#     {"name": "python3.12", "version": "3.12.1", "type": "library"},
#     {"name": "django", "version": "5.0.1", "type": "library", "purl": "pkg:pypi/django@5.0.1"},
#     {"name": "libcurl4", "version": "7.88.1", "type": "library"},
#     ... (145 components total)
#   ]
# }

# SBOM standards:
# • CycloneDX (OWASP) — JSON/XML, lightweight
# • SPDX (Linux Foundation) — ISO standard, more metadata

# Why SBOM matters for CNPA:
# • Compliance: Executive Order 14028 requires SBOMs for federal software
# • Incident response: "Do we use log4j?" → grep SBOM → answer in seconds
# • Supply chain transparency: Know exactly what's in your images
# • CVE matching: Match SBOM components against vulnerability databases
📖 SBOM in the CNPA Context

The CNPA exam expects you to understand SBOM as a supply chain security tool. Key points: (1) SBOM is generated at BUILD time (by Syft in CI), not at runtime. (2) SBOM is stored as a CI artifact alongside the image — not inside the image. (3) When a critical CVE (like Log4Shell) is announced, you query your SBOM repository — not your running clusters — to find affected images. (4) SBOM + vulnerability scanner = complete vulnerability management. SBOM says what's IN the image; the scanner says what's VULNERABLE.

SBOM Formats — SPDX vs CycloneDX: Which One Should anihpj Use?

Two SBOM standards dominate the industry. The CNPA exam expects you to know both exist and understand their differences — the choice impacts tooling compatibility, compliance reporting, and ecosystem integration:

📋 SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange)

Creator: Linux Foundation. Standard: ISO/IEC 5962:2021.

Strengths:

  • ISO standard — required for government compliance (Executive Order 14028)
  • Rich legal metadata: licenses, copyrights, attributions
  • Relationship tracking: "Library X DEPENDS_ON Library Y"
  • Mature ecosystem: Linux kernel, Yocto Project, Zephyr

Best for: Organizations needing ISO-standard compliance. Legal/license compliance teams. Government contractors.

📦 CycloneDX (OWASP)

Creator: OWASP Foundation. Standard: OWASP flagship project.

Strengths:

  • Security-focused: includes vulnerability info, exploitability data
  • Lightweight JSON — smaller files, faster parsing
  • Native support in Syft, Trivy, Dependency-Track
  • Extended beyond SBOM: SaaSBOM, HBOM (hardware), OBOM (operations)

Best for: Security teams. DevSecOps pipelines. Organizations using Syft + Trivy + Dependency-Track (all natively support CycloneDX).

💡 anihpj Recommendation: Generate BOTH. Syft with --output spdx-json for compliance/legal teams. Syft with --output cyclonedx-json for the security pipeline (Dependency-Track, Trivy integration). Storage is cheap. Compliance requirements change. Having both formats future-proofs your SBOM strategy.

Why Supply Chain Security Matters — The SolarWinds Anatomy

In 2020, attackers compromised SolarWinds' build pipeline and injected malicious code into a SIGNED software update. 18,000 organizations — including US government agencies — installed the trojaned update because it was "trusted." This is why every step in the CI/CD pipeline needs verification: signing, SBOM, and SLSA aren't academic concepts — they're defenses against the most dangerous class of attacks:

SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK ANATOMY — How SolarWinds Happened (And How We Prevent It)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  THE SOLARWINDS ATTACK (2020) — What Went Wrong                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  1. Attacker compromises CI/CD build server               │ │
  │  │  2. Attacker injects malicious DLL into source code       │ │
  │  │     BEFORE compilation                                    │ │
  │  │  3. CI pipeline builds + signs the COMPROMISED binary     │ │
  │  │  4. "Signed" update distributed to 18,000 customers       │ │
  │  │  5. Customers TRUST the signature → install immediately   │ │
  │  │  6. Attacker now has backdoor access to 18,000 networks   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ROOT CAUSE: The signature only proved "SolarWinds built  │ │
  │  │  this" — NOT that "the source code wasn't tampered with."  │ │
  │  │  Signing is necessary but INSUFFICIENT alone.            │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  HOW MODERN SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY PREVENTS THIS (anihpj):       │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  1. Source code in Git → PR requires 2-person review      │ │
  │  │     (SLSA 4 requirement — no unilateral changes)          │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  2. CI build runs on EPHEMERAL runner (not long-lived     │ │
  │  │     server that could be compromised over time)           │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  3. Build produces:                                       │ │
  │  │     • Signed image (Cosign — proves CI built it)          │ │
  │  │     • SBOM (Syft — lists ALL components)                  │ │
  │  │     • Provenance (SLSA — records build environment)       │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  4. Kyverno VerifyImages checks AT ADMISSION:             │ │
  │  │     • Is the signature valid? ✅                           │ │
  │  │     • Was it signed by anihpj CI? ✅                       │ │
  │  │     • Is the Rekor transparency log entry present? ✅      │ │
  │  │     • Does the SBOM show unexpected new components?       │ │
  │  │       → If yes → flag for review, DON'T auto-deploy       │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  5. Falco monitors runtime: unexpected outbound           │ │
  │  │     connections? → ALERT immediately                      │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  RESULT: Even if the build server is compromised, the     │ │
  │  │  combination of PR review + ephemeral runners +            │ │
  │  │  provenance + SBOM diffing + admission verification +     │ │
  │  │  runtime detection makes the attack EXTREMELY difficult. │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 THE CNPA LESSON: Signing alone is NOT enough. You need:     │
  │     Provenance (HOW it was built) + SBOM (WHAT's inside) +      │
  │     Admission verification (SHOULD it run) + Runtime detection  │
  │     (WHAT is it doing NOW). Each answers a different question.  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

11.5 Pipeline Security Best Practices — OIDC & SLSA

Two critical patterns define modern CI/CD security: OIDC eliminates long-lived credentials, and SLSA provides a framework for measuring supply chain integrity. Together, they address the two biggest pipeline risks: stolen credentials and tampered artifacts:

OIDC — No More Static Credentials

OIDC — Temporary Credentials Replace Static Keys
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ❌ THE OLD WAY (DANGEROUS):                                     │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  1. Create AWS IAM user                                     │ │
  │  │  2. Generate AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY     │ │
  │  │  3. Store in GitHub Secrets (hoping nobody leaks them)      │ │
  │  │  4. Keys NEVER EXPIRE — valid until manually rotated       │ │
  │  │  5. If keys leak (git commit, log output, CI output):      │ │
  │  │     → Attacker has PERMANENT AWS access 🔓                  │ │
  │  │     → Can provision resources, read S3, delete infra       │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ✅ THE NEW WAY (OIDC — SECURE):                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                             │ │
  │  │  GitHub Actions                    AWS IAM                  │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐                    ┌──────────────────┐     │ │
  │  │  │ OIDC     │─── 1. JWT token ──▶│ OIDC Provider     │     │ │
  │  │  │ Provider │     (repo+branch)  │ (trusts GitHub)   │     │ │
  │  │  └──────────┘                    └────────┬─────────┘     │ │
  │  │                                          │                 │ │
  │  │                                          ▼                 │ │
  │  │                                   ┌──────────────────┐     │ │
  │  │                                   │ IAM Role          │     │ │
  │  │                                   │ (assume-role)     │     │ │
  │  │                                   │ Condition:        │     │ │
  │  │                                   │  repo=anihpj/*    │     │ │
  │  │                                   │  branch=main      │     │ │
  │  │                                   └────────┬─────────┘     │ │
  │  │                                          │                 │ │
  │  │                    ◀── 2. Temporary ─────┘                 │ │
  │  │                        credentials (1 hour, auto-expire)   │ │
  │  │                                                             │ │
  │  │  ✅ NO static keys stored anywhere                          │ │
  │  │  ✅ Credentials auto-expire in 1 hour                       │ │
  │  │  ✅ Scoped to specific repo + branch (condition)            │ │
  │  │  ✅ If token leaks → already expired or wrong repo          │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 CNPA PRINCIPLE: OIDC is ALWAYS the answer for CI/CD auth.  │
  │     Static credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID) = WRONG answer.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SLSA Framework — Supply Chain Integrity Levels

SLSA (Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts, pronounced "salsa") defines four levels of supply chain integrity. Each level builds on the previous — the CNPA expects you to understand what each level provides:

LevelNameRequirementsWhat It Protects Against
SLSA 1DocumentationBuild process is documented. Automated build. Provenance generated (who built what, when).Basic visibility. Shows intent but no integrity guarantees.
SLSA 2Tamper ResistanceVersion control. Build service (not dev laptop). Signed provenance. Hosted build platform.Prevents casual tampering. "Was this built by CI or on someone's laptop?"
SLSA 3AuditabilityIsolated builds. SLSA-compliant build platform. Provenance is non-forgeable. Source and build are auditable.Prevents build process tampering. "Can I trust the CI pipeline itself?"
SLSA 4HermeticityHermetic builds. Reproducible. All dependencies pinned. Two-person review. Everything SLSA 3 + maximum isolation.Maximum protection. "Same source ALWAYS produces the same binary." Government/military grade.

💡 CNPA Context: Most platforms target SLSA 2-3. SLSA 4 is aspirational. The exam will present scenarios where a build runs on a developer's laptop → this violates SLSA 2 (build service requirement). The fix: move builds to a hosted CI platform (GitHub Actions, Tekton, Jenkins on dedicated infra).

Runtime Security — Falco: The Last Line of Defense

All the shift-left security in the world can't guarantee 100% prevention. A zero-day CVE, a misconfigured RBAC, or an insider threat could still slip through. Falco is the CNCF-standard runtime security tool that monitors system calls in real-time, detecting anomalous behavior as it happens. If every other security layer fails, Falco is your safety net:

FALCO RUNTIME DETECTION — Catching What Slips Through
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  HOW FALCO WORKS: System Call Monitoring at the Kernel Level    │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  KERNEL (eBPF or kernel module)                           │ │
  │  │       │                                                    │ │
  │  │       │ Every syscall is captured:                         │ │
  │  │       │ execve(), open(), connect(), bind(), ptrace()...  │ │
  │  │       ▼                                                    │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │  │              FALCO ENGINE (DaemonSet)                 │ │ │
  │  │  │                                                      │ │ │
  │  │  │  1. Captures syscall events from kernel               │ │ │
  │  │  │  2. Enriches with K8s metadata (pod, namespace,      │ │ │
  │  │  │     container, image)                                 │ │ │
  │  │  │  3. Evaluates against FALCO RULES (YAML)              │ │ │
  │  │  │  4. If rule matches → ALERT                            │ │ │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  CRITICAL FALCO RULES FOR PLATFORM SECURITY:                    │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  🐚 UNEXPECTED SHELL SPAWN                                │ │
  │  │  Rule: "A shell (bash/sh) was spawned in a container"     │ │
  │  │  Why: Production apps don't spawn shells. If someone is   │ │
  │  │       running /bin/bash in your prod container, it's      │ │
  │  │       either an attacker or a misconfig. Either way: ALERT.│ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ⛏️ CRYPTOMINER DETECTION                                  │ │
  │  │  Rule: "Outbound connection to known mining pool ports"   │ │
  │  │  Why: Compromised containers are often used to mine       │ │
  │  │       crypto. Connections to stratum+tcp:// pools on      │ │
  │  │       ports 3333, 4444, 8888 = IMMEDIATE ALERT.          │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  📁 SENSITIVE FILE ACCESS                                  │ │
  │  │  Rule: "Reading /etc/shadow, /root/.ssh, or K8s secrets"  │ │
  │  │  Why: Production apps don't need to read /etc/shadow.     │ │
  │  │       If they try, someone is attempting privilege         │ │
  │  │       escalation or credential theft.                     │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  🌐 UNEXPECTED OUTBOUND CONNECTION                         │ │
  │  │  Rule: "Container connected to IP NOT in allowlist"       │ │
  │  │  Why: anihpj-api should only talk to anihpj-db, Redis,    │ │
  │  │       and the K8s API. Connection to unknown IP →         │ │
  │  │       potential data exfiltration or C2 channel.          │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  🔑 PRIVILEGED CONTAINER STARTED                          │ │
  │  │  Rule: "Container started with privileged: true"          │ │
  │  │  Why: PSA should block this at admission, but if someone  │ │
  │  │       bypassed it (or PSA is misconfigured), Falco       │ │
  │  │       catches it at runtime. Defense-in-depth.            │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 FALCO INTEGRATION IN THE ANIHPJ STACK:                      │
  │  Falco (DaemonSet) → Alert → Prometheus Alertmanager →          │
  │  PagerDuty → On-call engineer. Runtime detection completes      │
  │  the security pipeline: Pre-commit→PR→Build→Deploy→RUNTIME.   │
  │  Every stage catches what earlier stages missed.                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

11.6 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of shift-left security, vulnerability scanning, image signing, SBOM, OIDC, and SLSA.

Security Q1 of 10
Where should secret detection (git-secrets) run in the anihpj pipeline?
A) At deploy time — Kyverno can check for secrets in pod specs
B) At build time — after the Docker image is created
C) At pre-commit time — BEFORE secrets are ever committed to Git. Shift-left means catching issues at the EARLIEST possible stage.
D) At runtime — Falco can detect when secrets are accessed
✅ Correct Answer: C — Pre-commit is the earliest (cheapest) stage

Shift-left principle: the EARLIER you catch an issue, the cheaper it is to fix. If git-secrets catches an AWS key at pre-commit: fix the file, recommit = 2 minutes. If caught at PR review: 5 minutes. At build: 30 minutes (rebuild). At deploy: 2 hours (rollback). At runtime: DAYS of incident response. The CNPA answer is always the LEFTMOST stage that can detect the issue.

Security Q2 of 10
Trivy scan finds 2 CRITICAL and 8 HIGH CVEs in your image. What should happen?
A) Deploy anyway — CVEs are common and usually not exploitable
B) FAIL the pipeline — CRITICAL CVEs must be fixed. Update the base image, rebuild, re-scan until zero CRITICAL CVEs.
C) Create a Jira ticket and deploy — fix later
D) Ignore the scan results — Trivy has many false positives
✅ Correct Answer: B — CRITICAL CVEs FAIL the pipeline

CRITICAL CVEs (CVSS 9.0+) are remotely exploitable and can lead to complete system compromise. The anihpj policy: CRITICAL → fail pipeline immediately, don't even push to registry. HIGH → block deployment to production but allow dev/staging. MEDIUM → create ticket, fix within 30 days. LOW → log for awareness. The key: fix CVEs BEFORE the image reaches the registry — not after it's running in production.

Security Q3 of 10
What is the advantage of Cosign keyless signing (Sigstore) over traditional key-based signing?
A) Keyless signing is faster — no cryptographic operations needed
B) Keyless signing doesn't require a container registry
C) Keyless signing produces smaller signatures
D) NO long-lived private keys to manage, protect, or steal. Ephemeral keys generated per signature. Identity verified via OIDC. Public auditability via Rekor transparency log.
✅ Correct Answer: D — No key management = no key theft

Traditional signing: generate a private key, store it securely (HSM, vault), distribute the public key, rotate keys, revoke compromised keys — massive operational burden. Keyless signing: Cosign authenticates via OIDC (GitHub Actions identity), Fulcio issues a SHORT-LIVED certificate (10 minutes), the ephemeral key signs the image and is discarded. The certificate + signature are recorded in Rekor (immutable public ledger). No key to steal. No key to rotate. Every signature is publicly auditable. This is the CNPA-preferred approach.

Security Q4 of 10
What does Kyverno's VerifyImages rule check at admission time?
A) That the container image has a VALID cryptographic signature from a TRUSTED identity — and rejects pods with unsigned or invalidly signed images
B) That the image has passed a Trivy scan with zero CVEs
C) That the image exists in the container registry
D) That the image tag follows semantic versioning
✅ Correct Answer: A — VerifyImages checks cryptographic signatures

Kyverno VerifyImages checks: (1) Does the image have an OCI signature? (2) Is the signature cryptographically valid? (3) Was it signed by a trusted identity (verified via public key or Fulcio certificate chain)? (4) Is there a Rekor transparency log entry? If ANY check fails → admission DENIED. This is separate from vulnerability scanning (Trivy) — signing proves WHO built it; scanning checks WHAT's in it. Both are needed for defense-in-depth.

Security Q5 of 10
What is the primary value of an SBOM in incident response?
A) SBOM automatically patches vulnerable components
B) When a critical CVE (like Log4Shell) is announced, you query your SBOM repository to find EVERY image containing the vulnerable component — in minutes instead of weeks
C) SBOM replaces vulnerability scanning — it's a more modern approach
D) SBOM is required by Kubernetes to run pods
✅ Correct Answer: B — SBOM enables rapid CVE impact analysis

Without SBOM: "Do we use Log4j?" → manually check every repo, every Dockerfile, every running container → takes WEEKS. With SBOM: grep -r "log4j" sboms/ → answer in MINUTES. SBOM is a COMPLETE inventory of every library, OS package, and dependency in every image. Generated at build time by Syft. Stored as a CI artifact. Queryable at any time. This is why Executive Order 14028 mandates SBOMs for federal software — and why CNPA expects you to understand the pattern.

Security Q6 of 10
Why are static credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID) in CI/CD dangerous?
A) They're too short — they expire too quickly
B) They require a hardware security module (HSM)
C) They can only be used once
D) They NEVER expire, are stored as plaintext in CI variables, and if leaked (git commit, logs, CI output) → attacker has permanent cloud access with no time limit
✅ Correct Answer: D — Static keys = permanent, stealable access

Static credentials are the #1 CI/CD security anti-pattern. They NEVER expire. They're stored as plaintext in CI/CD variables. If they leak (accidental git commit, debug logging, CI output capture), the attacker has PERMANENT access — no time limit, no automatic revocation. The fix: OIDC. GitHub Actions authenticates to AWS via OIDC, gets TEMPORARY credentials (1-hour expiry) scoped to the specific repo and branch. No static keys anywhere. Even if the token leaks, it's already expired. This is ALWAYS the CNPA correct answer for CI/CD authentication.

Security Q7 of 10
A developer builds Docker images on their laptop and pushes to the registry. Which SLSA level does this VIOLATE?
A) SLSA 1 — builds must be documented (the developer can document the process)
B) SLSA 4 — only hermetic builds are affected
C) SLSA 2 — requires a HOSTED BUILD SERVICE (CI platform, not developer laptop). Laptop builds are not tamper-resistant.
D) No SLSA level is violated — any build method is acceptable
✅ Correct Answer: C — SLSA 2 requires a hosted build service

SLSA 2's key requirement: builds MUST run on a HOSTED BUILD SERVICE (GitHub Actions, Tekton Pipelines, Jenkins on dedicated infra) — NOT on a developer's laptop. Why? (1) Build service provides an AUDIT TRAIL (who triggered the build, when, with what source). (2) Build service isolates the build from the developer's environment. (3) Build service generates signed provenance. A developer could tamper with the build on their laptop — SLSA 2 prevents this by requiring a trusted, auditable build platform.

Security Q8 of 10
You find an AWS access key committed to a public GitHub repository. What should you do FIRST?
A) IMMEDIATELY revoke/delete the key in AWS IAM — assume it's compromised. Then git-secrets to prevent future commits. The key has been public — revocation is urgent.
B) Delete the file from the repository and force-push — removing the commit fixes the leak
C) Add the repository to .gitignore — that prevents future leaks
D) Rotate the key — create a new one and update the application
✅ Correct Answer: A — Revoke FIRST, then fix the process

When a secret is committed to a public repo, assume it's ALREADY COMPROMISED (bots scan GitHub commits for keys within seconds). Step 1: REVOKE the key in AWS IAM immediately — stop the bleeding. Step 2: Remove the secret from Git history (BFG Repo-Cleaner, git filter-branch) — but know that if it was public, it's already been copied. Step 3: Install git-secrets to prevent future leaks. Step 4: Implement pre-commit hooks. Order matters: revoke first because every second the key is valid is a second an attacker can use it.

Security Q9 of 10
Trivy scan shows a CRITICAL CVE in openssl with CVSS 9.8 and a fix version available. What's the most efficient remediation?
A) Add a NetworkPolicy to block traffic to the affected pod — network isolation mitigates the CVE
B) Update the base image (apt-get upgrade or bump python:3.12-slim → python:3.12.2-slim), rebuild, re-scan. Fix the ROOT CAUSE — the vulnerable library.
C) Deploy a WAF to block exploit attempts — application-level protection
D) Accept the risk — CVSS 9.8 is just a number
✅ Correct Answer: B — Fix the root cause: update the vulnerable library

When a fix version EXISTS, ALWAYS fix the root cause. Updating the base image is the simplest fix: apt-get update && apt-get upgrade or bump the base image tag. Rebuild, re-scan to verify the CVE is gone. A, C, and D are compensating controls — they might reduce the attack surface but don't ELIMINATE the vulnerability. The CNPA principle: if a patch exists, APPLY IT. Only use compensating controls when no patch is available (zero-day).

Security Q10 of 10
Design the complete security toolchain for anihpj's pipeline — from pre-commit to runtime.
A) Just Trivy at build time — it covers all security needs
B) Kyverno VerifyImages at deploy time — admission control is sufficient
C) Pre-commit: git-secrets → PR: bandit + safety → Build: trivy scan + cosign sign + Syft SBOM → Deploy: Kyverno VerifyImages → Runtime: Falco. Defense-in-depth at EVERY stage.
D) Manual code review before merge — humans catch what tools miss
✅ Correct Answer: C — Defense-in-depth across ALL pipeline stages

The complete shift-left toolchain: Pre-commit (git-secrets) catches leaked credentials before they reach Git. PR review (bandit SAST + safety SCA) catches code vulnerabilities and vulnerable dependencies. Build (trivy CVE scan + cosign sign + Syft SBOM) catches OS/library CVEs, signs images for trust, and generates SBOM for compliance. Deploy (Kyverno VerifyImages) enforces only signed, trusted images run. Runtime (Falco) detects anomalous behavior. Each stage catches what earlier stages miss. This is defense-in-depth applied to the CI/CD pipeline — the CNPA ideal.

📊 Chapter 11 Summary — Key Takeaways

⬅️Shift-LeftPre-commit→PR→Build→Deploy→Runtime. Security at EVERY stage. Catch issues at the cheapest stage.
🔍Trivy ScanCRITICAL→fail pipeline. HIGH→block prod. MEDIUM→ticket. LOW→log. Fix CVEs BEFORE registry push.
✍️Cosign SignKeyless signing via Sigstore. No keys to manage. Fulcio certs + Rekor log = auditable trust chain.
📋SBOMComplete component inventory. Syft generates CycloneDX/SPDX. Rapid CVE impact analysis in minutes.
🔑OIDCNO static credentials. Temporary tokens (1hr). Scoped to repo+branch. Auto-expire. Always the CNPA answer.
🏗️SLSALevels 1-4: Documentation→Tamper Resistance→Auditability→Hermeticity. Most platforms target SLSA 2-3.

🟡 Part 3: Continuous Delivery & Platform EngineeringCNPA 16% · Ch 12-16

Chapter 12: CI Pipelines Deep Dive — The Build Factory

Continuous Integration isn't just "running tests on push." It's a software factory — a pipeline that converts raw source code into production-ready artifacts through a series of automated, repeatable stages. Each stage is a GATE — if any fails, the pipeline stops. No artifacts escape the factory without passing every quality check. This chapter dissects the CI pipeline stage by stage: triggers, caching, parallelization, artifact management, notifications, and Git integration — all applied to the anihpj/jobpost GitHub Actions workflow that builds, scans, signs, and packages our Django application.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours ⚙️ CI/CD 🎯 Domain 3: 16% 🔧 Pipeline Engineering

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ CI Pipeline Complete Flow — trace source code from git push through lint→test→build→scan→sign→artifact
  • ✅ Triggers & Stages — push, PR, schedule, manual. Parallel vs sequential stages. Pipeline dependency graphs
  • ✅ Caching & Artifacts — pip cache, Docker layer cache, cache key strategies. Artifact storage for images, SBOMs, reports
  • ✅ Notifications & Git Integration — Slack alerts, GitHub status checks, required checks before merge. Branch protection
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Continuous Delivery 16% Foundation for CI/CD Security (Ch 11) Foundation for GitOps (Ch 15-16)
⚠️ The Pipeline Is a GATE Factory — Not a Suggestion Box

The CNPA exam tests CI pipelines as a quality enforcement mechanism. Key patterns:

  • Fail fast, fail early. Put fast checks (lint, unit tests) BEFORE slow checks (build, integration tests). If lint fails in 30s, don't waste 4 minutes building.
  • Caching is a platform engineering concern. The platform team configures caching so developers don't have to. A pipeline without caching wastes 50-70% of its time on redundant work.
  • Artifacts are the OUTPUT of CI and the INPUT of CD. The CI pipeline produces versioned, signed, scanned artifacts. The CD pipeline consumes them. Never rebuild in CD — use the CI artifact.

12.1 CI Pipeline — Complete Flow from Push to Artifact

A CI pipeline is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of stages. Each stage depends on the previous one succeeding. The pipeline converts raw code into a versioned, tested, scanned, and signed artifact. Here's the complete anihpj flow:

CI PIPELINE — Complete anihpj Flow
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  git push (trigger)                                             │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────▼────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐          │
  │  │  LINT   │─▶│  TEST  │─▶│ BUILD+   │─▶│  DEPLOY  │          │
  │  │  ruff   │  │ pytest │  │ SCAN     │  │  ArgoCD  │          │
  │  │  30s    │  │  2min  │  │  4min    │  │  auto    │          │
  │  └─────────┘  └────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘          │
  │       │             │          │                                 │
  │       └───── FAIL ──▶ PIPELINE STOPS ◀── FAIL ─────────────────┘│
  │                                                                 │
  │  STAGE DETAILS:                                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ LINT (30s): ruff checks Python code style + errors        │ │
  │  │   → Catches: syntax errors, unused imports, type issues   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ TEST (2min): pytest runs 147 unit + integration tests     │ │
  │  │   → Catches: broken API endpoints, DB query errors,       │ │
  │  │     Django view logic bugs, model validation failures     │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ BUILD+SCAN (4min):                                        │ │
  │  │   1. docker build → anihpj/jobpost:abc1234                │ │
  │  │   2. trivy image scan → check for CVEs                    │ │
  │  │   3. cosign sign → keyless signature                      │ │
  │  │   4. syft sbom → cyclonedx-json                           │ │
  │  │   5. docker push → registry.anihpj.com                    │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ARTIFACTS PRODUCED:                                            │
  │  • Docker image: anihpj/jobpost:abc1234 (sha256:def...)        │
  │  • SBOM: sbom.cdx.json (145 components)                        │
  │  • Cosign signature: Rekor transparency log entry               │
  │  • Test report: coverage.xml (87% coverage)                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

GitHub Actions — The Complete anihpj CI Workflow

.github/workflows/ci.yml — Complete Pipeline 
name: CI Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: astral-sh/setup-ruff@v4
    - run: ruff check anihpj/ jobpost/   # Catches: syntax, style, bugs

  test:
    needs: lint          # Only runs if lint PASSES
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: {POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test}
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      with: {python-version: "3.12", cache: pip}
    - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
    - run: pytest --cov=jobpost --cov-report=xml -v

  build-and-scan:
    needs: test          # Only runs if test PASSES
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      image-tag: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Build & Push
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        push: true
        tags: registry.anihpj.com/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}
        cache-from: type=gha      # GitHub Actions cache
        cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
    - name: Trivy Scan
      uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
      with:
        image-ref: registry.anihpj.com/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}
        exit-code: 1
        severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    - name: Cosign Sign
      run: cosign sign registry.anihpj.com/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}
    - name: Generate SBOM
      run: syft registry.anihpj.com/jobpost:${{ github.sha }} -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.cdx.json
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with: {name: sbom, path: sbom.cdx.json}

The CI Pipeline as a Quality Factory — A Mental Model

Think of CI not as a script, but as a factory assembly line. Raw materials (source code) enter at one end. They pass through quality inspection stations (lint, test, scan). At each station, defective parts are rejected and sent back. Only parts that pass EVERY inspection reach the packaging station (artifact publication). This mental model explains every CI design decision:

CI AS A QUALITY FACTORY — Raw Code → Tested Artifact
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  RAW MATERIALS          INSPECTION STATIONS         SHIPPING    │
  │  (Source Code)         (Quality Gates)          (Artifacts)    │
  │       │                                                   │     │
  │  ┌────▼────┐   ┌────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐ │     │
  │  │INSPECT  │──▶│VERIFY  │──▶│ASSEMBLE  │──▶│  PACKAGE │ │     │
  │  │STATION 1│   │STATION 2│   │STATION 3│   │ STATION  │ │     │
  │  │(lint)   │   │(test)   │   │(build+  │   │ (push+   │ │     │
  │  │         │   │         │   │ scan)   │   │  sign)   │ │     │
  │  │ 30 sec  │   │ 2 min   │   │ 4 min   │   │  30 sec  │ │     │
  │  └────┬────┘   └────┬────┘   └────┬─────┘   └────┬─────┘ │     │
  │       │              │             │               │        │     │
  │       └── FAIL ──────┴── FAIL ─────┴── FAIL ───────┘        │     │
  │                     REJECTED — SENT BACK                      │     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  FACTORY PRINCIPLES THAT APPLY TO CI:                           │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1. FAIL FAST: Inspect the EASIEST things FIRST. Lint      │ │
  │  │    catches syntax errors in 30 seconds. Don't spend 4     │ │
  │  │    minutes building code that won't even compile.          │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ 2. INDEPENDENT STATIONS RUN IN PARALLEL: Lint and test    │ │
  │  │    don't depend on each other. Run them simultaneously.    │ │
  │  │    Assembly depends on both passing → run it after.        │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ 3. REJECTED PARTS GO BACK TO THE SUPPLIER: A failed       │ │
  │  │    pipeline sends the code back to the developer — with    │ │
  │  │    clear feedback about WHAT failed and WHY. The factory   │ │
  │  │    doesn't try to "fix" defective parts.                   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ 4. ONLY PASSED PARTS GET PACKAGED: An artifact is         │ │
  │  │    published ONLY if ALL stations pass. A partially        │ │
  │  │    inspected artifact is a SECURITY AND QUALITY RISK.      │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ 5. THE PACKAGE IS IMMUTABLE: Once packaged, the artifact  │ │
  │  │    NEVER changes. CD deploys the exact package CI built.   │ │
  │  │    Re-packaging invalidates ALL prior inspections.         │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 This model explains WHY we do CI the way we do. Every      │
  │     decision — parallel stages, caching, artifact immutability, │
  │     fast-fail ordering — follows from treating CI as a quality  │
  │     factory, not as a deploy script.                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

12.2 CI Pipeline Triggers & Stages — What Starts the Pipeline?

CI pipelines don't run themselves. They're triggered by events. Choosing the right trigger for each scenario is a CNPA-tested skill — the wrong trigger wastes CI minutes or misses critical checks:

CI TRIGGERS — What Starts the Pipeline?
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  EVENT           TRIGGER              TYPICAL USE               │
  │  ──────────────  ───────────────────  ──────────────────────────│
  │  git push        on: push             Every commit → CI          │
  │                  branches: [main]      Fast feedback (< 5 min)   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Pull Request    on: pull_request     PR checks visible in UI   │
  │                  branches: [main]      ✅ / ❌ blocks merge       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Schedule        on: schedule         Nightly full scan         │
  │                  cron: "0 2 * * *"    Long-running tests (E2E)  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Manual          on: workflow_dispatch Emergency hotfix deploy   │
  │                                       One-off migration run     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Tag push        on: push tags        Release trigger           │
  │                  tags: ["v*"]         v1.2.3 → build + sign     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Repository      on:                 Cross-repo pipeline        │
  │  Dispatch        repository_dispatch  (shared lib updated)      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Pipeline Stage Dependency Graph — Parallel vs Sequential

Not all stages need to run sequentially. Understanding which stages can parallelize is how you reduce pipeline time from 12 minutes to 5. The CNPA exam tests your ability to identify independent stages:

PIPELINE DEPENDENCY GRAPH — Parallelization Opportunities
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  SEQUENTIAL (Slow — 12 minutes):                                │
  │  lint → test → build → trivy → cosign → syft → push             │
  │  30s    2min    3min    45s      20s      15s     30s           │
  │  = 7m30s actual work + 4m30s waiting = 12 MINUTES              │
  │                                                                 │
  │  PARALLEL (Fast — 5 minutes):                                   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐     ← Run in PARALLEL             │  │
  │  │  │  LINT  │  │  TEST  │        (independent stages)       │  │
  │  │  │  30s   │  │  2min  │                                    │  │
  │  │  └───┬────┘  └───┬────┘                                    │  │
  │  │      │            │                                         │  │
  │  │      └─────┬──────┘  BOTH must pass                        │  │
  │  │           │                                                 │  │
  │  │  ┌────────▼──────────────────────────────────────────┐    │  │
  │  │  │              BUILD + SCAN (sequential)              │    │  │
  │  │  │  build ──▶ trivy ──▶ cosign ──▶ syft ──▶ push     │    │  │
  │  │  │  3min      45s       20s        15s      30s      │    │  │
  │  │  │  = 4m50s (these DEPEND on build succeeding)       │    │  │
  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  TOTAL: max(30s, 2min) + 4m50s = 6m50s → ROUNDED ~7 MINUTES    │
  │  SAVINGS: 12min → 7min = 42% faster!                           │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 RULE: Stages that don't depend on each other → PARALLEL.    │
  │     Stages that need previous stage output → SEQUENTIAL.        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

12.3 CI Pipeline Caching & Artifacts — Speed and Traceability

Caching is the difference between a 12-minute pipeline and a 5-minute pipeline. Artifacts are the pipeline's output — the evidence of what was built, tested, and scanned. Both are platform engineering responsibilities:

Caching Strategy — What to Cache and Why

What to CacheCache KeyTypical SavingsHow It Works
Python packages (pip)hash(requirements.txt)2 min → 15s (88% faster)Cache ~/.cache/pip. Only re-download when requirements.txt changes.
Docker layersLayer hash (automatic)3 min → 30s (83% faster)Each Dockerfile instruction produces a layer. Unchanged layers reused. COPY . . always rebuilds (code changed).
Node moduleshash(package-lock.json)1.5 min → 20s (78% faster)Cache node_modules. Only reinstall when dependencies change.
Go moduleshash(go.sum)1 min → 10s (83% faster)Go module cache. Deterministic builds, fast downloads.

Artifacts — What the Pipeline Produces

Artifacts are the CI pipeline's deliverables. They're immutable, versioned, and stored outside the CI runner (which is ephemeral). The CNPA exam tests the artifact boundary — this is where CI ends and CD begins:

📦
Docker Image

Stored in: Container Registry (ECR, GCR, Docker Hub)
Tagged with: git SHA + semantic version
Immutable: Never overwrite tags. Each build = new tag.
Example: registry.anihpj.com/jobpost:abc1234

📋
SBOM

Stored in: Artifact repository (GitHub Artifacts, OCI)
Format: CycloneDX JSON or SPDX
Purpose: Compliance, CVE matching, supply chain transparency
Example: sbom.cdx.json

✍️
Cosign Signature

Stored in: Container Registry (OCI signature) + Rekor log
Purpose: Prove WHO built the image, WHEN
Verifiable by: Kyverno at admission time
Example: Transparency log entry #847291

📊
Test Report

Stored in: CI artifact store or Codecov
Format: JUnit XML, coverage.xml
Purpose: Historical tracking, coverage trends
Example: 147 tests, 87% coverage

12.4 CI Notifications & Git Integration — Closing the Feedback Loop

A pipeline that runs silently is a pipeline nobody trusts. Notifications close the feedback loop — developers know instantly if their commit passed or failed. Git integration makes CI status visible in pull requests, blocking merges until checks pass:

Notification Channels — Who Gets Told What

💬
Slack Notifications

Success: "✅ Build #1247 passed — anihpj-api (3m42s)" → #deployments channel
Failure: "❌ Build #1247 FAILED — 3 tests broken in jobpost.views" → #platform-alerts
Ping: @commit-author — the person who pushed gets a direct mention

🔗
GitHub Status Checks

PR shows ✅ (all passed) or ❌ (failed) next to each check. Required checks: lint, test, build-and-scan MUST pass before merge. Branch protection: main branch requires passing CI + 1 review.

📧
Email Digests

Daily summary: "3 successful builds, 1 failed build, 87% average coverage." Sent to platform-team@anihpj.com. Not for urgent alerts — for trend awareness.

🚨
PagerDuty (Critical)

Only for: main branch build failure (blocks all deploys). Security scan found CRITICAL CVE. Rare but needs IMMEDIATE human attention.

💡 The Notification Hierarchy — CNPA Best Practice

Commit author: Always notified of THEIR commit's status (Slack DM or GitHub notification). Team channel: All build results for visibility. On-call: Only for main branch failures and security critical issues. Never page on-call for feature branch failures — that's the developer's responsibility.

CI Pipeline Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do

🚫
"It Works on My Machine" Pipeline

CI passes locally but fails in the pipeline. Cause: different Python version, missing env vars, different OS. Fix: Use EXACT same container image in CI as production. Pin versions. Docker-based CI runners.

🚫
Flaky Tests Ignored

"That test fails sometimes, just re-run." Each re-run erodes trust in CI. Fix: Quarantine flaky tests. Fix them within 1 sprint. Never ignore. Flaky tests = unreliable CI = developers ignore failures.

🚫
No Caching

Pipeline downloads ALL dependencies from scratch every run. 70% of pipeline time is redundant downloads. Fix: Cache pip packages, Docker layers, and build artifacts. Cache key = hash of lock file.

🚫
Rebuilding in CD

CI builds and tests an image. CD rebuilds it. The image running in production was NEVER tested. Fix: CI produces the artifact ONCE. CD deploys the exact same artifact. Never rebuild.

Docker Layer Caching — How It Actually Works

Docker layer caching is the single biggest CI speed improvement you can make — taking builds from 3 minutes to 30 seconds. But it only works if you understand HOW Docker decides which layers to reuse and which to rebuild:

DOCKER LAYER CACHING — How Docker Decides What to Rebuild
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  DOCKERFILE:                                                    │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ FROM python:3.12-slim          ← Layer 1: CACHED ✅        │ │
  │  │                                  (hash: base image digest) │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ RUN apt-get update && \         ← Layer 2: CACHED ✅        │ │
  │  │     apt-get install -y curl     (hash: RUN command text)   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ COPY requirements.txt .         ← Layer 3: CACHED ✅        │ │
  │  │                                  (hash: file contents)     │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ RUN pip install -r \            ← Layer 4: CACHED ✅        │ │
  │  │     requirements.txt            (depends on Layer 3)       │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ COPY . .                        ← Layer 5: REBUILT ❌       │ │
  │  │                                  (source code CHANGED!)    │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │ CMD ["python", "manage.py", \   ← Layer 6: REBUILT ❌       │ │
  │  │      "runserver"]               (everything after Layer 5) │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  THE CACHING RULES:                                             │
  │  1. Docker checks each instruction's cache key.                 │
  │  2. If the key matches → reuse cached layer. SKIP this step.   │
  │  3. If the key differs → REBUILD this layer AND ALL SUBSEQUENT │
  │     layers. This is the "cache busting" chain reaction.         │
  │                                                                 │
  │  WHY ORDER MATTERS (CRITICAL FOR CI SPEED):                     │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  ❌ BAD ORDER:                                              │ │
  │  │  COPY . .                    ← Changes EVERY commit        │ │
  │  │  RUN pip install -r req.txt  ← ALSO rebuilds every commit  │ │
  │  │  → pip install runs on EVERY build = 2 min wasted         │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ✅ GOOD ORDER:                                             │ │
  │  │  COPY requirements.txt .     ← Only changes when deps do  │ │
  │  │  RUN pip install -r req.txt  ← Cached until deps change   │ │
  │  │  COPY . .                    ← Code changes → only this   │ │
  │  │                                 layer rebuilds             │ │
  │  │  → pip install cached 95% of builds = saves 2 min         │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Build Matrix — Test Against Multiple Configurations

When your application needs to run on multiple Python versions or operating systems, a build matrix tests ALL combinations in parallel. This is the CNPA pattern for ensuring cross-version compatibility:

GitHub Actions — Build Matrix Strategy
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"]
        django-version: ["4.2", "5.0", "5.1"]
        # Generates 3 × 3 = 9 parallel test jobs!
      fail-fast: false
      # false = run ALL jobs even if one fails (see full picture)
      # true  = cancel ALL jobs when first fails (faster feedback)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      with: {python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}}
    - run: pip install django==${{ matrix.django-version }}
    - run: pytest
    # Result: 9 jobs run in parallel.
    # anihpj tested on Python 3.11/3.12/3.13 × Django 4.2/5.0/5.1
    # Coverage: 9 combinations. Parallel time = slowest job (~3 min)

12.5 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of CI pipelines, triggers, caching, artifacts, and notifications.

CI/CD Q1 of 10
In the anihpj CI pipeline, lint runs in 30s and test runs in 2min. Both must pass before build. What's the most efficient execution strategy?
A) Run lint → test → build sequentially — this is the simplest approach
B) Run everything in parallel — it's always faster
C) Skip lint — tests will catch the same issues
D) Run lint AND test in PARALLEL — they're independent. Build runs AFTER both pass. Total time: max(30s, 2min) + 4min = 6min instead of 6m30s sequential.
✅ Correct Answer: D — Parallel independent stages, sequential dependent ones

lint and test are INDEPENDENT — neither needs the other's output. Run them in parallel. build DEPENDS on both passing — run it after. Total time = max(parallel stages) + sequential stages. This is the fundamental principle of pipeline optimization: identify independent stages and run them simultaneously. Skipping lint (C) is wrong — lint catches issues tests don't (style, type errors, security patterns).

CI/CD Q2 of 10
A developer pushes a commit at 2am. Which trigger should run the full CI pipeline (lint + test + build + scan)?
A) on: push — every commit to main triggers CI. The developer gets fast feedback even at 2am.
B) on: schedule at 9am — CI should only run during business hours
C) on: pull_request — only PRs need CI, not direct pushes
D) Manual trigger — the developer should run CI when they're ready
✅ Correct Answer: A — on: push triggers CI on every commit

CI must run on EVERY push to main. This provides immediate feedback — the developer knows within minutes if their commit broke something. Running only during business hours (B) creates a dangerous gap — bad code could sit on main for hours. PR-only (C) works for feature branches but not main. Manual (D) defeats the purpose of automation — CI must be automatic and mandatory.

CI/CD Q3 of 10
What's the correct cache key strategy for Python pip packages in CI?
A) Cache key: current date — refresh cache daily
B) No cache key — always cache, never invalidate
C) Cache key: hash of requirements.txt — only reinstall when dependencies CHANGE. Otherwise reuse cached packages.
D) Cache key: git commit SHA — every commit gets its own cache
✅ Correct Answer: C — Cache key = hash of lock file

The cache key should be based on the LOCK FILE (requirements.txt, package-lock.json, go.sum). When dependencies change → lock file changes → cache key changes → fresh install. When dependencies DON'T change → cache key matches → reuse cached packages → saves 2 minutes. Date-based (A) invalidates even when nothing changed. No key (B) means you never update when deps change. Per-commit (D) defeats caching — every commit is a different key.

CI/CD Q4 of 10
What artifact does CI produce that CD should consume — NOT rebuild?
A) Source code — CD should re-clone the repo and run its own build
B) Docker image — CI builds, scans, and signs the image. CD deploys the EXACT same image. Never rebuild in CD — you lose the scan results and signature.
C) Test results — CD should re-run all tests against the production environment
D) Nothing — CI and CD should be completely independent
✅ Correct Answer: B — Docker image is the CI→CD handoff artifact

The CI pipeline produces a versioned, scanned, signed Docker image. The CD pipeline DEPLOYS that exact image — no rebuild, no re-scan, no re-sign. Why? (1) Rebuilding produces a DIFFERENT image (timestamps, layer hashes differ). (2) The scan results from CI would be invalid for the new image. (3) The Cosign signature from CI wouldn't match the new image. The CI→CD artifact boundary is sacred — CI builds once, CD deploys many times.

CI/CD Q5 of 10
Pipeline fails at the "Trivy Scan" stage. The logs show: "CRITICAL: CVE-2026-1234 (openssl, CVSS 9.8)." What happens next?
A) Pipeline FAILS immediately. Image is NOT pushed to registry. Developer must update the base image, rebuild, and re-scan. CRITICAL CVEs are non-negotiable gates.
B) Pipeline continues — CVEs are informational only, never block deployment
C) Image is pushed with a warning label — deploy with caution
D) Pipeline pauses and asks the developer if they want to proceed
✅ Correct Answer: A — CRITICAL CVEs FAIL the pipeline

The Trivy scan is configured with exit-code: 1 on CRITICAL and HIGH severities. A CRITICAL CVE (CVSS 9.8 — remotely exploitable, no auth needed, full compromise) MUST block the pipeline. The image is never pushed to the registry, so it can never be deployed. The developer must: update the base image (apt-get upgrade or bump python:3.12), rebuild, re-scan until zero CRITICAL CVEs. This is a non-negotiable security gate.

CI/CD Q6 of 10
A developer force-pushes to main, bypassing PR review. The CI pipeline passes. What additional protection should be in place?
A) Nothing — CI passing is sufficient protection
B) Add more tests to CI — better test coverage prevents issues
C) Branch protection rules: require PR before merge, require CI to pass, require at least 1 review, block force-pushes. CI alone is insufficient — you need Git-level controls.
D) Add a notification to Slack — awareness is the best defense
✅ Correct Answer: C — Branch protection rules at the Git level

CI is a quality gate, not an access control. Branch protection rules operate at the GIT level: require pull request before merging, require status checks to pass (CI), require at least 1 approving review, block force pushes, and restrict who can push to main. CI only validates code quality — it can't prevent someone from pushing unreviewed code directly. This is defense-in-depth: Git protects the branch, CI validates the code.

CI/CD Q7 of 10
Your pipeline takes 12 minutes: lint(30s) → test(2min) → build(3min) → trivy(45s) → cosign(20s) → syft(15s) → push(30s). Which optimization reduces time the MOST?
A) Buy faster CI runners — hardware solves everything
B) Skip trivy scan — it's the slowest non-build stage
C) Skip lint — it only saves 30 seconds
D) Run lint + test in PARALLEL (they're independent). Then add Docker layer caching to the build stage. Combined savings: ~5 minutes (42% faster).
✅ Correct Answer: D — Parallelization + caching = 42% faster

Two independent optimizations: (1) Run lint and test in parallel — they don't depend on each other. Saves max(30s, 2min) = 2min from the sequential 2m30s. (2) Docker layer cache — unchanged layers (FROM, RUN apt-get, RUN pip install) are reused. Saves ~2m30s per build. Combined: ~5 minutes saved = 42% faster. B and C compromise security/quality for speed — never the CNPA answer. A is expensive and doesn't address the root cause (sequential dependency + no caching).

CI/CD Q8 of 10
What notification should the anihpj platform send when a PR build fails?
A) Page the on-call engineer — build failures are always critical
B) GitHub status check shows ❌ on the PR. Slack DM to the commit author. Team channel gets a notification. BUT do NOT page on-call — PR failures are the developer's responsibility, not a production incident.
C) Send an email to the entire engineering team
D) No notification — developers should check CI manually
✅ Correct Answer: B — Targeted notifications, no on-call page for PR failures

The notification hierarchy: (1) GitHub status check — visible on the PR itself. (2) Commit author gets a direct notification — they caused it, they fix it. (3) Team channel for visibility. But NEVER page on-call for a PR failure — this is development activity, not a production incident. On-call is reserved for main branch failures (block all deploys) and security critical alerts. Over-paging causes alert fatigue and reduces response to real incidents.

CI/CD Q9 of 10
You manage a monorepo with 3 apps (api, web, worker). How should you design the CI pipeline to avoid rebuilding all 3 when only api changes?
A) Build everything — monorepos always rebuild all apps
B) Split into 3 separate repos — monorepos are an anti-pattern
C) Use path-based triggers: api/** changes → only build api. web/** changes → only build web. Shared lib/** changes → rebuild all. This is the monorepo CI pattern.
D) Manually select which app to build via workflow_dispatch
✅ Correct Answer: C — Path-based triggers for selective builds

GitHub Actions supports on: push: paths: ["api/**"] to trigger workflows only when specific paths change. This is the monorepo CI pattern: each app has its own workflow file with path filters. When api/** changes → only the api workflow runs. When shared libraries change (lib/**) → all apps rebuild (they all depend on the shared code). This saves CI minutes and avoids unnecessary rebuilds of unchanged apps.

CI/CD Q10 of 10
What's the ideal CI pipeline structure for the anihpj platform from a CNPA perspective?
A) Fast checks first (lint, unit tests in parallel) → comprehensive checks (build, scan, sign) → artifact publication (push image, upload SBOM, store signature). Each stage is a gate — fail stops the pipeline. This provides fast feedback AND thorough validation.
B) One stage that does everything — simplicity is best
C) Skip testing — trust developers to write correct code. Only build and push.
D) Run everything in parallel — speed is the only metric that matters
✅ Correct Answer: A — Tiered gates: fast→comprehensive→publication

The ideal CI pipeline has THREE tiers: (1) FAST GATES — lint + unit tests in parallel (~2 min). Catch obvious issues quickly. (2) COMPREHENSIVE GATES — build + scan + sign (~5 min). Thorough validation. (3) PUBLICATION — push image, upload SBOM, store signature. Only reach publication if all gates pass. This structure provides: fast feedback (2 min for simple issues), thorough validation (7 min total), and artifact immutability (only published if everything passes).

📊 Chapter 12 Summary — Key Takeaways

⚙️CI PipelinePush→Lint→Test→Build→Scan→Sign→Artifact. Each stage = gate. Fail stops pipeline.
🔔TriggersPush (every commit), PR (review), Schedule (nightly), Manual (emergency), Tag (release).
⚡ParallelizationIndependent stages = parallel. Dependent stages = sequential. 42% faster pipelines.
💾Cachingpip cache + Docker layers. Key = hash of lock file. Cache invalidates only when deps change.
📦ArtifactsImage + SBOM + Signature + Report. CI builds ONCE, CD deploys MANY. Never rebuild in CD.
💬NotificationsGitHub checks + Slack DM to author. On-call only for main failures. No alert fatigue.

Chapter 13: Incident Response in Platform Engineering — From Alert to Resolution

Every platform will fail. The question isn't IF, but how fast you detect it, how effectively you respond, and how much you learn from it. Incident response is a structured discipline — a repeatable process that transforms chaos into controlled resolution. This chapter covers the complete incident lifecycle: detection through Prometheus alerts, triage and severity classification, mitigation strategies, blameless postmortems, and the metrics (MTTR, MTBF, MTTD) that measure your platform's reliability — all applied to real anihpj incidents.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🚨 Incident Response 🎯 Domain 3: 16% 📊 SRE Practices

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Incident Response Lifecycle — Detect → Respond → Resolve → Learn. The 4-phase loop that turns outages into improvements
  • ✅ Severity Classification — P1 (critical, all-hands) through P4 (cosmetic). How to triage and assign the right response level
  • ✅ Alerting & Monitoring — Alertmanager routing: P1→PagerDuty, P2→Slack, P3→Email. Silencing and inhibition to prevent alert storms
  • ✅ Runbooks, Playbooks & Postmortems — Step-by-step guides, blameless culture, and turning incidents into action items
  • ✅ Incident Metrics — MTTR (Mean Time to Recover), MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures), MTTD (Mean Time to Detect), MTTA (Mean Time to Acknowledge)
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Continuous Delivery 16% Builds on Observability (Ch 7) SRE Practices for Platform Teams
⚠️ Incident Response Is a Platform Capability — Not Just Ops

The CNPA exam tests incident response from a platform engineering perspective. Key patterns:

  • Automation reduces MTTR. A runbook that says "SSH in and run these 5 commands" has MTTR of 15 minutes. An auto-rollback triggered by a Prometheus alert has MTTR of 2 minutes. The platform should automate incident response wherever possible.
  • Blameless postmortems are MANDATORY. The exam will present scenarios where a team blames an individual. The correct answer is ALWAYS: "Focus on the SYSTEM — what allowed this to happen, and how do we prevent it?"
  • MTTR is the north star metric. Every platform decision should reduce MTTR. Better alerts → faster detection. Better runbooks → faster resolution. Better automation → no human needed.

13.1 What is Incident Response? — The Structured Approach to Chaos

Incident response is a structured, repeatable process for handling service disruptions. Without a process, every incident is a fire drill — people panic, communications break down, and fixes are applied without documentation. With a process, incidents become manageable — and every one makes your platform stronger:

INCIDENT RESPONSE LIFECYCLE — The 4-Phase Loop
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  🔔 DETECT          🏃 RESPOND         🔧 RESOLVE              │
  │  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐       ┌──────────┐            │
  │  │Prometheus│────▶│PagerDuty │──────▶│Engineer  │            │
  │  │ Alert    │     │ Pages    │       │ Fixes    │            │
  │  │ Fires    │     │ On-Call  │       │ Issue    │            │
  │  └──────────┘     └──────────┘       └──────────┘            │
  │       │                │                   │                    │
  │  MTTD < 1min     MTTA < 5min         MTTR < 15min             │
  │  (auto detect)   (human acks)        (resolve + verify)        │
  │                                                                 │
  │  📝 LEARN (Blameless Postmortem — within 24 hours)              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  • Timeline: What happened, when (with timestamps)        │  │
  │  │  • Root Cause: WHY did it happen (5 Whys technique)       │  │
  │  │  • Impact: How many users affected, duration, data loss   │  │
  │  │  • Resolution: What fixed it (step by step)               │  │
  │  │  • Action Items: OWNER + DEADLINE — concrete, measurable  │  │
  │  │  • NO BLAME: "The system allowed this. Fix the system."   │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 anihpj targets: Detect < 1min, Acknowledge < 5min,          │
  │     Resolve < 15min, Postmortem < 24h. Every incident           │
  │     generates at least 2 action items with owners.              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Incident Command Structure — Who Does What During a P1

During a critical incident, chaos is the enemy. A clear command structure ensures everyone knows their role — no duplication, no gaps, no confusion. The CNPA exam tests this as an operational maturity indicator:

  │                    • Decides when to escalate                   │
  │                    • Decides when incident is RESOLVED          │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────┼────────────────────┬────────────────────┐              │
  │  │    │                    │                    │              │
  │  ▼    ▼                    ▼                    ▼              │
  │  OPS LEAD           COMMS LEAD          SME (Subject          │
  │  "Fixes it"         "Talks about it"     Matter Expert)       │
  │  • Investigates     • Updates status     "Knows the system"   │
  │    root cause         page              • Deep knowledge of   │
  │  • Applies fix      • Notifies stake-     the failing system  │

Alert Fatigue — The Silent Killer of Incident Response

The most dangerous alert is the one everyone ignores. Alert fatigue happens when engineers receive so many low-quality alerts that they stop responding to ALL alerts — including critical ones. This is a platform reliability crisis:

❌ Platform WITH Alert Fatigue
  • 🔴 47 alerts/day. 45 are "CPU > 75%" warnings
  • 🔴 On-call engineer: "Another CPU alert. Ignore."
  • 🔴 The 46th alert is a REAL DB outage. Engineer doesn't notice — it looks like all the others
  • 🔴 MTTA: 45 minutes. Users reported it before the platform detected it
  • 🔴 Root cause: alerting on METRICS (CPU, memory) instead of SYMPTOMS (error rate, latency)
✅ Platform WITHOUT Alert Fatigue
  • 🟢 3 alerts/day. All actionable. All linked to runbooks
  • 🟢 "Error rate > 5%" → page. "P95 latency > 500ms" → page. CPU > 75% → dashboard, no page.
  • 🟢 Every page is a REAL issue. On-call TRUSTS every alert
  • 🟢 MTTA: 2 minutes. Platform detects issues before users notice
  • 🟢 Root cause: alerting on SYMPTOMS. Using inhibition and grouping in Alertmanager

💡 The CNPA Principle: Every alert must be: ACTIONABLE (requires human action), SYMPTOM-BASED (what users experience), and LINKED TO A RUNBOOK. If an alert doesn't meet all three criteria → it's a dashboard widget, not an alert.

13.2 Incident Management Lifecycle — From Alert to Postmortem

Every incident follows the same lifecycle. Understanding each phase ensures nothing is missed — from the moment an alert fires to the follow-up on action items weeks later:

1
Detection — Alert Fires (Prometheus → Alertmanager → PagerDuty)

Prometheus alert rule triggers: "error_rate{anihpj-api} > 5% for 5 minutes." Alertmanager routes to PagerDuty with severity=critical, team=jobpost-team. On-call engineer receives push notification + phone call.

2
Triage — Assess Severity (P1/P2/P3/P4)

Engineer acknowledges within 5 minutes. Opens Grafana dashboard. Assesses: (a) Is the service down or degraded? (b) How many users affected? (c) Is data at risk? (d) Is revenue impacted? Classifies as P1 (critical, all-hands) to P4 (cosmetic, backlog).

3
Mitigation — Stop the Bleeding FIRST

BEFORE finding root cause, mitigate impact. Options: rollback the last deploy (ArgoCD), scale up replicas, failover to standby, or enable circuit breaker. The goal: restore service NOW. Root cause investigation comes AFTER service is restored.

4
Resolution — Fix Root Cause

With service restored, investigate: What caused the error rate spike? Check Loki logs, Tempo traces, recent deploys. Fix: missing DB index → add index → deploy → verify metrics return to baseline. Close incident.

5
Postmortem — Learn and Improve

Within 24 hours: write blameless postmortem. Timeline, root cause, impact, resolution, action items. Each action item has an OWNER and DEADLINE. Follow up in 2 weeks. The incident isn't "done" until action items are complete.

Severity Levels — How to Classify Incidents

LevelNameDefinitionResponseanihpj Example
P1CriticalService DOWN. Users cannot access. Data loss. Revenue impact.All-hands. Page on-call. War room. Exec notification.anihpj-api returning 500 for ALL requests. DB is down.
P2MajorService DEGRADED. Some users affected. No data loss.Page on-call. Dedicated engineer. Team notification.P95 latency > 2s for 30% of requests. Partial outage.
P3MinorMinor issue. Workaround exists. Few users affected.Slack notification. Fix during business hours.Search filter not working. Manual workaround available.
P4CosmeticVisual issue. No functional impact.Backlog. Fix in next sprint.CSS alignment issue on job listing page.

13.3 Alerting & Monitoring for Incidents — Intelligent Routing

Alerts that go to the wrong person or get lost in noise are useless. Alertmanager provides intelligent routing, grouping, silencing, and inhibition — ensuring the RIGHT person gets the RIGHT alert at the RIGHT time:

ALERTMANAGER — Intelligent Alert Routing
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  Prometheus Alert Fires: "anihpj-api error rate > 5%"          │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────▼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │              ALERTMANAGER                                 │   │
  │  │                                                          │   │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │   │
  │  │  │ STEP 1: GROUPING — Merge similar alerts            │ │   │
  │  │  │ 3 pods all failing → 1 alert, not 3 separate pages │ │   │
  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │   │
  │  │                                                          │   │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │   │
  │  │  │ STEP 2: INHIBITION — Suppress dependent alerts     │ │   │
  │  │  │ NodeDown alert firing → suppress PodNotReady       │ │   │
  │  │  │ (pod is down BECAUSE node is down — fix the node)   │ │   │
  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │   │
  │  │                                                          │   │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │   │
  │  │  │ STEP 3: ROUTING — Send to the right channel        │ │   │
  │  │  │                                                    │ │   │
  │  │  │  severity=critical → PagerDuty (push + call)       │ │   │
  │  │  │  severity=warning  → Slack #platform-alerts        │ │   │
  │  │  │  severity=info     → Email daily digest            │ │   │
  │  │  │                                                    │ │   │
  │  │  │  team=jobpost-team → routes to that team's on-call │ │   │
  │  │  │  team=platform     → routes to platform on-call    │ │   │
  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │   │
  │  │                                                          │   │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │   │
  │  │  │ STEP 4: SILENCING — Mute during planned maintenance│ │   │
  │  │  │ "DB migration window: Sat 2am-4am — silence DB     │ │   │
  │  │  │  alerts for this period"                            │ │   │
  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 WITHOUT ALERTMANAGER: 50 alerts, 50 pages, 50 phone calls.  │
  │     WITH ALERTMANAGER: 1 alert, 1 page, 1 focused response.    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

On-Call Best Practices — Sustainable Incident Response

On-call isn't just about who carries the pager. It's about building a SUSTAINABLE system where engineers can respond effectively without burning out:

🔄
Rotation Schedule

Primary + Secondary per week. Follow-the-sun: 3 regions × 8 hours each = 24/7 without night shifts. Secondary escalates if primary doesn't ack within 5 min.

📊
SLO-Based Alerting

Page ONLY when SLO is at risk. Alert on SYMPTOMS (users getting 500s), not causes (CPU > 80%). Error budget burn rate > threshold → page.

🛌
No Blame, No Burnout

>2 pages/night? Fix the alerts or fix the system. Blameless culture: every page is a learning opportunity. The SYSTEM failed, not the person.

📝
Runbook-Driven Response

Every alert links to a runbook. "See this alert → follow these steps." No heroics. Written during calm hours, executed at 3am.

13.4 Runbooks, Playbooks & Blameless Postmortems

Runbooks are step-by-step guides for specific incidents. They transform "I think we should try..." into "Execute these verified steps." Blameless postmortems transform incidents from blame-fests into learning opportunities:

📖 Runbook: "anihpj-db Is Down"
  • Step 1: kubectl get pods -n anihpj-prod | grep db — is the pod running?
  • Step 2: kubectl describe pod anihpj-db-0 — check Events for OOMKilled, CrashLoop
  • Step 3: kubectl logs anihpj-db-0 --tail=50 — check for error messages
  • Step 4: Check PVC status — kubectl get pvc -n anihpj-prod
  • Step 5: If PVC full → expand PVC or clean old WAL logs
  • Step 6: If none of above → restore from Velero backup (runbook links to backup restore runbook)
  • If all else fails: Escalate to DBA on-call via PagerDuty
📝 Blameless Postmortem Template
  • Title: [P1] anihpj-api outage — June 15, 2026
  • Timeline (UTC): 14:28 — Deploy v2.1. 14:30 — Alert fires. 14:32 — Engineer acks. 14:35 — Rollback initiated. 14:37 — Service restored.
  • Root Cause (5 Whys): Why did error rate spike? → DB connections exhausted. Why? → New endpoint creating connection per request, not using pool. Why? → Missing connection pooling config in Django settings. Why? → Not in deployment checklist. Why? → Checklist doesn't exist for new endpoints.
  • Impact: 47 users affected. 7 minutes downtime. No data loss.
  • Action Items: [#1] Add connection pooling config — Owner: @alice, Due: Jun 17. [#2] Create deployment checklist — Owner: @bob, Due: Jun 20. [#3] Add alert for DB connection count > 80% — Owner: @charlie, Due: Jun 22.

13.5 Incident Metrics — MTTR, MTBF, MTTD, MTTA

You can't improve what you don't measure. Incident metrics provide the data to make your platform MORE reliable over time. The CNPA exam expects you to know these four metrics and how to improve each one:

INCIDENT METRICS VISUALIZED — The Timeline

  │                                                                 │
  │  Issue Starts         Alert Fires    Human ACKs  Fixed          │
  │      │                    │              │         │            │

  │      │  (Mean Time to     │              │         │            │
  │      │   Detect)          │              │         │            │

  │      │                    │              │         │            │

  │      │  (Mean Time to Recover — the NORTH STAR metric)          │

  │             incidents               (30 days)        testing,    │

  │  💡 WHY MTTR IS THE NORTH STAR:                                  │
  │  Every platform decision should ask: "Does this reduce MTTR?"   │
  │  • Better alerts? → Reduces MTTD.                               │
  │  • Better on-call? → Reduces MTTA.                              │
