The 5 Whys Technique — Finding Root Cause, Not Symptoms

When an incident occurs, the first answer is almost always a SYMPTOM, not a root cause. The 5 Whys technique iteratively asks "Why?" until you reach the SYSTEMIC root cause — the thing you can fix to prevent recurrence. Here's how it applies to a real anihpj incident:

THE 5 WHYS — anihpj-api Outage Root Cause Analysis
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  INCIDENT: anihpj-api returning 500 errors for all requests     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Why #1: Why did the API return 500s?                           │
  │  → DB connection pool exhausted (100/100 connections in use)   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Why #2: Why was the connection pool exhausted?                 │
  │  → New /api/jobs/search endpoint creates a NEW connection       │
  │    per request instead of using the pool                        │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Why #3: Why did the new endpoint create new connections?       │
  │  → Developer used raw psycopg2.connect() instead of Django's   │
  │    connection pooling (DATABASES['default']['CONN_MAX_AGE'])    │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Why #4: Why did the developer use raw connections?             │
  │  → The Django ORM couldn't express the complex search query.    │
  │    Developer didn't know about connection pooling config.       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Why #5: Why didn't the developer know about connection         │
  │          pooling — and why wasn't it caught in review?          │
  │  → Platform golden path doesn't include a code review checklist │
  │    for database connections. No automated check for raw          │
  │    psycopg2 usage in CI.                                        │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ │
  │  ROOT CAUSE (systemic): No automated guardrail in CI or review  │
  │  to prevent raw database connections without pooling.           │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ACTION ITEMS (fix the SYSTEM, not the person):                 │
  │  1. Add CI check: bandit rule to detect raw psycopg2.connect()  │
  │  2. Add code review checklist item: "Verify DB connection       │
  │     pooling is configured"                                      │
  │  3. Add DB connection count alert at 80% (early warning)        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Error Budgets & Incident Response — When to Stop Deploying

An error budget is 1 minus your SLO. If your SLO is 99.9% availability, your error budget is 0.1% — about 43 minutes of allowed downtime per month. When the budget is exhausted, the platform policy changes:

🟢 Budget Available — Deploy Freely
  • Error budget not exhausted
  • Developers can deploy anytime
  • Experiments and risky changes allowed
  • "We have 30 minutes of budget left this month — use it to learn"
🔴 Budget Exhausted — FREEZE Deployments
  • Error budget fully consumed
  • ALL deployments halted (except P1 fixes)
  • Focus shifts to reliability improvements
  • "We used all our downtime budget — no more risk this month"

💡 CNPA Insight: Error budgets make the speed vs. stability trade-off EXPLICIT. When the budget is green, ship fast. When it's red, slow down and fix reliability. This removes the emotional "should we deploy?" debate — the budget answers it objectively.

13.6 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of incident response, severity classification, Alertmanager, runbooks, and incident metrics.

CI/CD Q1 of 10
What is the correct order of the incident response lifecycle?
A) Learn → Respond → Detect → Resolve
B) Respond → Detect → Resolve → Learn
C) Resolve → Learn → Detect → Respond
D) Detect → Respond → Resolve → Learn
✅ Correct Answer: D — Detect → Respond → Resolve → Learn

The lifecycle is sequential: (1) DETECT — Prometheus alert fires, Alertmanager routes to PagerDuty. (2) RESPOND — On-call engineer acknowledges, assesses severity, mitigates impact. (3) RESOLVE — Fix root cause, verify service restored. (4) LEARN — Blameless postmortem, action items, follow-up. Each phase feeds into the next. Skipping "Learn" means the same incident WILL happen again.

CI/CD Q2 of 10
anihpj-api is returning 500 errors for ALL users. No workaround exists. Revenue is impacted. What severity level is this?
A) P2 — Major incident, assign one engineer
B) P1 — Critical. Service DOWN. All users affected. Revenue impact. All-hands response. War room. Exec notification.
C) P3 — Minor, fix during business hours
D) P4 — Cosmetic, backlog for next sprint
✅ Correct Answer: B — P1 Critical

P1 criteria: Service DOWN (all users getting 500s), no workaround, revenue impact. Response: Page on-call IMMEDIATELY (PagerDuty), all-hands war room, notify exec team, resolve with maximum urgency. P2 = degraded, some users affected. P3 = minor with workaround. P4 = cosmetic only. The severity drives the response — under-classifying delays the fix and increases impact.

CI/CD Q3 of 10
A K8s node goes down. Alertmanager receives 47 alerts: 1 NodeDown + 46 PodNotReady for pods on that node. What should Alertmanager do?
A) INHIBIT the 46 PodNotReady alerts — they're a SYMPTOM of the NodeDown. Page on-call ONCE for NodeDown. Fixing the node fixes all pods.
B) Send all 47 alerts to PagerDuty — on-call needs every alert
C) Group them into one Slack message — but still send 47 separate pages
D) Silently drop all alerts — if the node is down, on-call will figure it out
✅ Correct Answer: A — Inhibit dependent alerts

Alertmanager's INHIBITION feature suppresses alerts that are DEPENDENT on a root cause alert. Rule: "If NodeDown is firing for node X, suppress PodNotReady for all pods on node X." The on-call engineer gets ONE page (NodeDown), fixes the node, and all pods recover. Without inhibition: 47 pages, 47 phone calls, 47 acknowledgements — alert fatigue destroys response quality. Inhibition rules are configured in Alertmanager YAML.

CI/CD Q4 of 10
What is the PRIMARY goal of a postmortem?
A) Identify who caused the incident so they can be held accountable
B) Document the incident for legal/compliance purposes only
C) Learn from the incident to prevent recurrence. Identify SYSTEM improvements (not people to blame). Produce actionable items with owners and deadlines.
D) Create a record of who responded fastest for performance reviews
✅ Correct Answer: C — Learn and improve the SYSTEM

Postmortems are BLAMELESS by design. The question isn't "Who caused this?" but "How did our system ALLOW this to happen?" Focus on: missing safeguards, insufficient testing, unclear documentation, broken processes. Every postmortem produces ACTION ITEMS with owners and deadlines. A postmortem without action items is just an incident diary — it doesn't prevent recurrence. The CNPA exam will ALWAYS choose the answer that focuses on system improvement over individual blame.

CI/CD Q5 of 10
anihpj-api error rate spikes at 14:30. The on-call engineer acks at 14:32. Service restored at 14:37. The issue actually started at 14:28. What are MTTD, MTTA, and MTTR?
A) MTTD=2min, MTTA=5min, MTTR=9min
B) MTTD=2min (14:28→14:30), MTTA=2min (14:30→14:32), MTTR=9min (14:28→14:37)
C) MTTD=0min, MTTA=7min, MTTR=7min
D) MTTD=2min, MTTA=5min, MTTR=7min
✅ Correct Answer: B — MTTD=2min, MTTA=2min, MTTR=9min

MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) = Issue start (14:28) → Alert fires (14:30) = 2 minutes. MTTA (Mean Time to Acknowledge) = Alert fires (14:30) → Human acks (14:32) = 2 minutes. MTTR (Mean Time to Recover) = Issue start (14:28) → Service restored (14:37) = 9 minutes. Note: MTTR includes the ENTIRE incident duration — from when the issue started to when service was restored. Some definitions use "alert → resolution" instead, but the CNPA exam typically uses "issue start → resolution."

CI/CD Q6 of 10
What's the MOST effective way to reduce MTTR from 15 minutes to 2 minutes?
A) Hire more on-call engineers — more people = faster response
B) Send more alerts — earlier detection = faster response
C) Write longer runbooks — more detail = faster resolution
D) Automate the response. If the platform auto-rolls back on error rate spike, MTTR drops from 15 min (human investigates + manually rolls back) to 2 min (automated detection + automated rollback).
✅ Correct Answer: D — Automation is the ultimate MTTR reducer

The MTTR hierarchy: Automation > Runbooks > Human investigation. An auto-rollback triggered by a Prometheus alert eliminates the human from the critical path. The platform: detects the error rate spike (MTTD < 1min) → automatically rolls back the last deploy (2min) → service restored. No pager. No war room. No 3am phone call. The CNPA exam favors AUTOMATION as the answer for reducing MTTR because it removes human latency and error from the equation.

CI/CD Q7 of 10
What should you do FIRST when a P1 incident alert fires?
A) MITIGATE — stop the bleeding. Rollback the last deploy. Scale up. Failover. Restore service NOW. Root cause investigation comes AFTER service is restored.
B) Investigate root cause — understand WHY before taking action
C) Notify all stakeholders — communication is the first priority
D) Write the postmortem — document everything as it happens
✅ Correct Answer: A — Mitigate FIRST, investigate SECOND

The #1 incident response rule: RESTORE SERVICE FIRST, then investigate. If the last deploy caused the issue → roll back NOW. Don't spend 30 minutes investigating the root cause while users are seeing 500 errors. The rollback restores service in 2 minutes. THEN investigate what went wrong with the deploy. The CNPA exam distinguishes between mitigation (stop the bleeding) and resolution (fix the root cause) — mitigation ALWAYS comes first.

CI/CD Q8 of 10
Your team schedules database maintenance for Saturday 2am-4am. How do you prevent alerts during this window?
A) Disable Prometheus during the maintenance window
B) Delete all alert rules related to the database
C) Create an Alertmanager SILENCE for the maintenance window. Specify: matchers (alertname=~"Database.*"), time range (Sat 2am-4am), creator, and reason.
D) Ask on-call to ignore database alerts during the window
✅ Correct Answer: C — Use Alertmanager Silences

Alertmanager Silences temporarily suppress alerts matching specific criteria. Create a silence with: matchers (which alerts to suppress), start/end time, creator name, and reason ("Planned DB maintenance — ticket PROJ-1234"). During the silence window, matching alerts are NOT routed to PagerDuty/Slack. After the window ends, alerting resumes automatically. A and B are destructive and risk forgetting to re-enable. D relies on human memory — unreliable at 2am.

CI/CD Q9 of 10
What distinguishes a runbook from a playbook?
A) They are the same thing — the terms are interchangeable
B) Runbook: Step-by-step guide for a SPECIFIC incident ("anihpj-db is down → do X, Y, Z"). Playbook: Higher-level plan for incident RESPONSE ("Who gets paged? Who communicates with stakeholders? Who writes the postmortem?")
C) Runbook is for developers; Playbook is for managers
D) Runbook is automated; Playbook is manual
✅ Correct Answer: B — Runbook = specific fix guide, Playbook = response plan

Runbooks answer "HOW do I fix this specific issue?" — they contain commands, checks, and step-by-step instructions for common incidents. Playbooks answer "HOW do we handle incidents as a team?" — they define roles (incident commander, communications lead), escalation paths, stakeholder notification procedures, and postmortem processes. A well-prepared team has BOTH: runbooks for the technical fix, and playbooks for the human coordination.

CI/CD Q10 of 10
Your platform's MTTR has been 25 minutes for the last quarter. The target is 15 minutes. What's the most effective improvement strategy?
A) Analyze the MTTR components: MTTD (detection time) vs MTTA (ack time) vs resolution time. Improve the WEAKEST component. If MTTD is 10 min → better alerting. If resolution is 15 min → better runbooks + auto-rollback.
B) Set a stricter MTTR target (10 min) — ambitious goals drive improvement
C) Increase on-call rotation frequency — fresh engineers respond faster
D) Add more alerts — earlier detection always helps
✅ Correct Answer: A — Decompose MTTR and fix the bottleneck

MTTR is composed of MTTD + MTTA + resolution time. You can't improve MTTR without knowing WHICH component is the bottleneck. If MTTD is 10 minutes (alert takes too long to fire) → tighten Prometheus alert thresholds. If MTTA is 5 minutes (on-call slow to respond) → improve on-call rotation, add escalation policies. If resolution is 10 minutes → invest in runbooks, automate rollbacks, add self-healing. Arbitrary targets (B) and more alerts (D) don't address the root cause. Data-driven decomposition is the CNPA approach.

📊 Chapter 13 Summary — Key Takeaways

🔄LifecycleDetect→Respond→Resolve→Learn. Repeatable. Every incident feeds into improvement.
🏷️SeverityP1 (critical, all-hands) → P4 (cosmetic, backlog). Severity drives response level.
🔔AlertmanagerGroup + Inhibit + Route + Silence. 47 alerts → 1 page. No alert fatigue.
📖RunbooksStep-by-step fix guides. Transform "try X" → "Execute verified steps." Reduce MTTR.
📝PostmortemsBlameless. Focus on SYSTEM. Action items + owners + deadlines. Prevent recurrence.
⏱️MTTRThe north star. Decompose into MTTD+MTTA+resolution. Automate to reduce.

Chapter 14: CI/CD Relationship & Deployment Strategies

CI builds it. CD ships it. But HOW you ship it — rolling update, blue/green, canary, or A/B testing — determines your risk profile, rollback speed, and user experience during deploys. This chapter clarifies the CI/CD boundary, distinguishes Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment, and dives deep into deployment strategies with visual comparisons — all applied to anihpj/jobpost deployments across dev, staging, and production.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔄 Deployment 🎯 Domain 3: 16% 🚀 Release Strategies

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ CI vs CD Boundary — where CI ends (artifact), where CD begins (deployment). Never rebuild in CD
  • ✅ Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment — manual approval vs fully automated to production
  • ✅ Deployment Strategies — Rolling update, Blue/Green, Canary, A/B Testing. When to use each
  • ✅ Feature Flags — Decouple deploy from release. Deploy hidden, release gradually
  • ✅ Deployment Automation Tools — ArgoCD, Flux, Spinnaker, Harness. CNPA focus on ArgoCD
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Continuous Delivery 16% Foundation for GitOps (Ch 15-16) Deployment Strategy Selection

14.1 What is Continuous Delivery (CD)? — Always Deployable

Continuous Delivery means your software is ALWAYS in a deployable state. Every merge to main produces a tested, scanned, signed artifact that can be deployed to production at any moment. The deployment itself may require a manual approval — but the software is READY. This is the goal: make deployment a business decision, not a technical hurdle:

📖 The CD Principle

"Your software is ALWAYS in a deployable state." Main branch is production-ready at ALL times. If main is broken, the team stops ALL other work and fixes it. Deploying to production should be BORING — a routine, low-risk operation you can do any time. If deploying is scary, your CD pipeline isn't mature enough yet.

14.2 CI vs CD — Where One Ends, the Other Begins

CI vs CD — The Boundary
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌────────────── CI (Continuous Integration) ──────────────┐   │
  │  │  Push → Lint → Test → Build → Scan → Sign → Artifact    │   │
  │  │                                                         │   │
  │  │  Output: Docker image + SBOM + Signature + Test report  │   │
  │  └────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                           │                                     │
  │                           │ ARTIFACT (immutable, versioned)     │
  │                           ▼                                     │
  │  ┌────────────── CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) ──────┐   │
  │  │                                                         │   │
  │  │  Deploy Staging → Verify → Manual Approval → Deploy     │   │
  │  │  Production → Verify → Monitor → (Rollback if needed)   │   │
  │  │                                                         │   │
  │  │  Key: CD deploys the EXACT artifact CI produced.        │   │
  │  │  No rebuild. No re-scan. No re-sign.                   │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 THE GOLDEN RULE: CI builds ONCE. CD deploys MANY TIMES.     │
  │     Never rebuild in CD — you lose scan results and signatures.│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.3 Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment — The Human Gate

📦 Continuous DELIVERY (anihpj's choice)

Pipeline: Auto to staging → MANUAL approval → deploy to production

  • Human decides WHEN to deploy to production
  • Safer for business-critical apps
  • Compliance-friendly (audit trail of approvals)
  • Allows scheduled deploys (not at 4:55pm Friday)
🚀 Continuous DEPLOYMENT (advanced)

Pipeline: Auto ALL the way to production — no human gate

  • Every merge to main → auto-deploy to production
  • Requires EXTREME confidence in testing and automated rollback
  • Used by: Netflix, Amazon (1000s of deploys/day)
  • Requires: comprehensive canary analysis, auto-rollback, feature flags

14.4 Deployment Strategies — Choosing Your Release Pattern

DEPLOYMENT STRATEGIES COMPARISON
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ROLLING UPDATE (K8s default)                                   │
  │  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐     Gradual replacement of old pods with new    │
  │  │v1│→│v2│→│v2│     maxSurge: 1 extra, maxUnavailable: 1       │
  │  └──┘ └──┘ └──┘     ✅ Simple, zero downtime                    │
  │                      ⚠️  Mixed versions during rollout           │
  │                      ⚠️  Slow rollback (reverse the process)     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  BLUE/GREEN                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   v1 (BLUE, active)                 │
  │  │ v1 (BLUE)│ │v2 (GREEN)│   v2 (GREEN, standby)               │
  │  │  active  │ │ standby  │   Switch ALL traffic at once         │
  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘   ✅ Instant, atomic switch           │
  │       ↓ traffic switch        ✅ Instant rollback (switch back)  │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐   ⚠️  Double resource usage          │
  │  │ v1 (old) │ │v2 (GREEN)│                                      │
  │  │ standby  │ │  active  │                                      │
  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘                                      │
  │                                                                 │
  │  CANARY                                                         │
  │  90% → v1  10% → v2      Gradual traffic shift                  │
  │  → verify metrics → 25% → verify → 50% → 100%                   │
  │  ✅ Safest for risky changes                                     │
  │  ✅ Auto-rollback if metrics degrade                             │
  │  ⚠️  Requires sophisticated traffic management (Istio/Argo)     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  A/B TESTING                                                    │
  │  User-A → v1   User-B → v2   Route by user identity/headers    │
  │  ✅ User-specific feature testing                                │
  │  ✅ Measure business metrics per variant                         │
  │  ⚠️  Requires Istio/Envoy header-based routing                  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ANIHPJ STRATEGY:                                                │
  │  • Patches (v2.1 → v2.2) → Rolling update (safe, simple)       │
  │  • Major releases (v2 → v3) → Blue/Green (fast rollback)       │
  │  • Risky changes (DB migration) → Canary (validate gradually)   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Deployment Strategy Decision Tree — Which Strategy When?

DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY DECISION TREE
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  START: "I need to deploy a change"                             │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────▼────────────────────────────┐                           │
  │  │ Is this a NEW FEATURE (not fix)?│                           │
  │  └────┬──────────────┬─────────────┘                           │
  │       │ YES          │ NO                                       │
  │       ▼              ▼                                          │
  │  FEATURE FLAG    Is it HIGH RISK? → YES → CANARY (DB migration) │
  │  (deploy off)                    → NO  → ROLLING UPDATE (patch) │
  │                                                                 │
  │  If HIGH RISK + DOUBLE RESOURCES → BLUE/GREEN (instant rollback)│
  │  If HIGH RISK + SINGLE RESOURCES → CANARY (gradual validation)  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Rollback Strategies — How Each Deployment Strategy Recovers

Every deployment strategy has a different rollback profile. The CNPA exam tests your ability to match the rollback speed to the deployment risk:

StrategyRollback MethodSpeedWhen to Use
Rolling Updatekubectl rollout undo — reverses pod-by-podSlow (same as forward deploy)Low-risk changes, patches
Blue/GreenSwitch 100% traffic Blue→GreenINSTANT (one operation)Major releases, risky changes
CanaryAuto-rollback via Argo Rollouts analysisAutomatic (no human)All changes with metric analysis
Feature FlagDisable flag — code stays, feature offINSTANT (no redeploy)New features, experiments

Rolling Update Math — Exactly How Many Pods Run During an Update

The CNPA exam tests precise understanding of maxSurge and maxUnavailable. Here's the math — knowing this lets you calculate exactly how many pods are running at any moment during a deployment:

ROLLING UPDATE MATH — maxSurge=2, maxUnavailable=1, replicas=10
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  maxUnavailable=1: At most 1 pod can be DOWN at any time.       │
  │  → MINIMUM running pods = 10 - 1 = 9                            │
  │                                                                 │
  │  maxSurge=2: At most 2 EXTRA pods can exist during update.      │
  │  → MAXIMUM total pods = 10 + 2 = 12                             │
  │                                                                 │
  │  DURING THE UPDATE: Pods oscillate between 9 and 12.             │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌───────┐   ┌───────┐   ┌───────┐   ┌───────┐   ┌───────┐    │
  │  │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v2   │   │  v2   │   │  v2   │    │
  │  │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v2   │   │  v2   │    │
  │  │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v2   │    │
  │  │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │    │
  │  │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │   │  v1   │    │
  │  │ 10 v1 │   │ 9 v1  │   │ 9 v1 │   │ 8 v1  │   │ 7 v1  │    │
  │  │       │   │  +1 v2│   │+2 v2 │   │+3 v2 │   │  ...   │    │
  │  └───────┘   └───────┘   └───────┘   └───────┘   └───────┘    │
  │  STEP 0      STEP 1       STEP 2       STEP 3      ...STEP 10   │
  │  All v1      1 v1 down    1 v1 down    1 v1 down    All v2      │
  │              2 v2 up      2 v2 up      3 v2 up                  │
  │  Pods:10     Pods:11      Pods:11      Pods:11      Pods:10     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  KEY INSIGHTS:                                                  │
  │  • Service capacity: MIN 9 pods serving (10-1). Safe if 9 can   │
  │    handle the load.                                             │
  │  • Resource headroom: MAX 12 pods running. Node must have       │
  │    capacity for 2 extra pods.                                   │
  │  • Rollback is SLOW: kubectl rollout undo does the SAME process  │
  │    in reverse — pod by pod. Not instant like Blue/Green.        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Canary Analysis — How Argo Rollouts Decides to Promote or Rollback

Canary deployments are only as good as their analysis. Argo Rollouts uses AnalysisTemplate to query Prometheus metrics at each step — the same metrics an SRE would check manually, but automated and continuous:

Argo Rollouts — AnalysisTemplate for Canary Verification
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: canary-analysis
spec:
  metrics:
  - name: error-rate
    interval: 30s          # Check every 30 seconds
    count: 10              # Run 10 times (5 minutes total)
    successCondition: result[0] < 0.01
    # PROMOTE if error rate < 1%
    failureCondition: result[0] >= 0.05
    # ROLLBACK if error rate >= 5%
    failureLimit: 3        # Allow 3 failures before aborting
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.platform-monitoring:9090
        query: |
          rate(http_requests_total{
            app="anihpj-api",status=~"5.."}[2m])
          /
          rate(http_requests_total{app="anihpj-api"}[2m])

  - name: p95-latency
    interval: 30s
    count: 10
    successCondition: result[0] < 0.5
    # PROMOTE if P95 < 500ms
    failureLimit: 3
    provider:
      prometheus:
        query: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{
              app="anihpj-api"}[2m]))

# RESULT:
# At each canary step (10%→25%→50%→100%), Argo Rollouts runs
# this analysis for 5 minutes. If error rate stays < 1% AND
# P95 latency stays < 500ms → PROMOTE to next step.
# If error rate exceeds 5% 3 times → AUTO-ROLLBACK.

14.5 Feature Flags — Decoupling Deploy from Release

Feature flags separate the TECHNICAL act of deploying code from the BUSINESS decision of releasing a feature. Deploy the code HIDDEN behind a flag. Enable for 10% of users → verify → 50% → 100%. If issues occur: DISABLE the flag (instant). No rollback needed:

📖 Deploy ≠ Release

Deploy: Code is running in production (technical). Release: Feature is visible to users (business). Feature flags make these independent. You can deploy at 2pm on Friday (code is there, hidden) and release on Monday at 9am (flip the flag). This is the CNPA-recommended pattern for risk-free deployments.

14.6 Deployment Automation Tools

🐙
ArgoCD (CNPA Focus)

GitOps declarative. Pull-based. K8s-native. Application CRD. Auto-sync. Self-heal. The CNPA exam's primary CD tool.

🌊
Flux

GitOps alternative. Lighter weight. HelmController. Image automation (auto-update image tags). Good for smaller platforms.

🎯
Spinnaker

Multi-cloud. Advanced deployment strategies (canary, red/black). Netflix-originated. Complex setup. Used in large enterprises.

🤖
Harness

AI-powered CD. Continuous verification (compares metrics before/after deploy). Auto-rollback. Commercial (not open source).

14.7 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

CI/CD Q1 of 10
Where does CI end and CD begin?
A) CI and CD are the same thing — no boundary
B) CI ends with a versioned ARTIFACT (Docker image + SBOM + signature). CD begins by deploying that artifact. The artifact is the handoff — never rebuild in CD.
C) CI ends when tests pass. CD begins when tests pass.
D) CI ends at merge. CD begins at merge.
✅ B — Artifact is the CI→CD boundary

CI produces a versioned, scanned, signed artifact. CD consumes that exact artifact. The artifact boundary ensures what was tested and scanned in CI is exactly what runs in production. Rebuilding in CD would produce a DIFFERENT artifact — invalidating all CI quality gates.

CI/CD Q2 of 10
anihpj is a banking app. Should it use Continuous Delivery or Continuous Deployment?
A) Continuous DELIVERY — auto to staging, manual approval to production. Banking requires human oversight for compliance and risk management.
B) Continuous Deployment — automate everything for speed
C) Neither — banking apps shouldn't use CI/CD
D) Both simultaneously — deploy to some users automatically, others manually
✅ A — Delivery (manual prod approval) for regulated industries

Continuous Delivery provides the automation benefits (auto to staging, always deployable) while keeping the human approval gate for production. Banking, healthcare, and government apps typically require this for compliance. Continuous Deployment (fully automated to prod) is for organizations with extreme testing confidence and automated rollback — like Netflix, not banks.

CI/CD Q3 of 10
You have 10 replicas of anihpj-api and deploy a new version with RollingUpdate, maxSurge=2, maxUnavailable=1. How many pods run during the update?
A) Always 10 — no change
B) Between 8 and 10
C) Between 9 and 12 — maxUnavailable=1 (minimum 9 running), maxSurge=2 (maximum 12 total during update)
D) Between 5 and 15
✅ C — Between 9 and 12 pods

maxUnavailable=1: at most 1 pod can be down at any time → minimum 9 running (10-1). maxSurge=2: at most 2 extra pods can be created during the update → maximum 12 total (10+2). During the rolling update: old pods are terminated one at a time, new pods are created. The cluster oscillates between 9 and 12 pods until all 10 are the new version.

CI/CD Q4 of 10
What is the primary advantage of Blue/Green over Rolling Update?
A) Blue/Green uses fewer resources
B) Blue/Green is faster to deploy
C) Blue/Green requires no additional infrastructure
D) INSTANT rollback — switch traffic back to Blue. Rolling update must roll back pod-by-pod, which takes time. Blue/Green rollback is one traffic switch.
✅ D — Instant rollback via traffic switch

Blue/Green keeps the old version (Blue) running alongside the new version (Green). If Green has issues → switch traffic back to Blue INSTANTLY. Rolling update must terminate Green pods and recreate Blue pods one-by-one — rollback takes as long as the forward deploy. The trade-off: Blue/Green requires DOUBLE the resources during deploy.

CI/CD Q5 of 10
You're deploying a risky DB schema migration. Which strategy provides the SAFEST rollout?
A) Canary — send 10% of traffic to new version, monitor error rates and latency for 5 minutes. If metrics are healthy → 25% → 50% → 100%. If metrics degrade → auto-rollback.
B) Rolling update — gradual pod replacement
C) Blue/Green — switch all traffic at once
D) Direct deploy — replace all pods immediately
✅ A — Canary for risky changes

Canary deployment MINIMIZES blast radius. Only 10% of users see the new version initially. If the DB migration causes errors → only 10% of users are affected, and auto-rollback kicks in. Rolling update would affect 100% of users (albeit gradually). Blue/Green would affect 100% at once. For risky changes, canary is the CNPA-recommended strategy.

CI/CD Q6 of 10
What does a feature flag enable that deployment strategies alone cannot?
A) Faster deployments — feature flags improve CI speed
B) Decoupling DEPLOY from RELEASE. Deploy code hidden behind a flag at 5pm Friday. Release (enable flag) at 9am Monday. Rollback = disable flag (instant, no redeploy).
C) Better monitoring — feature flags include built-in metrics
D) Automatic rollback — feature flags detect errors and self-disable
✅ B — Deploy ≠ Release

Feature flags separate the technical (deploy code) from the business (release feature). Code can be deployed and dormant. The feature is toggled ON for specific users, percentages, or environments. Rollback is instant — disable the flag, no redeploy needed. This is the CNPA-recommended pattern for reducing deployment risk and enabling trunk-based development.

CI/CD Q7 of 10
Match the deployment strategy to the scenario: (1) Hotfix for a critical bug, (2) Major version upgrade, (3) New experimental feature
A) (1) Canary, (2) Canary, (3) Canary
B) (1) Blue/Green, (2) Blue/Green, (3) Blue/Green
C) (1) Rolling update (fast, simple), (2) Blue/Green (instant rollback if major version fails), (3) Canary (gradual exposure to validate)
D) (1) Direct, (2) Direct, (3) Direct
✅ C — Strategy matches risk profile

Hotfix → Rolling: simple, fast, low risk (it's a fix, not new functionality). Major upgrade → Blue/Green: if the upgrade breaks things, instant rollback minimizes downtime. New feature → Canary: gradual exposure validates the feature with minimal blast radius. The CNPA exam tests your ability to MATCH the strategy to the scenario's risk profile.

CI/CD Q8 of 10
Why is ArgoCD the CNPA-preferred CD tool over traditional push-based CI/CD?
A) ArgoCD is faster than all other tools
B) ArgoCD is the only tool that supports Kubernetes
C) ArgoCD is free and open source
D) ArgoCD uses PULL-based GitOps — the agent runs INSIDE the cluster with no external credentials. It continuously reconciles cluster state with Git. Traditional push-based tools need cluster credentials stored externally (security risk).
✅ D — Pull-based GitOps = security + continuous reconciliation

ArgoCD runs INSIDE the cluster. It pulls desired state from Git. No external system has cluster credentials. It continuously reconciles — if someone manually edits a deployment, ArgoCD reverts it in 3 minutes. Push-based tools (Jenkins, traditional CI/CD) push into the cluster using kubectl — they need credentials stored outside the cluster, creating a security risk. GitOps = PULL, inside the cluster. This is the CNPA-preferred architecture.

CI/CD Q9 of 10
Canary deployment: 10% of traffic goes to v2. Error rate on v2 jumps to 15%. What should happen?
A) AUTO-ROLLBACK — the canary analysis detects error rate > threshold and automatically shifts 100% traffic back to v1. The canary is aborted. No human intervention required.
B) Continue to 25% — the error might be a false positive
C) Page on-call to manually decide
D) Deploy a third version to compare
✅ A — Auto-rollback on metric degradation

Argo Rollouts (with Prometheus analysis) continuously compares canary metrics against stable metrics. If error rate exceeds the threshold (e.g., > 5%), latency exceeds P95 threshold, or any defined metric degrades → auto-rollback. No human decision. No pager. The canary is aborted and traffic returns to the stable version. This is why canary + metric analysis is the safest deployment strategy — it catches issues automatically before they affect all users.

CI/CD Q10 of 10
What's the ideal CI/CD pipeline design for anihpj from a CNPA perspective?
A) Push to main → manual deploy to production
B) Push → CI (lint+test+build+scan+sign) → auto-deploy to staging → automated tests → manual approval → Blue/Green deploy to production with auto-rollback. Every stage is automated except the production approval gate.
C) Push → manual review → manual deploy
D) Push → auto-deploy to production immediately
✅ B — Automated CI + automated staging CD + manual prod gate

The CNPA ideal pipeline: CI builds and validates. CD auto-deploys to staging. Automated tests run against staging. Human approves production deployment. Blue/Green deploys to production with auto-rollback. This gives: developer autonomy (auto to staging), safety (human gate to prod), and resilience (Blue/Green + auto-rollback). It balances speed (automated where safe) with control (manual where it matters).

📊 Chapter 14 Summary — Key Takeaways

🔀CI→CD BoundaryCI builds artifact. CD deploys it. Never rebuild. Artifact = immutability guarantee.
🚦Delivery vs DeployDelivery = human gate to prod. Deployment = fully automated. anihpj uses Delivery.
🔄Rolling UpdatePod-by-pod. Simple. K8s default. Best for patches and low-risk changes.
🔵Blue/GreenAtomic switch. Instant rollback. Double resources. Best for major releases.
🐤CanaryGradual traffic shift. Auto-rollback on metric degradation. Best for risky changes.
🚩Feature FlagsDeploy ≠ Release. Deploy hidden, release gradually. Instant disable. No redeploy.

Chapter 15: GitOps Basics & Workflows — Declarative Cluster Management

GitOps is the operational model that makes Kubernetes platforms manageable at scale. Git is the single source of truth. An agent inside the cluster continuously reconciles the running state with Git. No one runs kubectl apply manually — every change flows through Git. Every change is versioned, reviewed, and auditable. This chapter covers the four GitOps principles, the push vs pull debate, ArgoCD architecture, the Application CRD, sync strategies, and repository structure — all applied to the anihpj/platform monorepo.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2.5 hours🚀 GitOps🎯 Domain 3: 16%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ GitOps Principles — Declarative, Versioned, Pulled Automatically, Continuously Reconciled. The 4 defining characteristics
  • ✅ Push vs Pull Models — Why PULL-based (ArgoCD in cluster) is more secure than PUSH-based (CI/CD with cluster credentials)
  • ✅ ArgoCD Architecture — API Server, Repository Server, Application Controller, Redis Cache. How they work together
  • ✅ Application CRD & Sync Strategies — The core ArgoCD resource. Auto-sync, self-heal, pruning. App-of-apps pattern
  • ✅ GitOps Repository Structure — Kustomize overlays, environment separation, monorepo patterns
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Continuous Delivery 16% ArgoCD is THE CNPA GitOps tool Foundation for Ch16 (Application Environments)

15.1 What is GitOps? — Git as the Single Source of Truth

GitOps means: Git defines the DESIRED state of your cluster. An agent INSIDE the cluster continuously ensures the ACTUAL state matches Git. No manual kubectl. No external CI/CD pushing changes. Everything flows through Git — every change is a commit, every commit is auditable, every mistake is revertible:

GITOPS — Push vs Pull Models
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ❌ PUSH MODEL (Traditional CI/CD)                               │
  │  Git → CI/CD Pipeline (has cluster creds) → kubectl apply → K8s │
  │  Risk: CI/CD compromised → attacker has cluster admin           │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ✅ PULL MODEL (GitOps — ArgoCD/Flux)                            │
  │  Git ← ArgoCD (in K8s, pulls every 3min) → reconciles → K8s    │
  │  Safe: Agent IN cluster. No external creds. Continuous reconcile.│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

15.2 GitOps Principles — The 4 Defining Characteristics

📝
1. Declarative

Desired state expressed as CODE (YAML manifests). Not scripts. Not CLI commands. "I want 3 replicas" — not "run kubectl scale."

🔄
2. Versioned & Immutable

Every change is a Git commit. Full history. Who changed what, when, why. Rollback = git revert. Audit trail = git log.

⬇️
3. Pulled Automatically

Agent IN cluster pulls from Git. No external system pushes. Agent has cluster access because it's IN the cluster — no credentials exposed externally.

🔁
4. Continuously Reconciled

Agent constantly compares Git vs Cluster. Drift detected → auto-corrected. Someone manually edits a deployment? Reverted in 3 minutes.

15.3 Push vs Pull Deployment Models — The Security Argument

❌ PUSH (CI/CD with kubectl)
  • CI/CD stores cluster credentials as secrets
  • If CI/CD compromised → attacker deploys anything
  • CI/CD pushes → no continuous reconciliation
  • Manual kubectl edits → undetected drift
✅ PULL (ArgoCD inside cluster)
  • No external system has cluster credentials
  • ArgoCD IN cluster → can only affect ITS cluster
  • Continuous reconciliation → drift auto-corrected
  • Every sync logged: "synced commit abc123 at 14:30"

15.4 ArgoCD Architecture — How It Works

ARGOCD ARCHITECTURE
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Git Repo ←── ArgoCD (in K8s) ──→ Kubernetes API                │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                   │
  │  │Repo      │──▶│App       │──▶│K8s       │                   │
  │  │Server    │   │Controller│   │Cluster   │                   │
  │  │(clone    │   │(sync K8s)│   │          │                   │
  │  │ Git)     │   │          │   │          │                   │
  │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘                   │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐                                    │
  │  │API Server│   │  Redis   │  Sync cycle: Every 3 minutes       │
  │  │(WebUI+CLI│   │ (Cache)  │  Compare Git vs Cluster →          │
  │  │ +gRPC)   │   │          │  If different → update cluster     │
  │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘                                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ArgoCD Sync — What Happens During a Sync Cycle (Step by Step)

1
Git Poll

Every 3 minutes, Application Controller triggers sync. Repository Server clones/pulls the Git repo at targetRevision.

2
Manifest Generation

Kustomize merges overlays with base. Helm templates with values. Output: list of K8s resource objects (the desired state).

3
Diff

Application Controller queries K8s API for ACTUAL state. Compares: "Git says replicas=3. Cluster has 5." Every diff = drift to correct.

4
Apply

kubectl apply equivalent for each resource with a diff. Existing → updated. New → created. prune:true → deleted if removed from Git.

5
Health Check

Monitors resource health after apply. Deployment → Healthy (all pods ready). StatefulSet → ordered ready. Timeout → sync FAILED.

15.5 ArgoCD Application CRD — The Core Resource

anihpj-prod-application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
spec:
  project: default
  source:                     # WHERE is the config?
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/platform
    path: apps/anihpj/overlays/prod
    targetRevision: main
  destination:                # WHERE to deploy?
    server: https://prod-cluster.anihpj.com
    namespace: anihpj-prod
  syncPolicy:                 # HOW to sync?
    automated:
      prune: true             # Delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true          # Revert manual kubectl edits
    syncOptions:
    - CreateNamespace=true

15.6 ArgoCD Sync Strategies

🖐️
Manual Sync

Human clicks "Sync" in ArgoCD UI. Changes only applied when explicitly triggered by a person.

🤖
Automated Sync

ArgoCD auto-syncs when Git changes (every 3min, or webhook). No human needed.

✂️
Pruning

Delete manifest from Git → ArgoCD DELETES resource from cluster. prune: true required.

🩹
Self-Heal

Someone runs kubectl edit → ArgoCD detects drift → REVERTS to Git state within 3 minutes.

ArgoCD Webhooks — Instant Sync (No 3-Minute Wait)

By default, ArgoCD polls Git every 3 minutes. For faster deployments, configure a webhook — GitHub/GitLab notifies ArgoCD the moment a push occurs. Sync happens in SECONDS, not minutes:

⏰ Polling (Default)
  • ArgoCD checks Git every 3 minutes
  • Push at 14:30:00 → ArgoCD sees it at 14:33:00
  • Maximum delay: 3 minutes
  • Simple. No configuration needed.
  • OK for most use cases
⚡ Webhook (Fast)
  • GitHub sends POST to ArgoCD on push
  • Push at 14:30:00 → ArgoCD syncs at 14:30:02
  • Maximum delay: 2 seconds
  • Requires: ArgoCD accessible from internet or webhook relay
  • Best for production where speed matters

ArgoCD RBAC & AppProject — Multi-Tenant GitOps

In a multi-team platform, you need to control WHO can sync WHAT to WHERE. ArgoCD's AppProject CRD defines boundaries — Team A can only deploy to their namespaces, from their repos, to their clusters:

ArgoCD AppProject — Multi-Tenant Boundaries
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: anihpj-project
spec:
  description: "anihpj team project — dev/staging/prod"
  # ─── SOURCE: Which Git repos can this team use? ───
  sourceRepos:
  - https://github.com/anihpj/platform

  # ─── DESTINATION: Which clusters + namespaces? ───
  destinations:
  - namespace: anihpj-*          # Wildcard: dev/staging/prod
    server: https://prod-cluster.anihpj.com

  # ─── WHAT can they deploy? ───
  clusterResourceWhitelist:      # Cluster-scoped resources
  - group: ""
    kind: Namespace
  namespaceResourceBlacklist:    # Resources they CANNOT deploy
  - group: ""
    kind: ResourceQuota
  - group: ""
    kind: LimitRange

  # ─── ROLES: Who can do what? ───
  roles:
  - name: developer
    policies:
    - p, proj:anihpj-project:developer, applications, sync, anihpj-project/*, allow
    # Developers can SYNC apps but not delete or modify projects

# RESULT:
# Team anihpj CAN: deploy to anihpj-* namespaces from their repo
# Team anihpj CANNOT: deploy to other namespaces, create ResourceQuotas
# Team anihpj developer: can sync apps but not change project settings

15.7 GitOps Repository Structure — App-of-Apps Pattern

GITOPS REPO STRUCTURE
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  platform/ (GitHub: anihpj/platform)                            │
  │  ├── apps/anihpj/                                               │
  │  │   ├── base/              ← Common manifests                  │
  │  │   └── overlays/{dev,staging,prod}/  ← Environment-specific   │
  │  ├── infra/terraform/       ← VPC, RDS, EKS                    │
  │  ├── policies/kyverno/      ← ClusterPolicies                  │
  │  └── root-app.yaml          ← App-of-Apps entry point           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

GitOps Anti-Patterns — What Breaks the Model

🚫
Manual kubectl Edits

"I'll just kubectl edit this real quick." Self-heal reverts it in 3 minutes. Always change via Git.

🚫
Git + kubectl Hybrid

Some things in Git, some via kubectl. Cluster state is UNKNOWN. Which is the source of truth?

🚫
Environment Branches

Dev/staging/prod branches. Fix: ONE branch (main). Kustomize overlays for environment differences.

🚫
No Self-Heal / No Prune

Without selfHeal: manual edits persist. Without prune: deleted Git resources keep running. Safety net OFF.

15.8 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

CI/CD Q1 of 10
Which scenario IS GitOps?
A) CI/CD pipeline runs kubectl apply after build succeeds
B) ArgoCD runs inside the cluster, pulls from Git every 3 minutes, and reconciles cluster state with Git. No external push.
C) Developer manually runs kubectl apply from their laptop
D) A cron job runs kubectl apply every hour
✅ B — PULL-based reconciliation from within the cluster

GitOps requires: (1) Git as source of truth, (2) PULL-based agent INSIDE the cluster, (3) Continuous reconciliation. A is PUSH-based (CI/CD pushes with kubectl). C is manual (not GitOps). D is scheduled push, not continuous reconciliation. Only B satisfies all GitOps principles.

CI/CD Q2 of 10
Why is the GitOps PULL model more secure than the PUSH model?
A) PULL: Agent runs INSIDE the cluster — no external system needs cluster credentials. PUSH: CI/CD stores cluster credentials externally — if compromised, attacker has cluster access.
B) PULL is faster — speed equals security
C) PULL uses encryption; PUSH uses plaintext
D) They are equally secure — the model doesn't matter
✅ A — No external cluster credentials in PULL model

In the PUSH model, your CI/CD system (Jenkins, GitHub Actions) stores kubeconfig or cluster credentials to run kubectl apply. If that system is compromised → attacker can deploy anything to your cluster. In the PULL model, ArgoCD is INSIDE the cluster — it has access because it's a native K8s workload with a ServiceAccount. No external system has cluster credentials. This is the fundamental security argument for GitOps.

CI/CD Q3 of 10
Which ArgoCD component clones Git repositories and generates manifests?
A) API Server
B) Application Controller
C) Repository Server — clones repos, generates manifests (Helm, Kustomize, plain YAML), and returns them to the Application Controller
D) Redis Cache
✅ C — Repository Server handles Git operations

ArgoCD components: (1) API Server — Web UI, CLI, gRPC API. (2) Repository Server — clones Git repos, runs Helm/Kustomize/Jsonnet to generate manifests. (3) Application Controller — compares generated manifests with cluster state, applies changes. (4) Redis — caches Git repo state. Repository Server is the Git-to-manifest bridge.

CI/CD Q4 of 10
What does an ArgoCD Application's syncPolicy with automated.prune=true and automated.selfHeal=true do?
A) Auto-sync only — no pruning or healing
B) Manual sync with pruning
C) Auto-heal only — drift detection without pruning
D) Auto-sync on Git change + DELETE resources removed from Git (prune) + REVERT manual kubectl edits (selfHeal). The cluster CANNOT drift from Git — ArgoCD enforces it.
✅ D — Auto-sync + prune + selfHeal = cluster locked to Git

automated: {} → ArgoCD auto-syncs when Git changes. prune: true → if you DELETE a manifest from Git, ArgoCD deletes the corresponding resource from the cluster. selfHeal: true → if someone manually edits a resource in the cluster, ArgoCD detects the drift and REVERTS it to match Git within 3 minutes. This combination makes Git the ENFORCED single source of truth.

CI/CD Q5 of 10
What happens when you DELETE a Deployment manifest from Git with prune:true and selfHeal:true?
A) Nothing — the Deployment keeps running in the cluster
B) ArgoCD detects the manifest no longer exists in Git → DELETES the Deployment from the cluster. Pruning removes resources that no longer exist in the desired state.
C) ArgoCD asks for manual confirmation before deleting
D) The Deployment is scaled to 0 but not deleted
✅ B — Pruning DELETES resources removed from Git

prune: true means: "If a resource exists in the cluster but NOT in Git → DELETE it." This is how you decommission services in GitOps: delete the YAML from Git → ArgoCD deletes the resources from the cluster. Without pruning, deleting from Git leaves orphaned resources running. This is the GitOps equivalent of "terraform destroy" — Git is the complete desired state, nothing more, nothing less.

CI/CD Q6 of 10
Someone runs kubectl edit deployment anihpj-api --replicas=10 at 2am to "fix" a performance issue. What happens with selfHeal: true?
A) ArgoCD detects DRIFT within 3 minutes (cluster has 10, Git says 3) → REVERTS to 3 replicas. The manual edit is undone.
B) The manual edit persists — kubectl edits are permanent
C) ArgoCD merges the change — sets replicas to the average of 3 and 10
D) ArgoCD sends a Slack message asking what to do
✅ A — Self-heal reverts manual edits to Git state

Self-heal is the GitOps enforcement mechanism. ArgoCD continuously compares cluster state with Git. When it detects drift (10 replicas in cluster, 3 in Git), it automatically reverts to Git state. The "fix" at 2am is undone. The correct fix: update replicas in Git (via PR), let ArgoCD sync. This prevents configuration drift and ensures the cluster ALWAYS matches the reviewed, approved state in Git.

CI/CD Q7 of 10
What is the App-of-Apps pattern in ArgoCD?
A) Running multiple ArgoCD instances
B) One Application that deploys everything directly
C) A ROOT Application that points to a directory containing child Application YAMLs. Deploying the root app deploys ALL child apps. One commit = deploy the entire platform.
D) Deploying apps to multiple clusters simultaneously
✅ C — Root app declares child apps

App-of-Apps: create a ROOT ArgoCD Application that points to a directory containing other Application YAMLs. When ArgoCD syncs the root app, it creates all child Applications, which then sync their respective resources. This enables: (1) One bootstrap command to deploy the entire platform. (2) Hierarchical management — update a child app without touching the root. (3) Self-bootstrapping — the root app can even deploy ArgoCD itself.

CI/CD Q8 of 10
Design the Git repo structure for anihpj with dev, staging, and prod environments using Kustomize.
A) Three separate repos: anihpj-dev, anihpj-staging, anihpj-prod
B) One flat directory with all YAMLs for all environments
C) Branch per environment: dev branch, staging branch, prod branch
D) BASE/ directory with common manifests + OVERLAYS/{dev,staging,prod}/ directories with environment-specific patches. One branch (main). Kustomize merges base + overlay.
✅ D — Base + Overlays (Kustomize pattern)

The Kustomize overlay pattern: BASE contains the common deployment (3 replicas, common env vars, common volumes). Each OVERLAY patches the base with environment-specific values (dev: 1 replica, debug=true. staging: 2 replicas. prod: 5 replicas, more resources). One branch (main). One source of truth. No copy-paste. ArgoCD points each environment's Application to its overlay directory. This is the CNPA-recommended GitOps repo structure.

CI/CD Q9 of 10
anihpj has clusters in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1. How do you deploy the same application to all three?
A) Create three separate ArgoCD instances
B) ArgoCD ApplicationSet — define ONE template, and it generates Applications for each cluster automatically. Add a new cluster? ApplicationSet auto-generates the new Application.
C) Copy-paste the Application YAML three times
D) Deploy to one cluster and use K8s federation
✅ B — ApplicationSet for multi-cluster deployments

ApplicationSet is an ArgoCD controller that GENERATES Applications from a template. Define: template (what to deploy), generators (list of clusters, Git directories, or matrix of both). When you add a new cluster to ArgoCD, ApplicationSet auto-generates a new Application for it. One template → N Applications → N clusters. This is the CNPA-recommended pattern for multi-cluster GitOps.

CI/CD Q10 of 10
ArgoCD Application shows "Unknown" health status. What should you check FIRST?
A) (1) Is the Git repo accessible? (2) Is the path correct? (3) Is the cluster reachable? (4) Check sync status and logs. "Unknown" usually means ArgoCD can't evaluate health — start with connectivity.
B) Restart ArgoCD — it usually fixes itself
C) Delete and recreate the Application
D) Ignore it — "Unknown" is normal for new applications
✅ A — Systematic connectivity check

"Unknown" health means ArgoCD can't determine the health status. Common causes: (1) Git repo unreachable (network, auth, deleted). (2) Path in source doesn't exist. (3) Cluster API server unreachable. (4) Sync hasn't completed yet. Debug in order: check repo connectivity, verify path, check cluster connectivity, check sync status in ArgoCD UI or via argocd CLI. Never restart or delete as first action — diagnose first.

GitOps doesn't stop at deploying to one cluster. Real platforms span dev, staging, and production clusters — each with different configurations, scaling, and security policies. This chapter covers environment-specific configuration with Kustomize overlays, progressive delivery with Argo Rollouts, secrets management in GitOps (Sealed Secrets, ESO, SOPS), and multi-cluster deployment with ApplicationSets — all applied to anihpj/jobpost across three environments.

16.1 Environment-Specific Configuration — Kustomize Overlays

KUSTOMIZE OVERLAYS — anihpj Example
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  base/deployment.yaml: replicas=3, image=anihpj/jobpost         │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────┼────────────┬──────────────────┐                        │
  │  │    │            │                  │                         │
  │  overlays/dev/  overlays/staging/  overlays/prod/               │
  │  replicas:1     replicas:2         replicas:5                   │
  │  debug:true     debug:false        debug:false                  │
  │  DB:sqlite      DB:PostgreSQL      DB:RDS (HA)                  │
  │  CPU:100m       CPU:250m           CPU:500m                     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Kustomize Patches Deep Dive — How Overlays Actually Work

Kustomize doesn't "template" YAML — it patches it. Understanding the patching model helps you debug "why is my overlay not applying?" and "why is this value different than expected?":

Kustomize — How Overlays Patch the Base
# base/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
- deployment.yaml

# base/deployment.yaml
replicas: 3
containers:
- name: api
  image: anihpj/jobpost
  resources:
    limits: {cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi"}
  env:
  - name: DEBUG
    value: "false"

# overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
- ../../base
patches:
- patch: |
    - op: replace
      path: /spec/replicas
      value: 1                  # Dev: 1 replica
    - op: replace
      path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/cpu
      value: "100m"             # Dev: smaller CPU
  target:
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj-api

# RESULT (base + overlay merged):
# replicas: 1 (overridden by dev overlay)
# cpu: "100m" (overridden by dev overlay)
# memory: "256Mi" (inherited from base — NOT overridden)
# DEBUG: "false" (inherited from base)
# image: anihpj/jobpost (inherited from base)

# 💡 PATCHING VS TEMPLATING:
# Kustomize: base is the TRUTH. Overlays selectively override.
# Helm: values.yaml is the TRUTH. Templates render from values.
# Kustomize = "start with base, change specific things"
# Helm = "render template with these values"

Helm vs Kustomize — Which One for anihpj?

AspectKustomizeHelm
ApproachPATCHING: base + overlay = final YAMLTEMPLATING: values.yaml → Go template → rendered YAML
Built into kubectl✅ kubectl apply -k (native, no install)❌ Requires helm CLI or Helm operator
ReusabilityOverlays — good for environment variantsCharts — excellent for sharing (Artifact Hub)
Complex logicLimited — JSON patches + strategic mergeGo templates — conditionals, loops, functions
Learning curveLow — same YAML you already knowMedium — Go template syntax, helper functions
CNPA ChoiceKustomize for simple env variants (what anihpj needs). Helm for reusable charts shared across teams/orgs. ArgoCD supports BOTH natively.

16.2 Progressive Delivery with Argo Rollouts

ARGO ROLLOUTS — Canary Deployment
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Step 1: stable (v1) = 100%                                     │
  │  Step 2: canary (v2) = 10% → wait 30s → check metrics           │
  │  Step 3: canary (v2) = 25% → wait 30s → check metrics           │
  │  Step 4: canary (v2) = 50% → wait 30s → check metrics           │
  │  Step 5: canary (v2) = 100% → PROMOTE (v2 is now stable)        │
  │  IF METRICS DEGRADE AT ANY STEP → AUTO-ROLLBACK to v1           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

16.3 Secrets in GitOps — Encrypt Before You Commit

🔐
Sealed Secrets

Encrypt Secret → safe to commit to Git → controller decrypts in cluster. Only the target cluster can decrypt. One-way: you can encrypt, only the controller can decrypt.

🔑
External Secrets Operator (ESO)

Syncs secrets from AWS/GCP/Vault into K8s Secrets. Secret never touches Git. ESO fetches at runtime. Auto-refresh on rotation.

🔏
SOPS

Encrypt YAML/JSON files with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or PGP. Decrypt during ArgoCD sync. Integrates natively with ArgoCD via Helm/Kustomize.

🚫
NEVER: Plaintext Secrets in Git

DB_PASSWORD: "MyS3cretP@ss!" in Git = EVERYONE with repo access can read it. Even if you delete it, it's in git history forever.

16.6 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

CI/CD Q1 of 10
Why use Kustomize overlays instead of copy-pasting YAML per environment?
A) Copy-paste is simpler and less error-prone
B) Kustomize is faster to apply than kubectl
C) Kustomize overlays apply PATCHES to a COMMON BASE. One base, N environments. Change the base → all environments get the update. Copy-paste means N copies to maintain — drift is inevitable.
D) Kustomize is required by ArgoCD
✅ C — DRY principle: one base, many patched overlays

Kustomize overlays eliminate copy-paste. Base defines the common configuration. Each overlay patches only what's DIFFERENT (replicas, image tag, resource limits). Change the base → all environments inherit the change. Copy-paste creates N independent copies that diverge over time. Kustomize is DRY, maintainable, and the CNPA-recommended approach.

CI/CD Q2 of 10
Argo Rollouts canary: metrics show P95 latency increased from 200ms to 800ms at 10% canary. What happens?
A) Continue to 25% — the increase might be temporary
B) Page on-call to manually decide
C) Increase canary to 50% to get more data
D) AUTO-ROLLBACK — the analysis step detects metric degradation and immediately shifts 100% traffic back to v1. No human intervention needed.
✅ D — Auto-rollback on metric degradation

Argo Rollouts with AnalysisTemplate continuously monitors Prometheus metrics during canary. If P95 latency exceeds the defined threshold (e.g., 500ms) → the canary is ABORTED and all traffic returns to the stable version. This is automated, requires no human decision, and minimizes impact (only 10% of users briefly affected). This is the CNPA gold standard for safe deployments.

CI/CD Q3 of 10
How does Sealed Secrets let you safely store secrets in Git?
A) You encrypt the Secret CLIENT-SIDE using the controller's public key. Only the controller (in the target cluster) can decrypt it with its private key. The encrypted (sealed) secret is safe to commit to Git — useless outside the cluster.
B) It base64-encodes the secret — safe enough for Git
C) It stores secrets in a separate private repo
D) It replaces secrets with references to a vault
✅ A — Asymmetric encryption: encrypt client-side, decrypt cluster-side

Sealed Secrets uses asymmetric encryption. The controller generates a keypair — public key for encryption, private key (stays in cluster) for decryption. kubeseal encrypts the Secret with the public key. The encrypted "SealedSecret" CR is safe to commit to Git. In the cluster, the controller decrypts it and creates a regular K8s Secret. Outside the cluster, the encrypted data is useless. Key rotation: controller can re-encrypt all secrets.

CI/CD Q4 of 10
What's the advantage of ESO (External Secrets Operator) over Sealed Secrets?
A) ESO is simpler to set up
B) ESO syncs secrets FROM external providers (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault). Secret never touches Git — not even encrypted. Secrets are fetched at runtime and auto-refreshed when rotated at the source.
C) ESO is free; Sealed Secrets requires a license
D) ESO doesn't require a controller in the cluster
✅ B — Secret never touches Git; auto-refresh from source

Sealed Secrets: secret IS in Git (encrypted). ESO: secret NEVER in Git — it's fetched from an external provider at runtime. Advantages: (1) No Git history of encrypted secrets. (2) Auto-refresh when the source secret rotates (AWS Secrets Manager rotates DB password → ESO updates K8s Secret within minutes). (3) Centralized secret management — rotate once in AWS, all clusters update. The CNPA exam presents ESO as the more mature, enterprise-grade solution.

CI/CD Q5 of 10
How does ArgoCD ApplicationSet deploy an app to 3 clusters with different configs?
A) Create 3 separate Application YAMLs manually
B) Use one Application with a wildcard cluster selector
C) ApplicationSet uses a GENERATOR (list of clusters) + TEMPLATE (how to deploy). It generates one Application per cluster. Each Application gets cluster-specific parameters. Add a new cluster → auto-generated Application.
D) ArgoCD can only deploy to one cluster
✅ C — Generator + Template = N Applications for N clusters

ApplicationSet uses the Generator/Template pattern. Generator provides the list of target clusters (from ArgoCD's managed clusters). Template defines the Application spec with placeholders ({{name}}, {{server}}, etc.). For each cluster in the generator, ApplicationSet creates an Application with cluster-specific values. Add a new cluster to ArgoCD → ApplicationSet automatically generates an Application for it. This is the CNPA pattern for multi-cluster GitOps.

CI/CD Q6 of 10
Canary deployment: you need to verify that the new version doesn't increase error rates. How do you configure this in Argo Rollouts?
A) Manually check Grafana after each step
B) Trust that the new version is fine
C) Run tests before the canary starts
D) Add an AnalysisTemplate that queries Prometheus: error_rate < 5% AND p95_latency < 500ms. Argo Rollouts runs this analysis at EACH canary step. If it fails → auto-rollback.
✅ D — AnalysisTemplate with Prometheus metric queries

Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate defines: (1) Which metrics to query (Prometheus PromQL). (2) Success/failure thresholds. (3) How long to measure. At each canary step, Argo runs the analysis: "P95 latency < 500ms for 30 seconds?" If YES → continue to next step. If NO → auto-rollback. This automates the verification that previously required a human watching Grafana. The analysis is the "canary in the coal mine" — it automatically detects problems before they affect all users.

CI/CD Q7 of 10
You discover a plaintext DB password committed to the GitOps repo 6 months ago. Even though the file was "deleted" later, what's the risk?
A) The password is STILL in git history. Anyone with repo access can git checkout the old commit and read it. The password must be ROTATED immediately — not just removed from HEAD. Git history is immutable.
B) No risk — deleting the file removes the password permanently
C) Only the commit author can see the password
D) Git automatically encrypts old commits
✅ A — Git history is FOREVER. Rotate the password.

Git NEVER truly deletes anything. Even if you remove the file and force-push, the old commits exist in: reflog, forks, local clones, and backups. The password in the commit 6 months ago is STILL readable by anyone who clones the repo and checks out that commit. The ONLY safe response: (1) IMMEDIATELY rotate the password in the source system. (2) Use git-filter-repo or BFG to rewrite history (optional — the password should already be rotated). (3) Use Sealed Secrets, ESO, or SOPS going forward. NEVER commit plaintext secrets.

CI/CD Q8 of 10
Rollback during a Blue/Green deploy vs rollback during a Canary deploy. What's the difference?
A) They are identical — both switch traffic back
B) Blue/Green rollback: switch 100% traffic from Green→Blue. INSTANT. Canary rollback: gradually shift traffic from canary→stable. Takes time but was already gradual. Blue/Green rollback is faster; Canary rollback was already safe.
C) Canary rollback is always faster
D) Neither supports rollback — you must redeploy
✅ B — Blue/Green: instant switch. Canary: gradual shift.

Blue/Green: at any point, you can switch 100% traffic back to Blue. Rollback is one atomic operation. Canary: at any step (10%, 25%, 50%), auto-rollback shifts the canary percentage back to 0% — but this still means gradually scaling down the canary pods while scaling up stable pods. Blue/Green rollback is faster but required double resources. Canary rollback is slightly slower but was already only affecting a small % of users. Different strategies, different rollback characteristics.

CI/CD Q9 of 10
Promote a canary from dev → staging → production. What's the GitOps promotion flow?
A) Manually copy YAML from dev/ to staging/ to prod/
B) Use one Application for all three environments
C) (1) Image passes dev canary → update staging overlay with new tag → ArgoCD syncs staging. (2) Image passes staging canary → update prod overlay → ArgoCD syncs prod. Promotion = Git commit updating the image tag in the next environment's overlay.
D) ArgoCD automatically promotes based on time
✅ C — Promotion = Git commit updating the overlay

GitOps promotion: the IMAGE TAG in the environment's Kustomize overlay is the promotion mechanism. Dev overlay has tag abc123. When tests pass in dev, update staging overlay to abc123 → ArgoCD syncs staging. When staging validates, update prod overlay to abc123 → ArgoCD syncs prod. Every promotion is a Git commit. Every promotion is auditable. Every promotion is revertible (git revert the tag change). This is the GitOps promotion pattern.

CI/CD Q10 of 10
Design the complete GitOps strategy for anihpj across 3 environments with safe deployments.
A) Kustomize base + overlays for config. ArgoCD for GitOps sync. Sealed Secrets or ESO for secrets. Argo Rollouts with AnalysisTemplate for canary deployments. ApplicationSet for multi-cluster. Promotion via Git commits updating image tags.
B) One flat repo with all YAML. kubectl apply from CI.
C) Separate repos per environment. Manual deploys.
D) Helm only. No overlays. Manual secret management.
✅ A — The complete GitOps stack

The CNPA GitOps stack: (1) Kustomize base+overlays for DRY environment config. (2) ArgoCD for GitOps sync with automated+prune+selfHeal. (3) Sealed Secrets or ESO for secret management (never plaintext). (4) Argo Rollouts with AnalysisTemplate for canary deployments with automated metric verification. (5) ApplicationSet for multi-cluster deployment. (6) Git-based promotion — commit the next environment's image tag. This stack provides: declarative config, automated deployment, safe rollouts, secure secrets, multi-cluster scale, and auditable promotion.

GitOps Promotion Walkthrough — anihpj v2.1 from Dev to Prod

Let's trace a real promotion of anihpj/jobpost v2.1 through the complete GitOps pipeline — from developer commit to production deployment. This is the end-to-end flow the CNPA exam tests:

1
Developer commits v2.1 code

PR merged to main. CI pipeline builds, tests, scans, and signs image anihpj/jobpost:abc123. Image pushed to registry.

2
Auto-deploy to DEV

CI updates overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml with new tag abc123. Commits to Git. ArgoCD detects change → syncs dev cluster. Dev canary: 10%→50%→100%. Metrics healthy.

3
Promote to STAGING (Git commit)

Platform engineer reviews dev metrics. Opens PR: update overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml tag to abc123. PR approved → merged. ArgoCD syncs staging. Staging canary validates.

4
Promote to PRODUCTION (Git commit + manual approval)

Platform engineer opens PR: update overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml tag to abc123. Requires 2 approvals (compliance). Merged. ArgoCD syncs prod with Blue/Green strategy.

5
Verify & Monitor (continuous reconciliation)

ArgoCD shows: anihpj-prod = Synced + Healthy. Prometheus: error rate 0.3%, P95=245ms. Grafana dashboard green. If metrics degrade → Argo Rollouts auto-rollback.

💡 Every step is a Git commit. Every promotion is auditable via git log. Rollback is git revert. This is GitOps — the pipeline doesn't deploy. Git deploys. ArgoCD enforces.
