Chapter 17: The Kubernetes Reconciliation Loop — The Heart of K8s

Every Kubernetes controller — from the Deployment controller to a custom Operator you write — runs the same fundamental algorithm: Observe current state → Compare with desired state → Act to converge. This infinite loop is the engine that makes Kubernetes declarative, self-healing, and resilient. Understanding it deeply transforms how you design, debug, and extend the platform. This chapter dissects the reconciliation loop, the controller pattern, level-triggered design, and idempotency — the principles that make K8s "just work" even when things crash.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🔄 K8s Internals🎯 Domain 4: 12%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Observe→Diff→Act — The reconciliation loop that runs in every controller. How Deployment controller maintains replica count
  • ✅ Controller Pattern — One controller per resource type. Built-in vs custom controllers (Operators)
  • ✅ Controller Manager — kube-controller-manager runs 30+ controllers. How they coexist
  • ✅ Level-Triggered vs Edge-Triggered — K8s is LEVEL-triggered. Why this matters for resilience
  • ✅ Controller Idempotency — Running reconcile 100 times = same result. Why this is essential
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Platform APIs & Infrastructure 12% Foundation for Operators (Ch 20) Foundation for CRDs (Ch 18)

17.1 Observe → Diff → Act — The Heart of K8s

THE RECONCILIATION LOOP — Every Controller Does This
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌───────────┐    ┌──────────┐                │
  │  │ OBSERVE  │───▶│ COMPARE   │───▶│   ACT    │                │
  │  │ (Get     │    │ (Diff?)   │    │ (Create/ │                │
  │  │  current │    │           │    │  Update/ │                │
  │  │  state)  │    │  Yes→Act  │    │  Delete) │                │
  │  └──────────┘    │  No→Sleep │    └──────────┘                │
  │                   └───────────┘                                │
  │  Deployment Controller: wants 3 replicas, has 2 →              │
  │  Act: create 1 more pod. Has 4 → Act: delete 1.               │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This loop runs INFINITELY. It never exits. It never says "done." Even when the cluster matches the desired state, the controller sleeps briefly and checks again. Why? Because reality drifts — pods crash, nodes fail, someone runs kubectl edit. The controller is the immune system that constantly heals the cluster back to the desired state.

The Thermostat Analogy — Understanding Reconciliation Through Everyday Objects

THE THERMOSTAT ANALOGY — Reconciliation in Everyday Life
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  THERMOSTAT                         KUBERNETES CONTROLLER        │
  │  Desired: 72°F (you set it)        Desired: 3 replicas (spec)   │
  │  Observed: 68°F (thermometer)      Observed: 2 pods (API server)│
  │  Compare: 72-68 = +4 (too cold)    Compare: 3-2 = +1            │
  │  Act: Turn HEATER ON                Act: CREATE 1 pod            │
  │  Later: Observed 74°F → ACT: OFF    Later: 4 pods → DELETE 1    │
  │  LOOP NEVER STOPS. Level-triggered. Idempotent.                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Controller Debugging — Why Isn't My Controller Reconciling?

🔍
Controller Logs

kubectl logs deploy/controller -n platform. Look for: "reconciling resource X," errors, or "nothing to do." No messages = informer not triggering.

📊
Status Conditions

kubectl describe <resource> → Status.Conditions. Stuck on Progressing? Degraded with error? Status tells you what the controller sees.

🔑
RBAC Check

Controller SA needs RBAC to watch/list/update CRDs AND create child resources. kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:ns:sa create deployments.

🔒
Finalizer Blocking

Resource stuck "Terminating"? Finalizer not removed. Check controller logs for cleanup errors. Never delete finalizers manually without understanding consequences.

Reconciliation Walkthrough — Tracing a Deployment Scale Event

Let's trace EXACTLY what happens when a user scales a Deployment from 3 to 5 replicas. Understanding this flow end-to-end — from kubectl to the new pods running — is what separates CNPA-level platform engineers from basic K8s users:

T+0s
User Submits Change

kubectl scale deployment anihpj-api --replicas=5 → API server receives the request → authenticates (who are you?) → authorizes (are you allowed to scale this Deployment?) → admission (do any webhooks reject this?) → writes to etcd: deployment.spec.replicas = 5. The write is an atomic etcd transaction. resourceVersion increments.

T+0.1s
WATCH Fires

The Deployment controller's informer has an open WATCH connection to the API server. The API server detects the etcd change → pushes a MODIFIED event over the still-open HTTP connection: {"type":"MODIFIED", "object":{"metadata":{"name":"anihpj-api"},"spec":{"replicas":5}}}. The informer's Reflector receives this event → updates the in-memory Indexer cache → triggers the registered event handler.

T+0.2s
Work Queue Enqueues

The event handler extracts the namespace/name key ("default/anihpj-api") and enqueues it into the work queue. The work queue's deduplication logic checks: is this key already queued? If yes → ignore (already scheduled for reconciliation). If no → add to queue. This ensures multiple rapid changes to the same resource produce ONE reconcile.

T+0.3s
Reconcile Runs

A worker goroutine pops "default/anihpj-api" from the queue. The reconcile function: (1) Reads the Deployment from the CACHE (in-memory Indexer — MICROSECOND latency, no API call). (2) Reads the ReplicaSet from the CACHE. (3) Calculates: desired 5 pods, currently 3 → need 2 more. (4) Calls API server: CREATE 2 new pods (API call, not cache — this is a WRITE).

T+0.5s
Pods Created, Scheduler Assigns Nodes

API server creates 2 Pod objects in etcd. Scheduler WATCH detects new unscheduled pods → assigns them to nodes → writes node assignments to etcd. Kubelet on each node WATCH detects pods assigned to it → pulls images → starts containers.

T+2s
Status Updated

Deployment controller creates or updates the ReplicaSet (spec.replicas=5). ReplicaSet controller detects the change → creates pods (already done by Deployment controller). Deployment controller updates Deployment.status: availableReplicas=3→4→5 as pods become ready. The user sees: kubectl get deploy anihpj-api → READY: 5/5.

📖 Why This Matters for the CNPA Exam

Every step above is a CNPA concept: (1) etcd as the source of truth (level-triggered). (2) WATCH for efficient change detection. (3) Informer + Cache for sub-millisecond reads. (4) Work queue for deduplication and rate-limiting. (5) Reconcile reads from cache, writes to API. (6) Multiple controllers cooperating via shared state (Deployment→ReplicaSet→Pods). (7) Status subresource for reporting. The exam tests your understanding of this FLOW, not just individual components. You should be able to trace any kubectl command through this pipeline.

17.2 Controllers and the Controller Pattern

Each resource type in Kubernetes has its OWN controller. The Deployment controller manages Deployments. The ReplicaSet controller manages ReplicaSets. The Job controller manages Jobs. They all follow the same pattern: Watch a resource type → Reconcile on changes → Update status. When you create a CRD and write a custom controller, you're creating an Operator — the same pattern, applied to YOUR resource.

📊
Deployment Controller

Watches: Deployments. Reconciles: Creates ReplicaSet → ReplicaSet controller creates Pods. Status: Available, Progressing, ReplicaFailure.

🔄
ReplicaSet Controller

Watches: ReplicaSets. Reconciles: Creates/deletes Pods to match desired replicas. Status: FullyLabeledReplicas, ReadyReplicas.

📋
Job Controller

Watches: Jobs. Reconciles: Creates Pods, monitors completion. Status: Active, Succeeded, Failed. Runs pod to completion.

🔌
EndpointSlice Controller

Watches: Services + Pods. Reconciles: Updates EndpointSlices when Pod IPs change. Ensures traffic routes to healthy pods.

Controller Cascading — How Controllers Cooperate via Shared State

Controllers don't call each other. They don't orchestrate. They communicate ENTIRELY through shared state in etcd — one controller writes to spec, another controller reads that spec and acts. This is the secret to K8s' composability:

CONTROLLER CASCADING — Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  USER: kubectl create deployment anihpj --replicas=3            │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────▼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  DEPLOYMENT (spec.replicas=3)          [etcd]              │ │
  │  │  Deployment Controller WATCHES this                        │ │
  │  │  RECONCILE: "No ReplicaSet exists → CREATE one"           │ │
  │  │  Writes: ReplicaSet{spec.replicas=3, selector=...}        │ │
  │  └────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                       │  (writes to etcd)                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  REPLICASET (spec.replicas=3)          [etcd]             │ │
  │  │  ReplicaSet Controller WATCHES this                        │ │
  │  │  RECONCILE: "0 Pods exist, need 3 → CREATE 3 Pods"      │ │
  │  │  Writes: Pod{name=anihpj-abc1}, Pod{abc2}, Pod{abc3}     │ │
  │  └────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                       │  (writes to etcd)                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  PODS (3×)                             [etcd]             │ │
  │  │  Scheduler WATCHES unassigned Pods → assigns nodes        │ │
  │  │  Kubelet WATCHES assigned Pods → runs containers          │ │
  │  │  ReplicaSet Controller updates RS.status.readyReplicas    │ │
  │  │  Deployment Controller updates Deploy.status.readyReplicas│ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                  │
  │  KEY INSIGHT: No controller "calls" another.                     │
  │  Deployment controller → writes ReplicaSet to etcd                │
  │  ReplicaSet controller → WATCH detects new RS → acts             │
  │  Each controller is independent. etcd is the shared medium.      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

17.3 Controller Manager — Running 30+ Controllers Together

The kube-controller-manager is a single binary that runs ALL built-in controllers in one process. Node controller, Replication controller, Endpoints controller, ServiceAccount controller, Token controller — 30+ controllers sharing the same process space, each watching different resource types, each running its own reconciliation loop. This design is efficient (shared caches, shared API connections) but means a crash in one controller could theoretically affect others — which is why controller isolation is improving in newer K8s versions.

How Controllers Work Under the Hood — Informers, Caches, and Work Queues

Controllers don't call the API server for every reconcile. That would overload etcd. Instead, they use a sophisticated architecture of informers (event-driven watchers), caches (in-memory state), and work queues (reconciliation scheduling). Understanding this is what separates CNPA-level platform engineers from basic K8s users:

CONTROLLER INTERNALS — Informers, Caches, Work Queues
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                    API SERVER (etcd)                       │ │
  │  └───────────────┬───────────────────┬───────────────────────┘ │
  │                  │ LIST (initial)    │ WATCH (streaming)        │
  │                  ▼                   ▼                          │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                     INFORMER                               │ │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │  │  REFLECTOR       │  │  INDEXER (In-Memory Cache)      │ │ │
  │  │  │  • LISTs API     │  │  • Full resource state in RAM   │ │ │
  │  │  │  • WATCHes API   │  │  • Indexed by namespace, labels │ │ │
  │  │  │  • Receives      │  │  • reconcile reads from HERE    │ │ │
  │  │  │    add/update/    │  │    (NOT from API server)       │ │ │
  │  │  │    delete events  │  │  • Serves GET requests in       │ │ │
  │  │  └─────────────────┘  │    microseconds (in-memory)      │ │ │
  │  │                       └─────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              │ Event handlers:                  │
  │                              │ "Deployment X changed → enqueue" │
  │                              ▼                                  │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                  WORK QUEUE                                │ │
  │  │  • Rate-limited: items processed one at a time             │ │
  │  │  • Deduplicated: multiple changes → ONE reconcile          │ │
  │  │  • Delayed retry: errors → exponential backoff            │ │
  │  │  • Fair: all resources get reconciled eventually          │ │
  │  └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                          │ Pop next item                       │
  │                          ▼                                      │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │              RECONCILE FUNCTION                             │ │
  │  │  • Reads current state from CACHE (fast, no API call)      │ │
  │  │  • Reads desired state from CACHE (fast, no API call)      │ │
  │  │  • Computes diff → Creates/Updates/Deletes via API         │ │
  │  │  • Updates status via API                                  │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 WHY THIS ARCHITECTURE MATTERS:                              │
  │  • Without informers: every controller polls API every second.  │
  │    With 30 controllers × 100 resources = 3000 API calls/sec.    │
  │    API server DIES under load.                                  │
  │  • With informers: WATCH streams changes. Cache serves reads.   │
  │    One WATCH connection per resource TYPE per controller.       │
  │    API calls only for WRITES (creates/updates/deletes).         │
  │  • This is why K8s scales to 5000+ nodes — the controller       │
  │    architecture is designed for efficiency, not simplicity.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

17.4 Level-Triggered vs Edge-Triggered — The K8s Design Choice

📡 Edge-Triggered (NOT K8s)
  • Reacts to EVENTS: "Pod created event!"
  • If controller crashes → misses events → state is LOST
  • Must persist event queue to survive crashes
  • Fragile: dropped event = incorrect state
  • Example: Traditional message queues
🔄 Level-Triggered (K8s)
  • Checks CURRENT STATE: "How many pods exist RIGHT NOW?"
  • If controller crashes → on restart, re-checks full state from etcd
  • No event queue needed. Desired state is ALWAYS in etcd
  • Resilient: the truth is in the database, not in a queue
  • Example: Every K8s controller

Why Not Both? — Comparing K8s, Terraform, and Event-Driven Systems

Different infrastructure tools use different reconciliation models. Understanding the tradeoffs helps you choose the right tool and design better controllers:

SystemModelWhen Reconciliation HappensCrash SafetyBest For
KubernetesLevel-TriggeredContinuously (every WATCH event + periodic re-sync). Desired state in etcd.Safe — reads full state on restartContainer orchestration. Continuous self-healing. Always-on systems.
Terraform / OpenTofuPlan-Apply (Manual)ON DEMAND (terraform plan/apply). State in a state file (local/S3).N/A — no controller running. State file must survive.Cluster bootstrap. One-shot infrastructure provisioning. Complex multi-resource orchestration.
CrossplaneLevel-TriggeredContinuously (same K8s controller pattern). Desired state in etcd (as CRDs).Safe — reads full state on restartDay 2 cloud infrastructure managed from within K8s. GitOps-native.
Event-Driven (SQS/Kafka)Edge-TriggeredOn each event: "UserCreated" → send email. Events MUST be processed in order.Fragile — missed events = incorrect state. Must persist event queue.Workflows. Async processing. Systems where event ORDER matters.
💡 The CNPA Insight

Kubernetes controllers and Crossplane use level-triggered reconciliation because they manage SYSTEMS that must self-heal continuously. Terraform uses plan-apply because it manages BOOTSTRAP infrastructure (create the cluster once, then K8s takes over). Event-driven systems handle WORKFLOWS where each event must be processed exactly once. The CNPA exam tests your ability to match the reconciliation model to the use case. Never use level-triggered for workflows (you'll reprocess on every restart). Never use edge-triggered for infrastructure (you'll miss drift).

Level-Triggered in Practice — The Idempotent Bash Script

Here's what level-triggered reconciliation looks like in code. Notice: there are NO event handlers. No callbacks. Just a loop that continuously checks state and acts:

🐚 BashLevel-Triggered Reconciliation — Bash Pseudocode
#!/bin/bash
# LEVEL-TRIGGERED RECONCILIATION LOOP
# This is what EVERY K8s controller does.

DESIRED_REPLICAS=3

while true; do
  # OBSERVE: Get CURRENT state (how many pods exist RIGHT NOW?)
  CURRENT_REPLICAS=$(kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj --no-headers | wc -l)

  # COMPARE: Diff desired vs current
  if [ $CURRENT_REPLICAS -lt $DESIRED_REPLICAS ]; then
    # ACT: Create missing pods
    MISSING=$((DESIRED_REPLICAS - CURRENT_REPLICAS))
    echo "[$(date)] Need $MISSING more pods. Creating..."
    for i in $(seq 1 $MISSING); do
      kubectl run anihpj-$RANDOM --image=anihpj/jobpost --restart=Always
    done

  elif [ $CURRENT_REPLICAS -gt $DESIRED_REPLICAS ]; then
    # ACT: Delete excess pods
    EXCESS=$((CURRENT_REPLICAS - DESIRED_REPLICAS))
    echo "[$(date)] Have $EXCESS extra pods. Deleting..."
    kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj --no-headers | tail -$EXCESS | \
      awk '{print $1}' | xargs kubectl delete pod

  else
    # NO-OP: State matches desired. Nothing to do.
    echo "[$(date)] ✅ $CURRENT_REPLICAS/$DESIRED_REPLICAS pods running. All good."
  fi

  sleep 10  # Check again in 10 seconds
done

# KEY PROPERTIES:
# • IDEMPOTENT: Running 100 times = same result.
#   If 3 pods exist, loop is a no-op forever.
# • LEVEL-TRIGGERED: Checks CURRENT state, not events.
#   If script crashes → on restart, reads current pod count.
# • SELF-HEALING: If someone deletes a pod → next loop creates it.
# • This script IS a (very basic) K8s controller!

17.5 Controller Idempotency — Safe to Retry Forever

Running reconcile 1 time = running reconcile 100 times = running reconcile 10,000 times. The result is the SAME. "Create pod if it doesn't exist" — after the first run, the pod exists, and all subsequent runs are no-ops. This idempotency is what makes K8s controllers safe to restart, safe to retry, and safe to run in HA (multiple replicas watching the same resources). If reconcile had side effects (like sending duplicate emails), retrying would be dangerous. Idempotency makes it safe.

The WATCH Mechanism — How Controllers Know Something Changed

Controllers don't poll. They WATCH. The API server supports long-lived HTTP connections where it streams changes as they happen. Combined with resourceVersion (an etcd-level version number), controllers always know exactly what changed and in what order:

WATCH API — How Controllers Stream Changes
# 1. Initial LIST: Get all Deployments + their resourceVersion
curl https://k8s-api/api/apps/v1/deployments?resourceVersion=0
# Returns: [{name: anihpj-api, spec: {replicas: 3}, ...}]
# resourceVersion: "47529"

# 2. WATCH: Open long-lived connection from that resourceVersion
curl https://k8s-api/api/apps/v1/deployments?watch=true&resourceVersion=47529
# Connection stays OPEN. API server streams changes as they happen:

# 3. Events stream in (HTTP chunked encoding):
# {"type": "MODIFIED", "object": {"name": "anihpj-api", "spec": {"replicas": 5}}}
# → Someone scaled anihpj-api to 5 replicas. Controller enqueues reconcile.

# {"type": "ADDED", "object": {"name": "anihpj-web", "spec": {"replicas": 2}}}
# → New Deployment created. Controller enqueues reconcile.

# {"type": "DELETED", "object": {"name": "old-service", ...}}
# → Deployment deleted. Controller cleans up (if Owner References don't handle it).

# 4. If connection drops → controller re-LIST + re-WATCH from last known resourceVersion.
# This is WHY K8s is level-triggered: on reconnect, LIST gets CURRENT state.
# No events are missed — the current state IS the truth.

Controller HA — Two Replicas Watching the Same Resource

What happens when TWO controller instances watch the same resource? Both receive the WATCH event. Both enqueue reconcile. Both try to create a missing Deployment. This is where idempotency becomes CRITICAL:

📖 HA Controllers in Practice

Instance A: WATCH event → enqueue → reconcile: "Need 3 pods, only 2 exist → create 1." Instance B: WATCH event → enqueue → reconcile: "Need 3 pods, already have 3 (A just created it) → no-op." No locking needed. No leader election for stateless controllers. Idempotent reconcile means duplicates are harmless. For stateful operations (like Operator provisioning a cloud DB), leader election prevents duplicate provisioning — but the reconcile itself remains idempotent.

17.6 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

APIs Q1 of 10
What are the three steps of the reconciliation loop?
A) Create → Read → Update
B) Observe → Diff/Compare → Act. The controller watches current state, compares with desired, and acts to converge.
C) Start → Process → Stop
D) Watch → Alert → Respond
✅ B — Observe → Diff → Act

Every K8s controller: (1) OBSERVE current state from API server. (2) COMPARE/DIFF with desired state (from spec). (3) ACT to converge (create, update, or delete resources). This infinite loop never exits — it continuously reconciles.

APIs Q2 of 10
Is Kubernetes level-triggered or edge-triggered? Why does it matter?
A) Edge-triggered — K8s reacts to events immediately
B) Both — K8s uses a hybrid approach
C) LEVEL-triggered. K8s checks CURRENT state against desired state. If controller crashes, on restart it reads the full state from etcd — no events are lost. The truth is in the database, not in a queue.
D) Neither — K8s uses a polling-based approach
✅ C — Level-triggered = resilient to crashes

K8s is LEVEL-triggered. Controllers evaluate "what SHOULD the world look like?" by comparing current state (from API server) to desired state (from spec). If a controller crashes, it doesn't "miss events" — on restart it reads the full current state from etcd and reconciles. Edge-triggered systems (like message queues) lose events on crash unless the queue is persisted.

APIs Q3 of 10
The Deployment controller crashes. What happens when it restarts?
A) It reads ALL Deployments from etcd, checks each one's current vs desired state, and reconciles any differences. No state is lost because desired state is stored in etcd.
B) It replays missed events from an event queue
C) All Deployments are paused until manual intervention
D) The API server recreates the controller automatically
✅ A — Level-triggered: reads full state on restart

Because K8s is level-triggered, the controller doesn't need to "remember" what happened while it was down. On restart, it queries the API server for ALL Deployments, compares each to its desired state, and acts. If a Deployment was updated while the controller was down, the new desired state is in etcd — the controller reconciles to the LATEST desired state, not catching up on intermediate states.

APIs Q4 of 10
Why must controller reconciliation be idempotent?
A) For performance — idempotent operations are faster
B) For security — idempotent operations prevent injection attacks
C) It doesn't need to be — controllers only run once per change
D) Because reconcile can run MULTIPLE times for the same resource (crashes, retries, HA replicas). Running it 100 times must produce the SAME result as running it once. Non-idempotent operations (like sending email on every reconcile) would cause duplicate side effects.
✅ D — Reconcile runs multiple times; must be safe to retry

Idempotency is NON-NEGOTIABLE for K8s controllers. Reasons: (1) Controllers restart frequently (crashes, upgrades). (2) HA deployments have multiple replicas watching the same resources. (3) Level-triggered design means reconcile runs on every state observation, not just on changes. A controller that sends an email "pod created" would send duplicate emails on every restart. Instead: "ensure pod exists" — after creation, subsequent runs are no-ops.

APIs Q5 of 10
How do controllers detect changes to resources they watch?
A) They poll the API server every second
B) Via WATCH — an HTTP long-poll connection to the API server. When a watched resource changes, the API server pushes the update. Combined with LIST (initial state) for the level-triggered pattern.
C) Via webhooks — resources push notifications to controllers
D) Via etcd directly — controllers read the database
✅ B — WATCH API (long-poll) + LIST (initial state)

Controllers use the WATCH API: open an HTTP connection to the API server with a resourceVersion parameter. When a watched resource changes, the API server sends the update over the still-open connection. Combined with an initial LIST to get current state (level-triggered), then WATCH for changes (efficient). This is far more efficient than polling — changes arrive within milliseconds, not at the next poll interval.

APIs Q6 of 10
Which of these is NOT a built-in controller managed by kube-controller-manager?
A) Node controller — monitors node health
B) ServiceAccount controller — creates default SA in new namespaces
C) Kyverno admission controller — this is an EXTERNAL webhook, not a built-in controller. Built-in controllers are compiled into kube-controller-manager.
D) Replication controller — ensures correct number of pod replicas
✅ C — Kyverno is external, not built-in

Built-in controllers run inside kube-controller-manager: Node, Replication, Endpoints, ServiceAccount, Token, Namespace, and 25+ others. External controllers (Kyverno, cert-manager, ArgoCD Application controller, custom Operators) run as separate pods in the cluster. They use the SAME controller pattern and reconciliation loop, but they're not compiled into the controller manager.

APIs Q7 of 10
What are finalizers and why are they needed in controllers?
A) Finalizers prevent a resource from being deleted until the controller CLEANS UP external resources (cloud databases, DNS records, storage volumes). The controller removes the finalizer only after cleanup is complete.
B) Finalizers speed up resource deletion
C) Finalizers are optional labels for categorization
D) Finalizers are Kubernetes garbage collection settings
✅ A — Finalizers block deletion until external cleanup completes

When you delete a resource with finalizers, K8s sets deletionTimestamp but does NOT remove the resource. The controller sees the deletion timestamp, cleans up external resources (deletes the cloud DB, removes DNS entry, releases the storage volume), then removes its finalizer from the list. Only when ALL finalizers are removed does K8s actually delete the resource. Without finalizers, deleting a Database CRD would leave the actual cloud database running (orphaned resource = $$$).

APIs Q8 of 10
Why do controllers write status to /status subresource instead of the main resource?
A) Status is faster to write
B) Status requires different authentication
C) There's no difference — it's convention only
D) SEPARATION OF CONCERNS: Users write to spec (desired state). Controllers write to status (observed state). RBAC can allow users to update spec but NOT status (preventing them from faking health). The controller owns the status.
✅ D — Separation: users own spec, controllers own status

The /status subresource separates: SPEC = what the USER wants (desired state). STATUS = what the CONTROLLER observes (actual state). RBAC can grant users write access to spec while blocking status writes — preventing users from manually setting "Ready: true" on a broken resource. The controller is the SOLE authority on status. This pattern is used by every K8s resource: Deployment.status.conditions, Pod.status.phase, etc.

APIs Q9 of 10
What's the relationship between a CRD, a custom controller, and an Operator?
A) They are three names for the same thing
B) CRD = the API extension (defines the resource type). Custom Controller = the reconciliation logic (watches CRD, runs Observe→Diff→Act). Operator = CRD + Custom Controller together — encoding human operational knowledge into software.
C) CRD = Operator; Controller is separate
D) Operator manages CRDs; Controllers manage Pods
✅ B — CRD + Custom Controller = Operator

A CRD alone is just a data store — you can create/read/update/delete resources, but nothing HAPPENS. A custom controller watches the CRD and runs reconciliation logic — creating child resources, updating status, cleaning up. Together, they form an Operator: software that automates what a human operator would do. CRD = the API. Controller = the brain. Operator = the complete package.

APIs Q10 of 10
A custom controller's reconcile function is being called repeatedly for the same resource but making no changes. Is this a bug?
A) Yes — reconcile should only be called once per change
B) Yes — the controller is in an infinite loop
C) NO — this is normal and EXPECTED. Level-triggered controllers re-reconcile on many triggers (resource changes, periodic re-sync, related resource changes). If the resource is in the desired state, reconcile should be a fast no-op. This is exactly how idempotent reconciliation works.
D) Yes — the controller should disable watching after first successful reconcile
✅ C — Normal behavior. Idempotent reconcile = fast no-op.

Controllers re-reconcile for many reasons: resource spec changed, resource status changed, related resources changed, periodic full re-sync (default: 10 hours), controller restart. If the resource is already in the desired state, reconcile should quickly determine "nothing to do" and return. This is NOT a bug — it's the level-triggered design working as intended. The controller should be efficient: check state → no diff → return immediately. No external API calls, no resource updates.

📊 Chapter 17 Summary — Key Takeaways

🔄ReconciliationObserve→Diff→Act. Infinite loop. Every controller. The engine of K8s.
📊ControllersOne per resource type. Built-in (30+ in controller-manager). Custom (Operators).
📡Level-TriggeredChecks CURRENT state. Crash-safe. Truth in etcd, not in event queues.
🔁IdempotentRun 100 times = same result. Safe to retry. No duplicate side effects.
🏷️FinalizersBlock deletion until cleanup. Prevent orphaned cloud resources. $$$ saver.
📋/statusUsers write spec. Controllers write status. Separation of concerns via RBAC.

Chapter 18: APIs for Self-Service Platforms — CRDs

Kubernetes isn't just a container orchestrator — it's an extensible API platform. Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) let you define YOUR OWN resource types with YOUR schema, YOUR validation, and YOUR behavior. Need a "Database" resource that provisions RDS? A "JobBoard" resource that deploys the entire anihpj stack? A "DeveloperEnvironment" that spins up a full dev setup? CRDs make K8s speak YOUR domain language. This chapter covers CRD design, OpenAPI validation, versioning, subresources, and platform API best practices — building the self-service APIs that make platforms powerful.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🔌 APIs🎯 Domain 4: 12%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ CRD Design — Extend K8s API with your resource types. kubectl get databases → shows your custom resources
  • ✅ OpenAPI v3 Validation — Field constraints, enums, required fields, min/max
  • ✅ CRD Versions & Conversion — v1alpha1→v1beta1→v1 lifecycle. Conversion webhooks
  • ✅ Subresources — /status for controller status, /scale for replica management
  • ✅ Self-Service APIs — REST, gRPC, GraphQL. From CRD to Backstage portal

18.1 Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) — Extending the K8s API

CRD — Extending the Kubernetes API
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kubectl get databases                                          │
  │  NAME          ENGINE     SIZE    STATUS   AGE                  │
  │  anihpj-db     postgres   20Gi    Ready    30d                  │
  │  anihpj-cache  redis      5Gi     Ready    15d                  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  kubectl create -f my-database.yaml                             │
  │  → CRD "Database" created                                       │
  │  → Operator sees new Database → provisions RDS                  │
  │  → 5 minutes later: Production PostgreSQL ready!                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

anihpj Database CRD — Full Definition

anihpj-database-crd.yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.anihpj.io       # plural.group
spec:
  group: anihpj.io
  names:
    kind: Database
    plural: databases
    singular: database
    shortNames: [db]
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              engine: {type: string, enum: [postgres, mysql, redis]}
              version: {type: string}
              size: {type: string, pattern: "^[0-9]+Gi$"}
              replicas: {type: integer, minimum: 1, maximum: 5}
            required: [engine, size]
          status:
            type: object
            properties:
              phase: {type: string, enum: [Pending, Creating, Ready, Failed]}
              endpoint: {type: string}
    subresources:
      status: {}
    additionalPrinterColumns:
    - name: Engine
      type: string
      jsonPath: .spec.engine
    - name: Size
      type: string
      jsonPath: .spec.size
    - name: Status
      type: string
      jsonPath: .status.phase

CRD Resource Lifecycle — From kubectl to etcd to Operator Action

When you create a CRD instance, it flows through the ENTIRE K8s machinery — the same pipeline a Deployment or Pod follows. Understanding this lifecycle is essential for debugging "my operator isn't working" issues:

1
kubectl apply -f database.yaml

kubectl sends an HTTP POST to the API server at /apis/anihpj.io/v1/namespaces/default/databases. The API server identifies this as a CRD resource (not a built-in one) by looking up the API group (anihpj.io) and version (v1) in its discovery information — which was registered when you created the CRD.

2
Authentication & Authorization

API server: "Who are you?" (AuthN — checks certificate/token). "Are you allowed to CREATE databases in the default namespace?" (AuthZ — RBAC check: the user's Role must have 'create' verb on 'databases' resource in the 'anihpj.io' group). If either fails → 401/403 immediately.

3
Admission — Mutating + Validating

Mutating admission webhooks run FIRST (can modify the resource — add labels, inject sidecars, set defaults). Then: OpenAPI v3 schema validation (from the CRD definition). Then: CEL validation rules (x-kubernetes-validations). Then: Validating admission webhooks (accept/reject — Kyverno policies, OPA constraints). Any rejection → 422 Unprocessable Entity with a clear error message.

4
Storage in etcd

The validated resource is serialized to JSON and written to etcd with an atomic transaction. etcd assigns it a resourceVersion (a monotonically increasing number). The resource is now PERSISTED. Even if the API server crashes, the resource exists in etcd.

5
WATCH Fires → Controller Acts

The Operator's controller (watching databases.anihpj.io) receives a WATCH event: "ADDED: anihpj-db". The informer caches it. The work queue enqueues "default/anihpj-db". The reconcile function: reads the Database from cache → provisions cloud resources → updates status.phase=Ready.

6
User Reads Status

kubectl get database anihpj-db → API server reads from etcd → returns the resource including status.phase=Ready and status.endpoint=db.anihpj.com. The spec is what the user wrote. The status is what the controller observed. Together: complete picture.

18.2 CRD Schema — OpenAPI v3 Validation

CRDs use OpenAPI v3 schemas for validation at the API server level — BEFORE the resource is stored in etcd. Invalid resources are REJECTED with clear errors:

🔤
String Validation

enum: [postgres, mysql, redis] — only these values. pattern: "^[0-9]+Gi$" — regex. minLength/maxLength — length bounds.

🔢
Integer Validation

minimum: 1, maximum: 5 — range. multipleOf: 2 — even numbers only. exclusiveMinimum — strict bounds.

📋
Required Fields

required: [engine, size] — must be present. Missing → REJECTED: "spec.engine is required."

🔒
Immutable Fields

x-kubernetes-validations: [{rule: "self == oldSelf", message: "engine is immutable"}] — CEL-based immutability in K8s 1.25+.

CEL Validation Rules — Beyond OpenAPI Schema

OpenAPI v3 validates individual fields. But what about cross-field rules? "If engine=postgres, version must be >= 12." "If encrypted=true, size must be >= 10Gi." K8s 1.25+ introduces CEL (Common Expression Language) — expressive, in-line validation that runs at the API server:

CRD CEL Validation — Cross-Field Rules
x-kubernetes-validations:
# Cross-field: PostgreSQL must be version >= 12
- rule: "self.engine == 'postgres' ? has(self.version) && int(self.version) >= 12 : true"
  message: "PostgreSQL requires version >= 12"

# Conditional: encrypted databases need minimum 10Gi
- rule: "self.encrypted && self.size != '' ? int(self.size) >= 10 : true"
  message: "Encrypted databases require minimum 10Gi"

# Immutability: engine can't change after creation
- rule: "self == oldSelf || self.engine == oldSelf.engine"
  message: "Engine is immutable after creation"

# Regex: size must be digits + Gi
- rule: "self.size.matches('^[0-9]+Gi$')"
  message: "Size must be in Gi format (e.g., 20Gi)"

# 💡 CEL vs OpenAPI: OpenAPI validates fields independently.
# CEL validates RELATIONSHIPS between fields. Both run BEFORE
# etcd storage. Both DECLARATIVE (no webhook needed).
# CEL is the CNPA pattern for cross-field validation.

The Validation Pipeline — Order of Operations at Admission

When a CRD resource is created or updated, the API server runs validation in a SPECIFIC order. Understanding this order is critical for debugging "why did my resource get rejected?" and for designing validation that works correctly with mutation:

VALIDATION PIPELINE — Every CRD Create/Update Goes Through This
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              API SERVER ADMISSION PIPELINE                        │
  │                                                                  │
  │  REQUEST: kubectl create -f database.yaml                       │
  │       │                                                          │
  │  ┌────▼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  1. AUTHENTICATION (AuthN)                                 │ │
  │  │  "Who are you?" — Certificate, Token, OIDC                │ │
  │  │  FAIL → 401 Unauthorized                                   │ │
  │  └────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                           │ PASS                                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  2. AUTHORIZATION (AuthZ — RBAC)                           │ │
  │  │  "Are you allowed to CREATE databases?"                   │ │
  │  │  FAIL → 403 Forbidden                                      │ │
  │  └────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                           │ PASS                                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  3. MUTATING ADMISSION WEBHOOKS                            │ │
  │  │  • Can MODIFY the resource (add labels, set defaults)      │ │
  │  │  • Run FIRST — before validation                          │ │
  │  │  • Example: Inject sidecar, add owner label               │ │
  │  │  • FAIL → rejected (but mutation already applied)         │ │
  │  └────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                           │ PASS                                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  4. OpenAPI v3 SCHEMA VALIDATION                           │ │
  │  │  • Field-level: enum, pattern, min/max, required          │ │
  │  │  • Runs on the MUTATED resource (after webhooks)           │ │
  │  │  • FAIL → 422 "spec.engine: Unsupported value"           │ │
  │  └────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                           │ PASS                                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  5. CEL VALIDATION (x-kubernetes-validations)              │ │
  │  │  • Cross-field rules: "if engine=postgres, version>=12"  │ │
  │  │  • Immutability: "self == oldSelf || engine unchanged"   │ │
  │  │  • Runs AFTER OpenAPI (fields are individually valid)      │ │
  │  │  • FAIL → 422 with custom CEL message                     │ │
  │  └────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                           │ PASS                                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  6. VALIDATING ADMISSION WEBHOOKS                          │ │
  │  │  • ACCEPT or REJECT the resource                           │ │
  │  │  • CANNOT modify (validating only)                        │ │
  │  │  • Example: Kyverno policy check, OPA constraint          │ │
  │  │  • FAIL → rejected with webhook's error message            │ │
  │  └────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                           │ PASS                                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  7. STORED IN etcd ✅                                      │ │
  │  │  Resource is PERSISTED. WATCH fires. Controller acts.      │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                  │
  │  💡 CNPA INSIGHT: Mutating webhooks → OpenAPI → CEL →            │
  │  Validating webhooks. This order matters: mutating webhooks      │
  │  can fix things BEFORE validation rejects them. CEL runs after   │
  │  OpenAPI so cross-field rules work on already-validated fields.  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Structural Schemas vs Validation Schemas — Why Both Matter

📋 Structural Schema (OpenAPI)
  • DEFINES the shape of your resource fields
  • Enables: kubectl explain, server-side apply, API discovery
  • Required for: /status and /scale subresources
  • Without it: CRD is "unstructured" — raw JSON blob, no field-level access
✅ Validation Schema
  • CONSTRAINS valid values (enum, pattern, min/max)
  • Rejects invalid resources BEFORE etcd storage
  • Built ON TOP of structural schema
  • OpenAPI + CEL rules together = complete validation

18.3 CRD Versions & Conversion — The API Evolution Path

CRDs follow the standard K8s API versioning: v1alpha1 (experimental, may break) → v1beta1 (stabilizing, likely no breaking changes) → v1 (stable, guaranteed no breaking changes). Multiple versions can be served simultaneously with conversion webhooks handling translation:

📖 Version Lifecycle

v1alpha1: Experimental. May change or be removed without notice. Use in dev only. v1beta1: Stabilizing. Breaking changes are rare and announced with migration time. Safe for limited production use. v1: Stable. NO breaking changes will ever be made. Safe for all production use. When you deprecate a version, you must support it for at least 3 releases before removal.

Conversion Webhook Internals — How Multi-Version CRDs Work

When a CRD serves multiple versions, resources may be STORED in one version (the storage version — e.g., v1) but REQUESTED in another (e.g., v1beta1). The conversion webhook translates between them on-the-fly. This is invisible to users but critical for API evolution:

CONVERSION WEBHOOK FLOW — v1beta1 Request, v1 Storage
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. User: kubectl get database anihpj-db -o yaml                │
  │     → API server receives request for v1beta1                    │
  │                                                                  │
  │  2. API server reads from etcd: STORED as v1 (the storage ver)  │
  │     spec:                                                        │
  │       engine: postgres        ← v1 field                         │
  │       size: "20Gi"                                              │
  │       replicas: 3             ← v1 added this field             │
  │                                                                  │
  │  3. API server calls CONVERSION WEBHOOK:                         │
  │     POST https://webhook-svc/platform/v1/convert                │
  │     Body: {desiredAPIVersion: "v1beta1", objects: [{v1 JSON}]}  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  4. Webhook converts v1 → v1beta1:                               │
  │     • Maps new field names to old: engineV → engineVersion       │
  │     • Drops new fields not in v1beta1: removes "replicas"       │
  │     • Transforms values: "20Gi" → {size: 20, unit: Gi}          │
  │                                                                  │
  │  5. Webhook responds: Converted to v1beta1 JSON                  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  6. API server returns v1beta1 resource to user                  │
  │     → User sees the old format, but storage is the new format    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ Conversion Webhook Critical Rules
  • Must be HA: If the webhook is down, ALL CRUD operations on the CRD FAIL. The API server calls the webhook on every request that crosses versions.
  • Must be idempotent: Converting v1→v1beta1→v1 must return the original v1 object (round-trip fidelity). Lossy conversion corrupts data.
  • Must handle "no-op" conversion: If the stored version matches the requested version, the webhook is NOT called — K8s returns the resource directly.
  • Must respond in < 10 seconds: The API server times out webhook calls. Slow conversion = API downtime.
  • CNPA Pattern: Use conversion webhooks for STRUCTURAL changes (field renames, type changes). Use CEL validation for cross-field rules within a single version.

18.4 CRD Subresources — /status and /scale

📊
/status Subresource

Separates spec (user writes desired state) from status (controller writes observed state). RBAC: users update spec, controllers update status. Prevents users from faking health. subresources: {status: {}}

📏
/scale Subresource

Enables kubectl scale database anihpj-db --replicas=3. Controller must implement the scale endpoint. Works automatically with HPA. subresources: {scale: {specReplicasPath: .spec.replicas}}

Subresources in Action — RBAC Separation with Code

The /status subresource isn't just convention — it's enforced by the API server at the RBAC level. Here's what happens when a user tries to fake status vs when a controller legitimately updates it:

🐚 BashRBAC Separation — Spec vs Status in Practice
# ─── USER TRIES TO FAKE STATUS ───
# User wants to mark a broken Database as "Ready"
$ kubectl patch database anihpj-db --type=merge -p '{"status":{"phase":"Ready"}}'
# ❌ Error: "databases.anihpj.io "anihpj-db" cannot update status"
# RBAC says: User CAN update spec, CANNOT update status.
# The /status subresource is PROTECTED.

# ─── CONTROLLER UPDATES STATUS LEGITIMATELY ───
# The Database Operator, using its ServiceAccount:
$ kubectl patch database anihpj-db --type=merge \
    --subresource=status -p '{"status":{"phase":"Ready","endpoint":"db.anihpj.com"}}'
# ✅ Success! Controller's ServiceAccount has RBAC to update /status.
# The --subresource=status flag targets the /status endpoint.

# ─── RBAC CONFIGURATION ───
# Developer Role: can manage spec, can ONLY READ status
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: database-developer
rules:
- apiGroups: ["anihpj.io"]
  resources: ["databases"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
  # NOTE: No access to "databases/status" — can't fake health!
- apiGroups: ["anihpj.io"]
  resources: ["databases/status"]
  verbs: ["get"]  # Read-only on status

# Operator ServiceAccount: CAN update status
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: database-operator
rules:
- apiGroups: ["anihpj.io"]
  resources: ["databases"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]  # Read-only on spec
- apiGroups: ["anihpj.io"]
  resources: ["databases/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]  # Write access on status
# Controller reads spec, writes status. Users write spec, read status.
# This separation is THE CNPA pattern for CRD subresources.

18.5 Self-Service APIs — From CRD to Developer Portal

CRDs are the foundation. Self-service APIs layer on top to give developers their preferred interface — REST for automation, gRPC for performance, GraphQL for portal UIs:

SELF-SERVICE API STACK — Backstage → API → CRD → Operator
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  🎭 Backstage Portal  ← Developer clicks "Create Database"      │
  │       │ REST / GraphQL                                          │
  │  📡 Platform API     ← Translates portal request → CRD          │
  │       │ kubectl apply -f                                       │
  │  📋 Database CRD     ← Stored in etcd                           │
  │       │ Watch (controller detects new CR)                       │
  │  🤖 DB Operator      ← Reconciliation: creates RDS, subnet, SG  │
  │       │ AWS API                                                 │
  │  ☁️  AWS RDS         ← Actual PostgreSQL instance provisioned   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL — Choosing the Right API Style

The platform API is the contract between developers and infrastructure. Choosing the right API style for each use case is a core CNPA design decision:

API StyleBest ForProtocolStrengthsWeaknesses
RESTPortal UIs, public APIs, automation scriptsHTTP/1.1 + JSONHuman-readable. curl-able. Universal tooling. Cacheable (GET). Mature ecosystem.Over-fetching data. Multiple round trips for related resources. No streaming.
gRPCService-to-service (controller→API, API→K8s)HTTP/2 + ProtobufBinary (smaller, faster). Multiplexing. Bidirectional streaming. Strong typing (.proto).Not browser-friendly. Harder to debug (binary). Requires .proto compilation step.
GraphQLPortal UIs with complex data needsHTTP + JSONClients request EXACTLY what they need. One query → nested resources. Schema-typed.Complex server implementation. N+1 query problem. Caching is harder than REST.
💡 The CNPA API Strategy

REST for public-facing platform APIs (Backstage calls, CLI tools, CI/CD scripts) — universal, debuggable, cacheable. gRPC for internal service-to-service (controller ↔ API server, Crossplane provider ↔ cloud API) — fast, typed, streaming-capable. GraphQL for Backstage portal UIs that need complex, nested resource queries ("show me this service, its deployments, its dependencies, and its alerts — all in one request"). Don't choose ONE — use the right style for each layer.

18.6 Platform API Design Best Practices

📌
Versioning

/v1/ → /v2/. Never break existing consumers. Old versions deprecated but served for N releases.

📝
Documentation

OpenAPI/Swagger specs. Auto-generate SDKs. Every field documented with examples.

⚠️
Deprecation

Announce → wait 9 months → remove. Set deprecationWarning header. Give migration guides.

🔒
RBAC

Fine-grained access per API. Developer role: create Database. Admin role: delete Database.

API Versioning Lifecycle — The Platform API Contract

Platform APIs are CONTRACTS with developers. Breaking the contract = breaking CI pipelines, Terraform scripts, and Backstage plugins that depend on your API. The versioning lifecycle ensures evolution without breaking existing consumers:

API VERSIONING LIFECYCLE — v1 → v2 Without Breaking Anyone
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    API VERSIONING TIMELINE                        │
  │                                                                  │
  │  MONTH 0:  /v1/ released (stable)                                │
  │     │      Developers build integrations against /v1/            │
  │     │      CI/CD, Terraform, Backstage plugins — all on /v1/     │
  │     │                                                            │
  │  MONTH 3:  /v2/ released (new features, same /v1/ still served) │
  │     │      Both /v1/ and /v2/ run simultaneously                 │
  │     │      New consumers use /v2/. Existing stay on /v1/         │
  │     │                                                            │
  │  MONTH 6:  /v1/ DEPRECATED (warning header, docs updated)       │
  │     │      HTTP Response: Deprecation: true                      │
  │     │      Sunset: "Sun, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT"              │
  │     │      Migration guide published: /v1/ → /v2/ changes       │
  │     │                                                            │
  │  MONTH 15: /v1/ SUNSET (9 months after deprecation)             │
  │     │      /v1/ removed. Only /v2/ remains.                      │
  │     │      By now, ALL consumers should have migrated.           │
  │     │      If not → 410 Gone with migration guide link.          │
  │                                                                  │
  │  RULES:                                                          │
  │  • NEVER remove a version without deprecation warning            │
  │  • Minimum 9 months between deprecation and removal              │
  │  • Deprecation header MUST be machine-readable                   │
  │  • Migration guide MUST be published at deprecation time         │
  │  • Monitor /v1/ traffic to confirm zero before removal          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🌐 HTTPDeprecation Headers — Machine-Readable Warnings
# When /v1/ is deprecated, EVERY response includes:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Deprecation: true
Sunset: Sat, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT
Link: <https://developer.anihpj.io/docs/migration-v1-to-v2>; rel="deprecation"

# Clients can detect this PROGRAMMATICALLY:
# CI/CD pipeline sees Deprecation header → logs warning → alerts team
# No human needs to notice the deprecation — automation does.

# When /v1/ is finally removed:
HTTP/1.1 410 Gone
Link: <https://developer.anihpj.io/docs/migration-v1-to-v2>; rel="deprecation"
# 410 Gone = "This resource is GONE, not just temporarily unavailable"
# 404 Not Found would be wrong — it implies the URL never existed.

18.7 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

APIs Q1 of 10
What does a CRD do WITHOUT a custom controller (Operator)?
A) Nothing — CRDs always require a controller
B) Automatically provisions cloud resources
C) Runs reconciliation logic automatically
D) Provides CRUD storage — you can kubectl create/get/update/delete Database resources, but nothing HAPPENS. The resources are stored in etcd. A controller is needed to ACT on them.
✅ D — CRD alone = data storage, no action

A CRD without a controller is like a database table with no application — you can insert/select/update/delete rows, but no business logic executes. A CRD + controller (Operator) is a complete application: the CRD defines the data model, the controller implements the behavior. CRD alone = API extension. CRD + Controller = Operator.

APIs Q2 of 10
User tries: kubectl create database --engine=mongodb. The CRD schema has engine: enum: [postgres, mysql, redis]. What happens?
A) The resource is created with engine=mongodb — validation is informational only
B) REJECTED by the API server: "spec.engine: Unsupported value: 'mongodb'. Supported values: postgres, mysql, redis." The CRD schema validates BEFORE etcd storage.
C) The resource is created but the controller ignores it
D) The API server crashes due to invalid input
✅ B — API server rejects invalid resources at admission

CRD OpenAPI v3 schemas are validated by the API server BEFORE the resource is stored in etcd. Invalid fields, missing required fields, or values outside constraints → immediate REJECTION with a clear error message. This is server-side validation — no controller needed. The controller never sees invalid resources because they never reach etcd.

APIs Q3 of 10
Your CRD has v1alpha1 and v1beta1 versions. You want to remove v1alpha1. What's the correct process?
A) 1) Announce deprecation. 2) Wait at least 3 K8s releases (or your stated support window). 3) Set served: false on v1alpha1. 4) Existing v1alpha1 resources must be converted to v1beta1 (via conversion webhook or manual migration) before removal.
B) Just delete the v1alpha1 definition — it's alpha, no obligations
C) Rename v1beta1 to v1 and delete v1alpha1 immediately
D) CRD versions cannot be removed once created
✅ A — Announce, wait, convert, then remove

CRD version removal follows the K8s API deprecation policy: announce deprecation, wait at least 3 releases (or 9-12 months), ensure all existing resources are stored in the new version (via storage version migration), then set served: false on the old version. Conversion webhooks handle on-the-fly conversion between versions. Rushing removal breaks clients that still use the old API version.

APIs Q4 of 10
What's the difference between Namespaced and Cluster-scoped CRDs?
A) No difference — all CRDs are the same
B) Cluster-scoped is faster
C) Namespaced: resource belongs to ONE namespace (like Deployments). Cluster: resource is cluster-wide (like Nodes, ClusterRoles). Set via scope: Namespaced or scope: Cluster in the CRD spec.
D) Namespaced is more secure; Cluster is less secure
✅ C — Namespaced vs Cluster scope

Namespaced CRDs (scope: Namespaced): resources exist within a namespace. RBAC can be namespace-scoped. kubectl get databases -n anihpj-dev. Cluster CRDs (scope: Cluster): resources are cluster-wide. kubectl get clusterdatabases. Used for resources that are not logically bound to a namespace — like cluster-level configuration, infrastructure definitions, or global policies.

APIs Q5 of 10
What does additionalPrinterColumns do in a CRD?
A) Adds security columns to the resource
B) Adds logging columns for debugging
C) Adds metadata columns for RBAC
D) Customizes kubectl get output. Without it: kubectl get databases shows only NAME and AGE. With it: shows NAME, ENGINE, SIZE, STATUS, AGE — extracted from JSON paths in the resource.
✅ D — Customizes kubectl get output columns

additionalPrinterColumns defines extra columns for kubectl get output. Each column specifies: name (header), type (string/integer/date), and jsonPath (where to read the value from). This makes kubectl get databases immediately useful — showing engine, size, and status at a glance — without needing kubectl describe or -o yaml. It's the CRD equivalent of a table view.

APIs Q6 of 10
When do you need a CRD conversion webhook?
A) For all CRDs — conversion webhooks are mandatory
B) When you have MULTIPLE versions (v1alpha1, v1beta1) with different schemas. The webhook converts resources between versions on-the-fly. Without it, you can only serve one version as storage.
C) For security — webhooks validate all CRD operations
D) For performance — webhooks cache CRD schemas
✅ B — Multi-version CRDs with schema differences

When a CRD serves multiple versions, resources may be stored in one version (storage version) but requested in another (served version). The conversion webhook translates between them. Example: stored as v1 (fields: engine, size, replicas), requested as v1alpha1 (different field names or structure) → webhook converts on-the-fly. Without a webhook, K8s can only do field-renaming conversions automatically — structural changes require a webhook.

APIs Q7 of 10
Design the self-service API flow: a developer wants to create a Database through the Backstage portal.
A) Backstage → POST /api/v1/databases → Platform API → kubectl apply -f database.yaml → CRD stored in etcd → Operator detects new Database → provisions RDS → updates status.ready=true. Developer sees "Ready" in Backstage.
B) Developer calls AWS directly from the portal
C) Backstage stores the request in a database for manual processing
D) Developer files a Jira ticket; platform team provisions manually
✅ A — Portal → API → CRD → Operator → Cloud → Status

The self-service flow: (1) Developer fills form in Backstage. (2) Backstage calls Platform API (REST/gRPC). (3) Platform API creates a CRD instance (kubectl apply). (4) CRD stored in etcd. (5) Operator's controller watches for new Database resources. (6) Controller reconciles: calls AWS API to create RDS, subnet group, security group. (7) Controller updates status.phase=Ready, status.endpoint=db.anihpj.com. (8) Backstage polls status and shows green checkmark. No human in the loop.

APIs Q8 of 10
What's the correct deprecation policy for a Platform API endpoint?
A) Remove it immediately — old versions cause confusion
B) Email users and remove in 1 week
C) 1) Announce deprecation with migration guide. 2) Add deprecation warning header. 3) Wait N months (minimum 9 for stable APIs). 4) Remove only after confirming zero traffic to the old endpoint.
D) Never remove API endpoints — they're permanent
✅ C — Announce → Warn → Wait → Confirm → Remove

API deprecation follows K8s conventions: announce with clear timeline, add deprecation headers so clients can detect it programmatically, wait sufficient time for migration (minimum 9 months for stable APIs), monitor traffic to confirm no clients still use it, then remove. Never surprise-deprecate — it breaks CI/CD pipelines, automation scripts, and developer trust in the platform.

APIs Q9 of 10
Why use gRPC instead of REST for platform service-to-service communication?
A) gRPC is easier to debug
B) gRPC is more human-readable
C) gRPC requires less code
D) gRPC uses Protocol Buffers (binary, smaller payloads) + HTTP/2 (multiplexing, streaming). Faster and more efficient for service-to-service communication. REST is better for browser/portal access and debugging.
✅ D — gRPC = binary + HTTP/2 = faster for internal services

gRPC advantages for internal platform services: (1) Protocol Buffers — binary encoding, smaller payloads than JSON. (2) HTTP/2 multiplexing — multiple requests over one connection. (3) Native streaming — server-side, client-side, bidirectional. (4) Strong typing via .proto files. REST advantages for portals: human-readable, browser-debuggable with curl, wider ecosystem. Best practice: gRPC between internal services, REST for external/portal APIs.

APIs Q10 of 10
Design the complete self-service platform API architecture for anihpj.
A) One monolithic API that handles everything
B) CRDs define the resource types (Database, Service, Environment). Platform API wraps CRDs with REST/gRPC endpoints. Backstage portal provides the UI. Operators in the background reconcile CRDs into real infrastructure. Versioned APIs, documented with OpenAPI, RBAC-controlled access.
C) Direct AWS API access for all developers
D) Manual ticket-based provisioning — no APIs needed
✅ B — CRD + API + Portal + Operator = Self-Service Platform

The CNPA self-service architecture: CRDs define the domain model (what resources exist). Platform API provides developer-friendly access (REST/gRPC/GraphQL). Backstage portal gives a UI. Operators reconcile CRDs into real infrastructure. This layered architecture separates concerns: data model (CRD), access (API), experience (portal), and automation (Operator). Developers get self-service. Platform team maintains guardrails.

✅ValidationOpenAPI v3. Enum, pattern, min/max, required. Server-side. Rejects BEFORE etcd.
📌Versioningv1alpha1→v1beta1→v1. Deprecation + migration. Conversion webhooks for multi-version.
