Chapter 19: Infrastructure Provisioning — From YAML to Cloud Resources

Kubernetes excels at managing workloads ON the cluster. But who provisions the cluster itself? And the databases, caches, and message queues your workloads depend on? Crossplane brings infrastructure provisioning INTO Kubernetes — using the same CRD + Controller pattern to manage cloud resources (RDS, S3, EKS, VPC) declaratively. Combined with Cluster API for managing K8s clusters themselves, and drift detection to keep reality matching desired state, this chapter covers the complete infrastructure-as-code-to-K8s pipeline for anihpj.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🏗️ Infra🎯 Domain 4: 12%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Crossplane — Kubernetes-native infrastructure provisioning. CRDs for cloud resources
  • ✅ XRD + Composition — Define YOUR platform API. Map it to cloud resources via Composition
  • ✅ Cluster API (CAPI) — Manage K8s clusters as K8s resources
  • ✅ Drift Detection — Detect and correct when cloud reality diverges from desired state

19.1 Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — Declarative Cloud

IaC tools (Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, Crossplane) define cloud infrastructure as declarative code. "I want a VPC with these subnets, an RDS PostgreSQL instance of this size, and these security groups." The tool computes the diff and applies changes. Git is the source of truth. Infrastructure is versioned, reviewed, and auditable.

The Terraform/OpenTofu Plan-Apply Workflow

Terraform (HashiCorp) and OpenTofu (community fork, Linux Foundation) follow the same workflow. Understanding this is essential because the CNPA exam tests when to use external IaC vs K8s-native (Crossplane):

1
Write (HCL)

Define infrastructure in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language): resource "aws_db_instance" "anihpj" { engine = "postgres", allocated_storage = 20 }. Files stored in Git — versioned, reviewed, auditable.

2
Plan

terraform plan reads current state (from state file or cloud API), compares with desired state (from .tf files), and outputs: "Plan: 3 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy." NO changes made yet — just a preview.

3
Apply

terraform apply executes the plan: calls cloud APIs (AWS, GCP, Azure) to create/update/delete resources. State file updated with new resource IDs. One-shot reconciliation — unlike K8s controllers, Terraform does NOT continuously reconcile.

4
State Management

State file (terraform.tfstate) maps HCL resources to real cloud resource IDs. Stored locally or remotely (S3, Terraform Cloud). State locking prevents concurrent modifications. State is THE source of truth for what Terraform manages.

Terraform vs OpenTofu — The IaC Landscape

🟣 Terraform (HashiCorp)
  • Original IaC tool. Mature ecosystem (3000+ providers)
  • Terraform Cloud for remote state + team collaboration
  • BSL license since 2023 (not fully open source)
  • HCL language. Plan → Apply workflow
  • Best for: Organizations already invested, need Terraform Cloud
🟢 OpenTofu (Linux Foundation)
  • Community fork after Terraform license change (2023)
  • Fully open source (MPL 2.0). CNCF-aligned
  • Drop-in replacement — same HCL, same workflow
  • Growing ecosystem, backward-compatible
  • Best for: CNCF-aligned organizations, open-source purists

IaC Principles — What Every Platform Engineer Must Know

📜
Declarative, Not Imperative

Define WHAT you want ("RDS instance, 20Gi, encrypted"), not HOW to create it ("call CreateDBInstance API"). The tool figures out the steps. Same philosophy as K8s — desired state over procedural steps.

🔄
Idempotent

Running apply 100 times = same result. If resource already exists in desired state → no-op. If someone manually changed it → revert to desired state. Same principle as K8s controller idempotency.

📊
State is Truth

The state file is the bridge between code and reality. Without state, Terraform can't know what it manages. Protect it: remote storage (S3), encryption at rest, state locking (DynamoDB), versioning.

🔍
Drift Detection

terraform plan detects drift: someone changed the security group in AWS console → plan shows it as "change" → apply reverts it. Unlike Crossplane (continuous), Terraform drift detection is ON-DEMAND (you run plan).

Terraform in Practice — The anihpj EKS Bootstrap

This is the Terraform code that bootstraps the anihpj platform. Terraform creates the foundational infrastructure (VPC, EKS, IAM roles). Once the cluster is running, Crossplane takes over Day 2 management from inside the cluster:

🏗️ HCL (Terraform)main.tf — anihpj EKS Bootstrap (what Terraform does best)
# ─── TERRAFORM: BOOTSTRAP THE PLATFORM ───
# Terraform creates the foundational infrastructure.
# Once the cluster exists, Crossplane manages everything inside.

# VPC — the network foundation
resource "aws_vpc" "anihpj" {
  cidr_block           = "10.0.0.0/16"
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  tags = { Name = "anihpj-vpc", Environment = "production" }
}

# EKS Cluster — the K8s control plane
resource "aws_eks_cluster" "anihpj" {
  name     = "anihpj-prod"
  role_arn = aws_iam_role.eks_cluster.arn
  version  = "1.29"

  vpc_config {
    subnet_ids = [aws_subnet.private_a.id, aws_subnet.private_b.id]
  }
}

# IAM Role for Crossplane (IRSA)
resource "aws_iam_role" "crossplane" {
  name = "crossplane-irsa-role"
  assume_role_policy = jsonencode({
    Version = "2012-10-17"
    Statement = [{
      Effect = "Allow"
      Principal = {
        Federated = aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.eks.arn
      }
      Action = "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"
      Condition = {
        StringEquals = {
          "oidc.eks.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/id/XXX:sub" =
            "system:serviceaccount:crossplane-system:provider-aws"
        }
      }
    }]
  })
}

# ─── RESULT ───
# terraform apply creates:
# ✅ VPC (10.0.0.0/16) with public + private subnets
# ✅ EKS Cluster (v1.29) with managed node groups
# ✅ IAM Role for Crossplane (IRSA — no static credentials)
# ✅ Security Groups, Route Tables, NAT Gateways
#
# After this: Crossplane runs INSIDE the cluster.
# Terraform's job is DONE. Crossplane takes over Day 2.
# This is the CNPA bootstrap pattern.

19.2 Crossplane — Kubernetes-Native Infrastructure

CROSSPLANE MODEL — Platform APIs for Infrastructure
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DEVELOPER (Claim)              PLATFORM TEAM (XRD)             │
  │  "I want a 20Gi PostgreSQL DB"  XRD: PostgreSQLInstance         │
  │       │                         Fields: engine, size, version    │
  │       ▼                         Composition maps to:             │
  │  Crossplane provisions →        • RDS Instance                  │
  │  AWS RDS PostgreSQL (20Gi)      • Subnet Group                  │
  │                                 • Security Group                │
  │                                 • IAM Role                      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Crossplane Architecture Deep Dive — Providers, Managed Resources, and the Reconciliation Engine

Crossplane isn't just "Terraform in K8s" — it's a complete reimagining of infrastructure management using the K8s controller pattern. Understanding the architecture explains WHY it integrates seamlessly with GitOps, WHY it continuously reconciles, and WHERE it fits in the platform:

CROSSPLANE ARCHITECTURE — How Providers Work Inside K8s
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    CROSSPLANE CONTROL PLANE                       │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  CROSSPLANE CORE (crossplane pod)                         │  │
  │  │  • XRD Controller: Watches XRDs → creates XR resources   │  │
  │  │  • Composition Controller: Watches Compositions           │  │
  │  │  • Claim Controller: Watches Claims → creates XRs        │  │
  │  │  • Package Manager: Installs/upgrades Providers          │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                              │                                   │
  │              ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐                  │
  │              ▼               ▼               ▼                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐   │
  │  │ PROVIDER-AWS     │ │ PROVIDER-GCP │ │ PROVIDER-AZURE   │   │
  │  │ (separate pod)   │ │ (separate    │ │ (separate pod)   │   │
  │  │                  │ │  pod)        │ │                  │   │
  │  │ • RDS Controller │ │ • CloudSQL   │ │ • PostgreSQL     │   │
  │  │ • S3 Controller  │ │   Controller │ │   Controller     │   │
  │  │ • EKS Controller │ │ • GKE Ctrl   │ │ • AKS Controller │   │
  │  │ • IAM Controller │ │ • ...        │ │ • ...            │   │
  │  └────────┬─────────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └────────┬─────────┘   │
  │           │                  │                   │              │
  │           ▼                  ▼                   ▼              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  CLOUD APIs (AWS / GCP / Azure)                          │  │
  │  │  Each Provider's controllers call cloud APIs to create,  │  │
  │  │  update, delete, and READ (drift detection) resources.   │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  HOW RECONCILIATION WORKS:                                       │
  │  1. Developer creates a Claim ("I want PostgreSQL")             │
  │  2. Claim Controller creates an XR (Composite Resource)         │
  │  3. Composition Controller matches XR to Composition → creates  │
  │     Managed Resources (MRs): RDSInstance, SubnetGroup, etc.     │
  │  4. Provider-AWS controllers watch their MRs → reconcile:       │
  │     Observe (call AWS API) → Diff → Act (create/update/delete)  │
  │  5. Provider updates MR.status with cloud resource state        │
  │  6. Composition Controller aggregates MR status → XR status     │
  │  7. Claim Controller propagates XR status → Claim status        │
  │  8. Developer sees: Claim.status.ready = true ✅                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

19.3 Crossplane Providers — AWS, GCP, Azure

Crossplane uses Providers to connect to cloud APIs. Each provider (provider-aws, provider-gcp, provider-azure) installs CRDs for that cloud's resources. ProviderConfig stores credentials (via IAM Roles or Service Accounts). Managed Resources are the individual cloud resources — RDSInstance, S3Bucket, EKSCluster — each represented as a K8s CRD.

ProviderConfig — How Crossplane Authenticates to AWS

The ProviderConfig is the SINGLE place where cloud credentials are configured. Every Managed Resource references a ProviderConfig — credentials are centralized, not duplicated across hundreds of resources:

☁️ YAMLProviderConfig — AWS IRSA (IAM Role for Service Account)
# ─── STEP 1: Create ProviderConfig (credentials ONCE) ───
apiVersion: aws.upbound.io/v1beta1
kind: ProviderConfig
metadata:
  name: anihpj-aws-production
spec:
  # IRSA: No static credentials. Pod assumes IAM role via STS.
  credentials:
    source: IRSA
    # Crossplane's ServiceAccount MUST be annotated:
    # eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/crossplane
  region: us-east-1

# ─── STEP 2: Every Managed Resource references THIS ProviderConfig ───
apiVersion: rds.aws.upbound.io/v1beta1
kind: Instance
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
spec:
  providerConfigRef:
    name: anihpj-aws-production  # ← References the ProviderConfig above
  forProvider:
    engine: postgres
    engineVersion: "15.4"
    allocatedStorage: 20
    instanceClass: db.t3.micro

# ─── ALTERNATIVE: Static credentials (less secure, for testing) ───
apiVersion: aws.upbound.io/v1beta1
kind: ProviderConfig
metadata:
  name: anihpj-aws-dev
spec:
  credentials:
    source: Secret
    secretRef:
      namespace: crossplane-system
      name: aws-credentials
      key: credentials  # Contains: [default]\naws_access_key_id=...\n...

Provider Architecture — How a Provider CRD Becomes a Cloud Resource

PROVIDER RECONCILIATION — From K8s CRD to Cloud API Call
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PROVIDER RECONCILIATION FLOW (example: provider-aws)            │
  │                                                                  │
  │  1. Platform team / Crossplane Composition creates an MR:        │
  │     apiVersion: rds.aws.upbound.io/v1beta1                      │
  │     kind: Instance  (a Managed Resource CRD)                     │
  │     spec: { engine: postgres, size: 20 }                        │
  │       │                                                          │
  │  2. Provider-AWS controller WATCH detects new Instance          │
  │       │                                                          │
  │  3. Reconcile:                                                   │
  │     ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │     │  OBSERVE: Call AWS API DescribeDBInstances              │ │
  │     │  → "No RDS instance named anihpj-db exists"             │ │
  │     │                                                          │ │
  │     │  DIFF: Desired (Instance CRD) vs Actual (AWS API)       │ │
  │     │  → "Need to CREATE RDS instance"                        │ │
  │     │                                                          │ │
  │     │  ACT: Call AWS API CreateDBInstance(                     │ │
  │     │    engine=postgres,                                      │ │
  │     │    allocatedStorage=20,                                  │ │
  │     │    instanceClass=db.t3.micro                             │ │
  │     │  )                                                       │ │
  │     │                                                          │ │
  │     │  UPDATE STATUS:                                          │ │
  │     │  Instance.status.atProvider.state = "creating"          │ │
  │     │  Instance.status.atProvider.arn = "arn:aws:rds:..."    │ │
  │     └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                  │
  │  4. Next reconcile (30s later):                                  │
  │     OBSERVE: DescribeDBInstances → state = "available" ✅       │
  │     DIFF: No diff — resource exists and matches spec             │
  │     ACT: No-op (idempotent)                                      │
  │     UPDATE STATUS: Instance.status.atProvider.state = "available"│
  │                                                                  │
  │  KEY INSIGHT: Each Provider is just a K8s controller that        │
  │  translates CRD spec ↔ cloud API calls. Same Observe→Diff→Act   │
  │  pattern. Same idempotency. Same level-triggered design.         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

19.4 Crossplane Compositions & XRD — Your Platform API

XRD (Composite Resource Definition) defines YOUR platform's resource types — "PostgreSQLInstance", "CacheCluster", "MessageQueue". Composition defines how each XRD maps to actual cloud resources. An XRD "PostgreSQLInstance" with fields (engine, size, encrypted) maps via Composition to 4-5 AWS resources. Developers create Claims (simple requests). Crossplane reconciles them into real infrastructure.

The Three Layers in Code — XRD, Composition, Claim

The Crossplane model has three layers. Each is a separate YAML file maintained by different teams. Understanding the separation of concerns is the key CNPA concept:

🏛️ YAMLLayer 1: XRD — Platform Team Defines the API Schema
# ─── LAYER 1: XRD (Platform Team) ───
# Defines: WHAT fields does our PostgreSQL API have?
apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1
kind: CompositeResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: xpostgresqlinstances.anihpj.io
spec:
  group: anihpj.io
  names:
    kind: XPostgreSQLInstance
    plural: xpostgresqlinstances
  claimNames:
    kind: PostgreSQL      # ← What developers create
    plural: postgresqls
  versions:
  - name: v1alpha1
    served: true
    referenceable: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            properties:
              engineVersion:
                type: string
                enum: ["14.8", "15.4", "16.1"]
              size:
                type: string
                pattern: "^[0-9]+Gi$"
                default: "20Gi"
              encrypted:
                type: boolean
                default: true
            required: ["engineVersion"]
    # Result: Developers see a SIMPLE API:
    # engineVersion: "15.4", size: "20Gi", encrypted: true
🔄 YAMLLayer 3: Claim — Developer Requests Infrastructure (THIS is what devs write)
# ─── LAYER 3: CLAIM (Developer) ───
# The ONLY YAML a developer writes. Everything else is platform.
apiVersion: anihpj.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgreSQL
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod-db
  namespace: production
spec:
  engineVersion: "15.4"
  size: "50Gi"
  encrypted: true

# ─── RESULT (CROSSPLANE RECONCILES) ───
# kubectl apply -f claim.yaml
#   ↓
# Crossplane:
#   1. Reads Claim → finds matching XRD (XPostgreSQLInstance)
#   2. Creates XR (Composite Resource) from XRD schema
#   3. Finds matching Composition (postgresql.anihpj.io)
#   4. Composition patches XR fields → Managed Resources:
#      • RDS Instance (engine=postgres, version=15.4, size=50)
#      • Subnet Group (auto-discovered by label)
#      • Security Group (with encryption policy)
#   5. Provider-AWS controller reconciles MRs → actual AWS resources
#   6. Status propagates back: Claim.status.ready = true ✅
#
# Developer experience: "I wanted a 50Gi PostgreSQL. I got one."
# Developer NEVER sees: RDSInstance, SubnetGroup, Composition, patches.

19.5 Cluster API (CAPI) — Managing K8s with K8s

Cluster API uses K8s to manage the lifecycle of K8s clusters. Define a Cluster CRD → CAPI provisions VMs, installs K8s, configures networking. Infrastructure providers (AWS, GCP, Azure, vSphere, Docker) handle the cloud-specific details. The result: "clusters as cattle" — spin up, scale, upgrade, and delete clusters declaratively.

CAPI in Code — The Cluster and Machine CRDs

Here's what a platform engineer writes to create a production K8s cluster. CAPI controllers reconcile these CRDs into actual VMs and K8s installations:

☸️ YAMLCAPI — Cluster + MachineDeployment + KubeadmControlPlane
# ─── CLUSTER: The top-level resource ───
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
spec:
  clusterNetwork:
    pods:
      cidrBlocks: ["192.168.0.0/16"]
    services:
      cidrBlocks: ["10.96.0.0/12"]
  controlPlaneRef:
    apiVersion: controlplane.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
    kind: KubeadmControlPlane
    name: anihpj-prod-cp
  infrastructureRef:
    apiVersion: infrastructure.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
    kind: AWSManagedCluster
    name: anihpj-prod-aws

---
# ─── CONTROL PLANE: 3 nodes, K8s v1.29 ───
apiVersion: controlplane.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeadmControlPlane
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod-cp
spec:
  replicas: 3
  version: v1.29.0
  machineTemplate:
    infrastructureRef:
      apiVersion: infrastructure.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
      kind: AWSMachineTemplate
      name: anihpj-prod-cp-machine

---
# ─── WORKER NODES: 5 nodes, auto-scaling ───
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: MachineDeployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod-workers
spec:
  replicas: 5
  template:
    spec:
      clusterName: anihpj-prod
      version: v1.29.0
      bootstrap:
        configRef:
          apiVersion: bootstrap.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
          kind: KubeadmConfigTemplate
          name: anihpj-prod-workers-config
      infrastructureRef:
        apiVersion: infrastructure.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
        kind: AWSMachineTemplate
        name: anihpj-prod-workers-machine
# ─── RESULT ───
# kubectl apply → CAPI reconciles:
# 1. AWSManagedCluster → creates EKS control plane
# 2. KubeadmControlPlane → 3 managed control plane nodes
# 3. MachineDeployment → 5 worker nodes in Auto Scaling Group
# 4. Cluster becomes Ready → kubeconfig available
#
# Scale workers: kubectl scale machinedeployment anihpj-prod-workers --replicas=10
# Upgrade K8s: change version: v1.30.0 → CAPI rolling upgrades all nodes

CAPI Architecture — The Meta-Cluster Pattern

Cluster API is the meta-K8s: one MANAGEMENT cluster runs CAPI controllers, which provision and manage multiple WORKLOAD clusters. This is the same Operator pattern applied to K8s itself:

CAPI ARCHITECTURE — Management Cluster → Workload Clusters
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MANAGEMENT CLUSTER (runs CAPI)                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  CAPI Controllers:                                        │  │
  │  │  • Cluster Controller: Watches Cluster CRs                │  │
  │  │  • Machine Controller: Watches Machine CRs                │  │
  │  │  • MachineDeployment Controller: Watches MD CRs           │  │
  │  │  • KubeadmControlPlane Controller: Manages CP nodes       │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                              │                                   │
  │     ┌────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐         │
  │     ▼                        ▼                        ▼         │
  │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐     │
  │  │ WORKLOAD     │    │ WORKLOAD     │    │ WORKLOAD     │     │
  │  │ CLUSTER A    │    │ CLUSTER B    │    │ CLUSTER C    │     │
  │  │ (dev)        │    │ (staging)    │    │ (prod)       │     │
  │  │              │    │              │    │              │     │
  │  │ K8s v1.29    │    │ K8s v1.29    │    │ K8s v1.28    │     │
  │  │ 3 CP nodes   │    │ 3 CP nodes   │    │ 5 CP nodes   │     │
  │  │ 5 workers    │    │ 10 workers   │    │ 20 workers   │     │
  │  │ AWS us-east-1│    │ AWS us-west-2│    │ AWS eu-west-1│     │
  │  └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘     │
  │                                                                  │
  │  CAPI RECONCILIATION FOR EACH WORKLOAD CLUSTER:                  │
  │  1. Infrastructure Provider creates VMs (AWS EC2, vSphere)      │
  │  2. Bootstrap Provider installs K8s binaries on VMs             │
  │  3. Control Plane Provider initializes the control plane        │
  │  4. KubeadmControlPlane joins additional CP nodes                │
  │  5. MachineDeployment joins worker nodes to cluster             │
  │  6. Cluster becomes Ready → CAPI updates status                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 CAPI vs Crossplane — Two Different "Infrastructure in K8s" Tools

CAPI manages KUBERNETES CLUSTERS (the platform itself). Crossplane manages CLOUD RESOURCES (databases, caches, buckets — the services running ON the platform). They're complementary: CAPI creates the K8s clusters. Crossplane provisions the resources those clusters need. Together they provide complete infrastructure-as-K8s. The CNPA exam expects you to know when to use each.

Crossplane Composition — How Platform API Maps to Cloud Resources

The Composition is the "translation layer" — it defines exactly how a developer's simple request becomes complex cloud infrastructure. Understanding patches is the key to designing effective platform APIs:

Crossplane Composition — XRD → Cloud Resources
apiVersion: apiextensions.crossplane.io/v1
kind: Composition
metadata:
  name: postgresql.anihpj.io
spec:
  compositeTypeRef:
    apiVersion: anihpj.io/v1
    kind: XPostgreSQLInstance    # The XRD this Composition implements

  resources:
  # ─── PATCH 1: RDS Instance ───
  - name: rds-instance
    base:
      apiVersion: rds.aws.upbound.io/v1beta1
      kind: Instance
      spec:
        forProvider:
          engine: postgres
          engineVersion: "15.4"
          allocatedStorage: 20
          storageEncrypted: true
          instanceClass: db.t3.micro
    patches:
    - fromFieldPath: spec.engineVersion
      toFieldPath: spec.forProvider.engineVersion
      # Developer's XRD field → RDS Instance engineVersion
    - fromFieldPath: spec.size
      toFieldPath: spec.forProvider.allocatedStorage
      transforms:
      - type: string
        string: {type: Regexp, regexp: {group: 1}}
        # "20Gi" → regex extracts "20" → transforms to integer 20

  # ─── PATCH 2: Subnet Group ───
  - name: subnet-group
    base:
      apiVersion: rds.aws.upbound.io/v1beta1
      kind: SubnetGroup
      spec:
        forProvider:
          region: us-east-1
          subnetIdSelector:
            matchLabels:
              network.anihpj.io/type: private
              # Auto-discovers private subnets by label

  # RESULT: One XRD "PostgreSQLInstance" → 2+ AWS resources.
  # Developer only fills: engineVersion, size.
  # Platform team designed the Composition — hidden complexity.

Terraform vs Crossplane — When to Use Which

Decision FactorTerraformCrossplane
Runs where?Externally (CLI, CI/CD, Terraform Cloud)Inside K8s as a controller
State managementState file (local/S3/Terraform Cloud)K8s etcd (no separate state file)
ReconciliationManual: terraform plan → applyAutomatic: continuous K8s control loop
Drift detectionterraform plan (on demand)Continuous (every reconcile cycle)
Self-serviceRequires wrapper API/platformNative via Claims (CRDs)
Multi-cloudNative, mature, all providersVia Providers (growing, not as complete)
Best forCluster bootstrap (create EKS), complex multi-resource orchestrationDay 2 management from within K8s, self-service platform APIs
anihpj StrategyTerraform bootstraps the EKS cluster. Crossplane manages everything inside (RDS, ElastiCache, S3, IAM). Together: Terraform creates the platform. Crossplane runs ON the platform.

19.6 Infrastructure Drift Detection

"Someone changed the security group manually in the AWS console." This is drift — reality ≠ desired state. Crossplane (and Terraform) continuously compare actual cloud state against desired state in Git/K8s. Drift is detected, reported, and auto-corrected — the same reconciliation loop that K8s controllers use, applied to cloud infrastructure. If someone opens port 22 on a security group, Crossplane re-closes it within minutes.

Drift Detection Scenario — Manual Console Change vs Crossplane Reconciliation

Here's exactly what happens when someone bypasses the platform and manually edits cloud resources. This is why "never manually edit platform-managed resources" is rule #1:

DRIFT DETECTION & AUTO-CORRECTION — The Timeline
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DRIFT SCENARIO: Operations engineer opens port 22 in AWS       │
  │                 console ("just for debugging")                  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  T+0s:  Crossplane desired state (in K8s CRD):                  │
  │         SecurityGroup.spec.forProvider.ingress = [              │
  │           {port: 5432, protocol: "tcp", cidr: "10.0.0.0/16"}  │
  │         ]                                                        │
  │         Actual AWS state: ingress = [{port: 5432, ...}]         │
  │         → STATE MATCHES. No action.                             │
  │                                                                  │
  │  T+5m:  Operations engineer opens AWS console.                  │
  │         Manually adds SSH rule: {port: 22, cidr: "0.0.0.0/0"} │
  │         AWS state NOW: ingress = [                               │
  │           {port: 5432, ...},                                    │
  │           {port: 22, cidr: "0.0.0.0/0"}  ← DRIFT!             │
  │         ]                                                        │
  │                                                                  │
  │  T+6m:  Crossplane Provider-AWS controller RECONCILE runs:      │
  │         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │         │  OBSERVE: DescribeSecurityGroups API call           │ │
  │         │  → AWS returns: ingress = [port 5432, port 22]     │ │
  │         │                                                      │ │
  │         │  DIFF: Desired (CRD: only port 5432)                │ │
  │         │        vs Actual (AWS: port 5432 AND port 22)       │ │
  │         │        → DRIFT DETECTED! Port 22 should NOT exist.  │ │
  │         │                                                      │ │
  │         │  ACT: UpdateSecurityGroup API call                  │ │
  │         │  → REMOVE port 22. Revert to desired state.         │ │
  │         │                                                      │ │
  │         │  UPDATE STATUS:                                      │ │
  │         │  SecurityGroup.status.conditions = [{               │ │
  │         │    type: "Synced", status: "True",                  │ │
  │         │    message: "Drift detected and corrected:           │ │
  │         │              removed unauthorized port 22"          │ │
  │         │  }]                                                  │ │
  │         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                  │
  │  T+7m:  Operations engineer: "Hey, who closed my SSH port?!"   │
  │         Platform engineer: "Crossplane. The platform manages    │
  │         that security group. Don't edit it manually."           │
  │                                                                  │
  │  KEY INSIGHT: This is the SAME reconciliation loop as K8s.      │
  │  Just like Deployment controller ensures 3 replicas,            │
  │  Crossplane ensures security groups match desired state.        │
  │  Manual changes are DRIFT — and drift gets corrected.           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

19.7 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

APIs Q1 of 10
How does Crossplane differ from Terraform for infrastructure provisioning?
A) Crossplane is faster; Terraform is slower
B) They are identical — both use HCL
C) Crossplane runs INSIDE K8s using CRDs + Controllers (same reconciliation loop). Infrastructure is defined as K8s resources. Terraform runs externally, manages state files, and uses HCL. Crossplane = K8s-native. Terraform = external tool.
D) Crossplane only works with AWS; Terraform is multi-cloud
✅ C — Crossplane = K8s-native CRDs. Terraform = external HCL.

Crossplane runs as a K8s controller. Infrastructure is defined as CRDs (same kubectl workflow). Continuous reconciliation from within the cluster. Terraform runs externally, manages state files (local/S3), and uses HCL. Key difference: Crossplane uses the K8s control loop for infrastructure; Terraform uses plan/apply lifecycle. Crossplane integrates natively with GitOps (ArgoCD).

APIs Q2 of 10
What is the relationship between XRD, Composition, and Claim in Crossplane?
A) XRD = defines YOUR platform API schema (PostgreSQLInstance with fields). Composition = maps YOUR API to cloud resources (XRD→RDS+Subnet+SG). Claim = developer request ("I want a 20Gi PostgreSQL"). Three layers: Platform API → Mapping → Developer Request.
B) They are three names for the same thing
C) XRD = developer request, Composition = cloud, Claim = platform
D) All three are optional; Crossplane works without them
✅ A — XRD (API) + Composition (Mapping) + Claim (Request)

Three-layer model: (1) Platform team defines XRD — the simplified API developers see (fields: engine, size, version). (2) Platform team defines Composition — how the XRD maps to 4-5 cloud resources behind the scenes. (3) Developer creates a Claim — "I want a PostgreSQL, 20Gi, encrypted." Crossplane reconciles: Claim → XRD → Composition → Provider resources → actual cloud infrastructure.

APIs Q3 of 10
How does Crossplane authenticate to AWS to provision resources?
A) Crossplane embeds AWS credentials in its configuration
B) ProviderConfig stores credentials (IRSA — IAM Role for Service Account, or static keys). Crossplane's controller assumes the IAM role and calls AWS APIs. No credentials in CRDs. Uses K8s Secrets for credential storage.
C) Crossplane doesn't need AWS credentials — it uses a built-in connection
D) Each CRD contains its own AWS credentials
✅ B — ProviderConfig with IRSA or static credentials

ProviderConfig references a K8s Secret containing AWS credentials (or uses IRSA for pod-level IAM roles). Crossplane's provider-aws controller uses these credentials to call AWS APIs. Credentials are stored ONCE in ProviderConfig, not in every resource. Best practice: use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) — ties the IAM role to Crossplane's ServiceAccount, no static keys needed.

APIs Q4 of 10
What is Cluster API (CAPI)?
A) A Kubernetes API for managing container images
B) A tool for managing API versions
C) A CRD for cluster-level RBAC
D) A K8s project that uses K8s to manage K8s clusters. Define a Cluster CRD → CAPI provisions VMs, installs K8s. "Clusters as cattle" — declarative lifecycle management of K8s clusters themselves.
✅ D — K8s managing K8s clusters

Cluster API is the meta-K8s: use one management cluster to provision and manage multiple workload clusters. Define Cluster + Machine + MachineDeployment CRDs. CAPI controllers provision VMs (via infrastructure providers: AWS, GCP, Azure, vSphere), bootstrap K8s on them, and join them to the cluster. Scale up: change replicas. Upgrade: change K8s version. Delete: kubectl delete cluster. Declarative cluster lifecycle.

APIs Q5 of 10
Someone manually changes an AWS security group that Crossplane manages. What happens?
A) Drift detection: Crossplane's controller continuously reconciles. It detects the security group doesn't match the desired state in the CRD → REVERTS the manual change. The security group returns to the desired state within minutes.
B) Crossplane accepts the manual change as the new desired state
C) Crossplane sends an alert but doesn't change anything
D) Crossplane deletes and recreates the entire infrastructure stack
✅ A — Drift detected → auto-corrected (reconciliation loop)

Crossplane uses the SAME reconciliation loop as K8s controllers. It continuously compares the actual cloud state (via AWS API) with the desired state (in the CRD). Drift detected → Crossplane updates the cloud resource to match. This is the same self-healing pattern as a Deployment controller ensuring 3 replicas exist. Never manually edit Crossplane-managed resources — the controller will revert your changes.

APIs Q6 of 10
Terraform vs Crossplane — when should anihpj use which?
A) Always Terraform — Crossplane is experimental
B) Always Crossplane — Terraform is legacy
C) Terraform for BOOTSTRAP (create the EKS cluster). Crossplane for DAY 2 (provision RDS, S3, IAM from WITHIN the cluster). Both have their place. Crossplane excels at K8s-native, GitOps-integrated provisioning. Terraform excels at initial cluster creation and multi-cloud orchestration.
D) Never use either — provision everything manually
✅ C — Terraform for bootstrap; Crossplane for Day 2

Common pattern: Terraform creates the EKS cluster (bootstrap). Crossplane runs INSIDE the cluster and manages Day 2 resources (RDS, S3, IAM, ElastiCache). Why? Crossplane integrates natively with GitOps (ArgoCD syncs infrastructure CRDs). Crossplane uses the K8s reconciliation loop for continuous drift correction. But Crossplane needs a K8s cluster to run on — hence Terraform for initial cluster creation.

APIs Q7 of 10
What's the security advantage of Crossplane's ProviderConfig with IRSA?
A) IRSA is faster than static credentials
B) NO static AWS credentials. Crossplane's ServiceAccount is annotated with an IAM Role ARN. AWS STS issues temporary, auto-rotating credentials. If the pod is compromised, creds expire in 1 hour. No keys to steal or rotate.
C) IRSA encrypts all API calls
D) IRSA requires MFA for every API call
✅ B — IRSA = temporary, auto-rotating credentials, no static keys

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) ties an AWS IAM Role to a K8s ServiceAccount. Crossplane's controller pod assumes this role via AWS STS. Credentials are: (1) Temporary (1 hour expiry). (2) Auto-rotated (STS refreshes before expiry). (3) Pod-scoped (only Crossplane pods get them). (4) No static keys stored anywhere. This is the CNPA-recommended pattern for Crossplane authentication. Equivalent to OIDC for CI/CD pipelines.

APIs Q8 of 10
Crossplane XRD Composition patches: how do you map a developer's "size: 20Gi" to an RDS instance?
A) Composition uses patch transforms: take spec.size from the XRD, transform it (e.g., "20Gi" → allocatedStorage: 20), and patch it into the RDSInstance resource. Compositions are templates that map platform API fields to provider resource fields.
B) The developer writes raw RDS YAML
C) Crossplane auto-generates the mapping
D) Each size requires a separate Composition
✅ A — Composition patches map XRD fields to provider fields

Composition defines how platform API fields become cloud resource configs. Patches can: (1) Copy values directly (spec.size → allocatedStorage). (2) Transform values (map "small" → 20, "medium" → 100). (3) Generate values (generate a random password for the DB). (4) Combine multiple fields (engine + version → DBInstanceClass). Compositions are the "translation layer" between developer-friendly APIs and complex cloud resource configs.

APIs Q9 of 10
How does GitOps work with Crossplane?
A) Crossplane cannot be used with GitOps
B) Crossplane requires a separate GitOps tool
C) GitOps is optional for Crossplane
D) Crossplane CRDs (XRD, Composition, Claim, Managed Resources) are regular K8s resources. Store them in Git. ArgoCD syncs them to the cluster. Crossplane controller reconciles them into cloud resources. Git → ArgoCD → Crossplane → Cloud.
✅ D — Git → ArgoCD → Crossplane → Cloud (full GitOps)

Crossplane resources are K8s CRDs — they work natively with GitOps. Store XRD, Composition, and ProviderConfig in Git. ArgoCD syncs to the cluster. Crossplane controller reconciles CRDs into cloud infrastructure. Result: cloud infrastructure managed through the same GitOps pipeline as application deployments. One workflow for everything — infrastructure AND applications.

APIs Q10 of 10
Design the complete infrastructure provisioning strategy for anihpj.
A) Manual AWS console — full control
B) Terraform bootstraps EKS + VPC. Crossplane (running in the cluster) manages Day 2 resources (RDS, ElastiCache, S3, IAM). XRD defines platform APIs (PostgreSQLInstance, CacheCluster). Compositions map to cloud resources. Developer Claims provision infrastructure. All CRDs stored in Git, synced via ArgoCD. Continuous drift detection and auto-correction.
C) Terraform only — manage everything externally
D) Crossplane only — no Terraform needed
✅ B — Terraform bootstrap + Crossplane Day 2 + GitOps

The CNPA infrastructure strategy: (1) Terraform creates the foundational infrastructure (VPC, EKS, IAM roles). This is a one-time bootstrap. (2) Crossplane runs INSIDE the cluster, managing all Day 2 resources. (3) Platform team defines XRD + Composition (the platform API). (4) Developers create Claims (self-service). (5) Everything stored in Git, synced via ArgoCD. (6) Continuous drift detection keeps cloud matching desired state. This combines Terraform's strength (cluster creation) with Crossplane's strengths (K8s-native, GitOps, self-service, drift correction).

📋XRDPlatform API schema. Developer-friendly. Composition maps to cloud resources.
☸️CAPICluster API. K8s managing K8s. Declarative cluster lifecycle.

Chapter 20: The Kubernetes Operator Pattern — Codifying Operations

An Operator is software that encodes human operational knowledge into code. A DBA knows how to provision, configure, backup, and failover a PostgreSQL database. An Operator automates all of that — watching a CRD for desired state and running reconciliation loops to achieve it. This chapter covers the Operator pattern end-to-end: CRD + Controller = Operator, Day 0/1/2 capabilities, SDK frameworks (Kubebuilder, Kopf, Operator SDK), OLM for lifecycle management, and best practices — building the anihpj JobBoard Operator that deploys the entire stack from a single custom resource.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🤖 Operators🎯 Domain 4: 12%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Operator Pattern — CRD + Custom Controller = Operator. One custom resource deploys the entire stack
  • ✅ Operator Capabilities — Day 0 (install), Day 1 (configure), Day 2 (backup, restore, scale, failover)
  • ✅ Operator SDKs — Kubebuilder (Go), Kopf (Python), Operator SDK (Go/Helm/Ansible)
  • ✅ OLM — Operator Lifecycle Manager. Install, upgrade, dependency management for operators
  • ✅ Best Practices — Idempotent reconciler, status conditions, finalizers, owner references, error handling

20.1 What is a Kubernetes Operator? — CRD + Controller

OPERATOR PATTERN — anihpj JobBoard Operator
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kubectl apply -f jobboard.yaml                                 │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────▼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  JobBoard CRD: name=anihpj-jobpost, replicas=3, db=20Gi │   │
  │  └────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                       │                                        │
  │  ┌────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  anihpj OPERATOR (Custom Controller)                    │   │
  │  │  Reconcile creates:                                     │   │
  │  │    ✅ Deployment (3 replicas)  ✅ Ingress (TLS)          │   │
  │  │    ✅ Service (ClusterIP)       ✅ NetworkPolicy         │   │
  │  │    ✅ PVC (20Gi)                ✅ ServiceMonitor         │   │
  │  │    ✅ ConfigMap                  ✅ Secret (ESO)           │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │  ONE kubectl apply → Operator handles EIGHT resources           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What the Developer Actually Writes — The JobBoard CR

The beauty of the Operator pattern: the developer writes a SIMPLE YAML file with their intent. The Operator handles ALL the complexity behind the scenes. This is the "platform as a product" philosophy in action — hide complexity, expose simplicity:

📋 YAMLjobboard.yaml — What the Developer Creates (ONE resource)
# ─── DEVELOPER WRITES THIS (20 lines) ───
apiVersion: anihpj.io/v1
kind: JobBoard
metadata:
  name: anihpj-jobpost
  namespace: production
spec:
  # Application config
  image: anihpj/jobpost:v2.4.1
  replicas: 3
  domain: jobpost.anihpj.io

  # Database config (Crossplane Claim)
  database:
    engine: postgres
    version: "15.4"
    size: 20Gi
    encrypted: true

  # Redis cache config
  cache:
    size: 5Gi

  # Django settings
  django:
    debug: false
    workers: 4
    allowedHosts: ["jobpost.anihpj.io"]

# ─── OPERATOR AUTOMATICALLY CREATES (200+ lines total) ───
# ✅ Deployment (anihpj-jobpost, 3 replicas)
# ✅ Service (ClusterIP :8000)
# ✅ Ingress (jobpost.anihpj.io, TLS via cert-manager)
# ✅ PVC (20Gi for PostgreSQL)
# ✅ NetworkPolicy (web→api→db)
# ✅ ServiceMonitor (Prometheus scraping)
# ✅ ConfigMap (Django settings from spec.django)
# ✅ Secret (DB password, synced via External Secrets Operator)

# The developer NEVER writes Deployment YAML.
# The developer NEVER configures Ingress.
# The developer NEVER sets up monitoring.
# ONE kubectl apply = production-ready in minutes.
# THIS is the Operator pattern. THIS is platform engineering.

Operator Reconciliation — Pseudocode of the Infinite Loop

Every operator, regardless of language or SDK, runs the same fundamental algorithm. Here's the pseudocode that captures the essence of EVERY K8s controller — from the built-in Deployment controller to your custom anihpj JobBoard operator:

🔄 PseudocodeThe Universal Operator Reconciliation Loop
# ─── THE UNIVERSAL OPERATOR LOOP (Pseudocode) ───
# Every operator framework (Kubebuilder, Kopf, Operator SDK)
# implements this EXACT pattern.

while True:  # This loop NEVER exits. It runs forever.

    # 1. WATCH for changes (via informer + work queue)
    # The framework handles WATCH automatically.
    # You just wait for the next reconcile request.
    request = work_queue.get()  # Blocks until something changes

    # 2. GET the custom resource (from IN-MEMORY CACHE)
    # This is a LOCAL read — sub-millisecond. No API call.
    cr = cache.get(request.namespace, request.name)

    # 3. CHECK if the resource still exists
    if cr is None:
        # Resource was deleted. Finalizer cleanup already happened.
        continue  # Nothing to reconcile

    # 4. OBSERVE current state (what EXISTS in the cluster)
    current_deployment = cache.get_deployment(cr.name)
    current_service = cache.get_service(cr.name)
    current_pvc = cache.get_pvc(cr.name)

    # 5. COMPUTE desired state (what the CR SPEC says)
    desired_deployment = build_deployment_from_cr(cr.spec)
    desired_service = build_service_from_cr(cr.spec)
    desired_pvc = build_pvc_from_cr(cr.spec)

    # 6. DIFF — compare current vs desired
    actions = []
    if current_deployment != desired_deployment:
        actions.append(("UPDATE", "Deployment", desired_deployment))
    if current_service is None:
        actions.append(("CREATE", "Service", desired_service))
    if current_pvc and current_pvc.size < desired_pvc.size:
        actions.append(("UPDATE", "PVC", desired_pvc))  # Expand

    # 7. ACT — execute the actions
    try:
        for action, kind, obj in actions:
            if action == "CREATE":
                api.create(kind, obj)  # API call — WRITE
            elif action == "UPDATE":
                api.update(kind, obj)  # API call — WRITE
            elif action == "DELETE":
                api.delete(kind, obj)  # API call — WRITE

        # 8. UPDATE STATUS — report what happened
        cr.status.phase = "Ready"
        cr.status.conditions = [
            {"type": "Available", "status": "True"},
            {"type": "Progressing", "status": "False"}
        ]
        api.update_status(cr)  # API call — WRITE to /status

    except ApiError as e:
        # 9. ERROR — requeue with backoff
        cr.status.phase = "Degraded"
        cr.status.conditions = [
            {"type": "Degraded", "status": "True",
             "message": str(e)}
        ]
        api.update_status(cr)
        work_queue.requeue(request, delay=backoff.next())
        # Exponential backoff: 1s → 2s → 4s → 8s → ... → max

# KEY PROPERTIES OF THIS LOOP:
# • IDEMPOTENT: Running 100 times = same result. No side effects.
# • LEVEL-TRIGGERED: Checks CURRENT state, not events.
# • CRASH-SAFE: On restart, re-reads full state from cache.
# • DECLARATIVE: "Ensure this state exists" not "Create this."

20.2 Operator Capabilities — Day 0, Day 1, Day 2

🚀
Day 0: Install/Create

Provision everything from scratch. Create Deployment, Service, Ingress, PVC, ConfigMap, Secrets. "One kubectl apply → production-ready stack."

⚙️
Day 1: Configure/Update

Rolling upgrade to new version. Scale replicas up/down. Change configuration. Update resource limits. "kubectl edit jobboard → change replicas → Operator rolling updates."

🔧
Day 2: Operate/Maintain

Backup, restore, failover, rebalance, monitor. "DB is full → Operator auto-scales PVC. Primary fails → Operator promotes standby."

🗑️
Day N: Deprovision

Delete the CR → Operator cleans up ALL child resources via Owner References + Finalizers. No orphaned cloud resources.

Operator Capability Levels — From Basic to Autonomous

The Operator SDK defines 5 capability levels. The CNPA exam expects you to know what each level means and where most operators in the ecosystem fall:

LevelNameCapabilitiesExample
Level IBasic InstallDay 0 only. CRD → creates Deployment, Service, PVC. No upgrades, no backups.Most Helm-based operators. Simple stateless app operators.
Level IISeamless UpgradesDay 0 + Day 1. Rolling upgrades, version tracking, configuration updates.Prometheus Operator (upgrades Prometheus version). cert-manager.
Level IIIFull LifecycleDay 0 + Day 1 + Day 2. Backup, restore, failover. Handles storage.Postgres Operator (Zalando/CloudNativePG). Strimzi (Kafka).
Level IVDeep InsightsLevel III + metrics, alerts, dashboards. Proactive monitoring. Auto-scaling based on metrics.Prometheus Operator (with Thanos integration). Elasticsearch Operator.
Level VAutonomousLevel IV + auto-pilot. Self-tuning, self-healing, self-optimizing. No human intervention needed.Rare. The goalpost. Most real operators are Level II-III.
💡 The CNPA Operator Maturity Insight

Most operators in the CNCF ecosystem are Level II-III. The anihpj JobBoard Operator targets Level II (Day 0 + Day 1 — it creates the stack and handles rolling upgrades). Level V operators are rare because they require domain-specific ML models and years of operational data. The exam expects you to know: (1) What each level means. (2) That most operators are Level II-III. (3) That Level V is the vision but not the reality. (4) That even a Level I operator adds value by eliminating manual installation toil.

20.3 Operator SDK Frameworks — Choosing Your Tool

FrameworkLanguageBest For
KubebuilderGoProduction operators. Used by K8s SIGs. Full-featured. The CNPA standard.
Operator SDKGo/Helm/AnsibleRed Hat's framework. Helm-based operators for simple config. Ansible for infra.
KopfPythonPython teams (like anihpj). Rapid prototyping. Less boilerplate than Go.
Java Operator SDKJavaJVM-based platforms. Quarkus/Spring integration.

Kopf Operator Example — Pythonic Reconciliation

Below is a Kopf (Kubernetes Operator Pythonic Framework) operator for the anihpj JobBoard. It watches JobBoard CRDs and reconciles them by creating Deployments, Services, and PVCs — all in Python, the same language as the Django application:

🐍 Python (Kopf Operator)jobboard_operator.py — anihpj JobBoard Operator
import kopf
import kubernetes
import yaml

# ─── ON CREATE/UPDATE: Reconcile JobBoard CR ───
@kopf.on.create('anihpj.io', 'v1', 'jobboards')
@kopf.on.resume('anihpj.io', 'v1', 'jobboards')
def reconcile_jobboard(spec, status, namespace, logger, **kwargs):
    """Reconcile a JobBoard CR into Deployment + Service + PVC + Ingress."""
    replicas = spec.get('replicas', 3)
    image = spec.get('image', 'anihpj/jobpost:latest')
    storage = spec.get('storage', '20Gi')

    # 1. Create PersistentVolumeClaim for Django media
    api = kubernetes.client.CoreV1Api()
    pvc = api.create_namespaced_persistent_volume_claim(
        namespace=namespace,
        body=kubernetes.client.V1PersistentVolumeClaim(
            metadata=kubernetes.client.V1ObjectMeta(
                name=f"jobboard-{spec['name']}-media"),
            spec=kubernetes.client.V1PersistentVolumeClaimSpec(
                access_modes=["ReadWriteOnce"],
                resources=kubernetes.client.V1ResourceRequirements(
                    requests={"storage": storage})
            )
        )
    )

    # 2. Create Deployment with Django app
    apps_api = kubernetes.client.AppsV1Api()
    deployment = apps_api.create_namespaced_deployment(
        namespace=namespace,
        body=kubernetes.client.V1Deployment(
            metadata=kubernetes.client.V1ObjectMeta(
                name=f"jobboard-{spec['name']}"),
            spec=kubernetes.client.V1DeploymentSpec(
                replicas=replicas,
                selector=kubernetes.client.V1LabelSelector(
                    match_labels={"app": spec['name']}),
                template=kubernetes.client.V1PodTemplateSpec(
                    metadata=kubernetes.client.V1ObjectMeta(
                        labels={"app": spec['name']}),
                    spec=kubernetes.client.V1PodSpec(containers=[
                        kubernetes.client.V1Container(
                            name="django",
                            image=image,
                            ports=[kubernetes.client.V1ContainerPort(
                                container_port=8000)],
                            env_from=[kubernetes.client.V1EnvFromSource(
                                secret_ref=kubernetes.client.V1SecretEnvSource(
                                    name=f"jobboard-{spec['name']}-db"))]
                        )
                    ])
                )
            )
        )
    )

    # 3. Create ClusterIP Service
    service = api.create_namespaced_service(
        namespace=namespace,
        body=kubernetes.client.V1Service(
            metadata=kubernetes.client.V1ObjectMeta(
                name=f"jobboard-{spec['name']}-svc"),
            spec=kubernetes.client.V1ServiceSpec(
                selector={"app": spec['name']},
                ports=[kubernetes.client.V1ServicePort(port=80, target_port=8000)]
            )
        )
    )

    # 4. Update status with created resources
    return {
        'deployment': deployment.metadata.name,
        'service': service.metadata.name,
        'pvc': pvc.metadata.name,
        'availableReplicas': 0  # Will update after pod ready
    }


# ─── ON DELETE: Cleanup hook ───
@kopf.on.delete('anihpj.io', 'v1', 'jobboards')
def delete_jobboard(spec, status, namespace, logger, **kwargs):
    """Finalizer: cleanup external resources before CR deletion."""
    logger.info(f"Cleaning up JobBoard: {spec['name']}")
    # Kopf automatically handles finalizer management.
    # The resource won't be removed from K8s until this handler
    # completes successfully — preventing orphaned resources.
    pass


# Kopf runs with: kopf run jobboard_operator.py --verbose
# Installs CRD, starts watch loop, handles reconciliation.
# PYTHONIC — same language as anihpj's Django app.

Helm-Based Operator — When You Don't Need Custom Code

Not every operator needs a custom controller in Go or Python. The Operator SDK supports Helm-based operators — where the "reconciliation logic" is a Helm chart, and the Operator SDK provides the controller wrapper. Ideal for stateless applications that already have a Helm chart:

⛵ YAMLHelm-Based Operator — Simple CRD → Helm Chart Reconciliation
# ─── STEP 1: Create the operator project ───
# operator-sdk init --plugins=helm --domain=anihpj.io
# operator-sdk create api --group=apps --version=v1 --kind=WebApp

# ─── STEP 2: Define the CRD schema (watches.yaml) ───
# The Operator SDK auto-generates a CRD from this + Helm values
apiVersion: anihpj.io/v1
kind: WebApp
metadata:
  name: anihpj-landing
spec:
  image: nginx:1.25
  replicas: 2
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    host: landing.anihpj.io

# ─── STEP 3: The "reconciliation" is a Helm chart ───
# operator-sdk uses the chart in /helm-charts/
# When a WebApp CR is created, the operator:
# 1. Reads CR spec → generates Helm values
# 2. Runs: helm template webapp ./helm-charts/ --values 
# 3. Applies the rendered manifests to the cluster
# 4. Watches for CR changes → re-render + re-apply
# 5. Watches deployed resources → detect drift → re-apply

# ─── WHEN TO USE HELM OPERATORS ───
# ✅ Stateless apps with existing Helm charts
# ✅ Simple Day 0 (install) only — no Day 2 logic needed
# ✅ Team knows Helm but not Go/Python
# ❌ Complex Day 2 operations (backup, failover)
# ❌ Cross-resource orchestration (need custom logic)
# ❌ External resource management (need finalizers)
#
# CNPA Insight: Helm operators are Level I (Basic Install).
# They're great for wrapping existing Helm charts as CRDs.
# For production database operators, use Kubebuilder/Kopf.

20.4 OLM — Operator Lifecycle Manager

OLM manages the lifecycle of Operators themselves — installation, upgrades, dependency resolution, and RBAC. Channels (stable, fast, candidate) control upgrade paths. Approval strategies (Manual vs Automatic) control when upgrades happen. OLM is what makes OperatorHub (OpenShift's marketplace) possible — and it's available for vanilla K8s too.

OLM Architecture — How Dependency Resolution Works

OLM is more than a package manager — it's a constraint solver that ensures Operators can coexist without breaking each other. This is the same problem Linux package managers solve, applied to K8s operators:

OLM ARCHITECTURE — Catalogs, Subscriptions, and Dependency Resolution
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    OLM COMPONENTS                                 │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐                   │
  │  │  CATALOGSOURCE   │    │  SUBSCRIPTION    │                   │
  │  │  (Where to find  │    │  (What to install│                   │
  │  │   operators)     │    │   + which channel│                   │
  │  │                  │    │   + approval)    │                   │
  │  │  Registry image  │    │                  │                   │
  │  │  or OperatorHub  │    │  channel: stable │                   │
  │  │  API             │    │  approval: Manual│                   │
  │  └────────┬─────────┘    └────────┬─────────┘                   │
  │           │                       │                              │
  │           ▼                       ▼                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  OLM RESOLVER (Constraint Solver)                         │  │
  │  │                                                           │  │
  │  │  "Install Prometheus Operator v0.65"                     │  │
  │  │    ↓                                                       │  │
  │  │  Resolver checks:                                         │  │
  │  │  ✅ Prometheus Operator v0.65 exists in Catalog?          │  │
  │  │  ✅ Depends on: ServiceMonitor CRD v1 (included)          │  │
  │  │  ✅ Depends on: PrometheusRule CRD v1 (included)          │  │
  │  │  ✅ No conflict with existing operators                   │  │
  │  │  ✅ K8s version compatible (>=1.25)                       │  │
  │  │    ↓                                                       │  │
  │  │  Resolver creates InstallPlan:                            │  │
  │  │  Step 1: Install CRDs (ServiceMonitor, PrometheusRule)    │  │
  │  │  Step 2: Create ServiceAccount + RBAC                     │  │
  │  │  Step 3: Create Deployment (Prometheus Operator pod)      │  │
  │  │  Step 4: Create ClusterServiceVersion (CSV)               │  │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  CHANNELS:                    APPROVAL STRATEGIES:               │
  │  ┌──────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐           │
  │  │ stable  → v1 │            │ Manual: Human approves│           │
  │  │ fast    → v2 │            │ each upgrade. Safe    │           │
  │  │ candidate→v3 │            │ for production.       │           │
  │  └──────────────┘            │ Automatic: OLM auto-  │           │
  │                               │ upgrades within the  │           │
  │  stable = tested, safe        │ channel. Fast updates│           │
  │  fast = new features,         │ for dev environments.│           │
  │         minor risk            └──────────────────────┘           │
  │  candidate = bleeding edge,                                      │
  │              preview features                                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

OLM in Practice — Subscription and OperatorGroup YAML

Installing an operator via OLM requires two resources: a Subscription (what to install) and an OperatorGroup (which namespaces it watches). Here's the actual YAML that installs the Prometheus Operator via OLM:

📦 YAMLOLM — Subscription + OperatorGroup (Installing Prometheus Operator)
# ─── STEP 1: OperatorGroup — which namespaces can this operator manage? ───
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1
kind: OperatorGroup
metadata:
  name: monitoring-operators
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  targetNamespaces:
  - monitoring    # Only manage resources in the monitoring namespace

---
# ─── STEP 2: Subscription — what to install, which channel, approval ───
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata:
  name: prometheus-operator
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  channel: stable           # stable | fast | candidate
  name: prometheus          # Package name in the catalog
  source: community-operators  # Which CatalogSource
  sourceNamespace: olm
  installPlanApproval: Manual  # Manual | Automatic
  # Manual = human approves each upgrade (production safe)
  # Automatic = OLM upgrades automatically within the channel

# ─── RESULT ───
# kubectl apply → OLM:
# 1. Resolves: prometheus operator from community-operators catalog
# 2. Creates InstallPlan (pending approval if Manual)
# 3. kubectl approve installplan-xyz → OLM executes:
#    • Creates ServiceAccount + RBAC for the operator
#    • Installs CRDs: ServiceMonitor, PrometheusRule, PodMonitor
#    • Creates Deployment: prometheus-operator pod
#    • Creates ClusterServiceVersion (CSV) — tracks installed version
# 4. Operator is now running and reconciling ServiceMonitors
#
# UPGRADE:
# • New version appears in stable channel
# • OLM creates new InstallPlan (pending if Manual approval)
# • Approve → OLM rolling-updates the operator Deployment
# • Old CSV replaced with new CSV
#
# CNPA INSIGHT: OLM handles what you'd otherwise script manually:
# RBAC creation, CRD installation, Deployment management, upgrades.
# It's the "operator for operators."

20.5 Operator Best Practices

🔄
Idempotent Reconciler

Run reconcile 100 times = same result. "Ensure resource exists" not "Create resource." No duplicate side effects.

📊
Status Conditions

Report: Available, Progressing, Degraded. Standard K8s condition format. Users and tools rely on these.

🔒
Finalizers

Block deletion until external cleanup completes. Delete cloud DB → THEN remove finalizer → THEN K8s deletes CR.

👨‍👩‍👧
Owner References

Child resources reference parent CR. Parent deleted → K8s garbage collects children automatically.

Error Handling — Retry with Backoff, Never Panic

Operator reconcile functions WILL fail — cloud APIs are temporarily unavailable, resources are being modified by someone else, rate limits are hit. The operator must handle failures gracefully. This is one of the most tested CNPA concepts:

✅ Correct Error Handling
  • Log the error with context (resource name, namespace, what failed)
  • Set Degraded status condition — users and dashboards see the problem
  • Return the error with a requeue — controller-runtime handles backoff
  • Exponential backoff: 1s → 2s → 4s → 8s → 16s → ... → max (e.g., 5 min)
  • Never panic / os.Exit — crashes reset all watches and caches
❌ Wrong Error Handling
  • Panic/Exit: "Cloud API error → log.Fatal" — kills the operator, resets ALL watches. Worst possible response.
  • Silent ignore: "error → return nil" — resource stays broken forever, no status update. Users never know.
  • Delete and recreate: "error → delete resource → create new" — destructive, loses state, may cause data loss.
  • Infinite retry without backoff: "error → retry immediately" — thundering herd, rate limit exhaustion.
📖 How Controller-Runtime Backoff Works

When you return an error from reconcile, the controller-runtime automatically: (1) Re-queues the request after a delay. (2) Uses exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s... up to a configurable max, default ~16 minutes). (3) Resets the backoff on successful reconcile. (4) Rate-limits per-resource (one resource failing doesn't block others). You get this for FREE — just return the error. Don't implement your own retry loop. The work queue handles deduplication, rate-limiting, and fair scheduling. This is the SAME work queue architecture used by built-in K8s controllers.

20.6 Common Operators in the CNCF Ecosystem

📊
Prometheus Operator

CRDs: ServiceMonitor, PrometheusRule, PodMonitor. Auto-discovers scrape targets. Manages Prometheus + Alertmanager.

📜
cert-manager

CRDs: Certificate, Issuer, ClusterIssuer. Auto-provisions and renews TLS certificates from Let's Encrypt.

🐘
Postgres Operator (Zalando/CloudNativePG)

CRDs: PostgreSQL cluster. Auto-provisions, backs up, failover. Full Day 2 operations automated.

📨
Strimzi (Kafka Operator)

CRDs: Kafka, KafkaConnect, KafkaMirrorMaker. Manages Kafka clusters on K8s with full lifecycle automation.

Operators in Code — What Each CRD Looks Like

The Operator pattern manifests differently for each domain, but the pattern is identical: CRD defines intent, Operator reconciles it into reality. Here are the actual CR YAML snippets developers write for each operator:

📊 YAMLPrometheus Operator — ServiceMonitor CR (Developer writes THIS)
# Prometheus Operator: Developer creates a ServiceMonitor
# Operator generates Prometheus scrape config automatically
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-monitor
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api       # Which Service to scrape
  endpoints:
  - port: metrics            # Scrape /metrics on this port
    interval: 30s            # How often
    path: /metrics
  # Result: Prometheus auto-discovers and scrapes anihpj-api.
  # No manual prometheus.yml editing. Declarative monitoring.
📜 YAMLcert-manager — Certificate CR (Auto-TLS)
# cert-manager: Developer creates a Certificate
# Operator auto-provisions TLS from Let's Encrypt and auto-renews
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: anihpj-tls
spec:
  secretName: anihpj-tls-secret   # Where the TLS cert is stored
  dnsNames:
  - jobpost.anihpj.io
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  # Result: cert-manager calls Let's Encrypt API, completes HTTP-01
  # challenge, stores cert in Secret, auto-renews 30 days before expiry.
  # Developer never touches TLS certs manually.
🐘 YAMLCloudNativePG — Cluster CR (Full PostgreSQL Lifecycle)
# CloudNativePG Operator: Developer creates a Cluster
# Operator auto-provisions PostgreSQL with HA, backups, monitoring
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
spec:
  instances: 3              # 3 PostgreSQL instances (1 primary + 2 replicas)
  imageName: ghcr.io/cloudnative-pg/postgresql:15.4
  storage:
    size: 20Gi              # PVC for each instance
  backup:
    barmanObjectStore:      # Automated backups to S3
      destinationPath: s3://anihpj-backups/
  monitoring:
    enablePodMonitor: true  # Auto-creates PodMonitor for Prometheus
  # Result: PostgreSQL cluster with streaming replication, automated
  # failover (primary down → replica promoted in <30s), scheduled
  # backups to S3, and Prometheus metrics. All from THIS YAML.

20.7 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

APIs Q1 of 10
What components make up a Kubernetes Operator?
A) A Deployment and a Service
B) A Helm chart and a values file
C) CRD (Custom Resource Definition — the API extension) + Custom Controller (reconciliation logic — the automation). Together they form an Operator that encodes human operational knowledge into software.
D) A Kubernetes pod and a service account
✅ C — CRD + Custom Controller = Operator

CRD defines the resource type and schema (WHAT you manage). Custom Controller runs the reconciliation loop (HOW you manage it). Together they automate what a human operator would do: provision, configure, backup, scale, failover. The controller watches CRD instances and reconciles them into the desired state by creating/updating/deleting child resources.

APIs Q2 of 10
What are Day 0, Day 1, and Day 2 operations for an Operator?
A) Day 0 = Install/Create (provision everything from scratch). Day 1 = Configure/Update (rolling upgrade, scale, config changes). Day 2 = Operate/Maintain (backup, restore, failover, monitor). A mature Operator handles ALL three.
B) They are development sprints — 3-week cycles
C) Day 0 = Monday, Day 1 = Tuesday, Day 2 = Wednesday
D) They are levels of operator certification
✅ A — Day 0 (create), Day 1 (configure), Day 2 (operate)

Operator Capability Levels: Day 0 = initial provisioning (the "easy" part — kubectl apply works). Day 1 = configuration updates (rolling upgrades, scaling, tuning). Day 2 = ongoing operations (backup, restore, failover, rebalancing, monitoring integration). Most basic operators handle Day 0. Mature operators handle Day 2 — that's where the real value is. A PostgreSQL operator that auto-failovers saves a DBA from 3am pages.

APIs Q3 of 10
Which Operator SDK should anihpj (a Python/Django shop) use?
A) Kubebuilder — it's the most popular
B) Go Operator SDK — it's the standard
C) Helm Operator — it's the simplest
D) Kopf (Python) — Pythonic operator framework. Same language as anihpj's Django app. Rapid prototyping. Less boilerplate than Go. Team can maintain it without learning Go.
✅ D — Kopf for Python teams. Kubebuilder for Go teams.

Choose the SDK based on your team's language: Python team → Kopf. Go team → Kubebuilder. Java team → Java Operator SDK. Ansible team → Ansible Operator SDK. The operator pattern is the same regardless of language — the SDK handles K8s API interactions, CRD generation, and reconciliation loop scaffolding. Use the language your team knows best.

APIs Q4 of 10
Why do operators use finalizers?
A) Finalizers speed up deletion
B) Finalizers prevent K8s from deleting the CR until the controller CLEANS UP external resources first. Without finalizers, deleting a Database CRD would orphan the actual cloud RDS instance — still running, still billing. Finalizers ensure cleanup BEFORE deletion.
C) Finalizers are optional labels
D) Finalizers cache resource state for faster reconciliation
✅ B — Finalizers ensure external cleanup before K8s deletion

When you delete a resource with finalizers, K8s sets deletionTimestamp but does NOT remove it. The controller sees the timestamp, cleans up external resources (deletes cloud DB, DNS entry, storage volume), then removes its finalizer. When ALL finalizers are gone, K8s finally deletes the resource. Finalizers are THE mechanism that prevents orphaned cloud resources. Every operator that manages external resources MUST use finalizers.

APIs Q5 of 10
How do Owner References help operators manage child resources?
A) Owner References are documentation only
B) Owner References control RBAC permissions
C) Child resources (Deployment, Service, PVC) reference the parent CR via ownerReferences. When the parent is deleted, K8s garbage collector AUTO-DELETES all children. No manual cleanup. The controller doesn't need to delete children individually.
D) Owner References speed up reconciliation
✅ C — K8s garbage collector auto-deletes children

Owner References create a parent-child relationship. The child resource's metadata.ownerReferences points to the parent CR's UID. When the parent is deleted, K8s garbage collector finds all resources with that ownerReference and deletes them automatically (cascading deletion). The controller creates children WITH ownerReferences, and K8s handles cleanup. Combined with finalizers for external resources, this gives complete lifecycle management.

APIs Q6 of 10
What status conditions should a mature operator report?
A) Available (True when service is ready), Progressing (True when reconciling/updating), Degraded (True when something is wrong). These are the standard K8s condition types — used by Deployments, used by operators, recognized by tools and dashboards.
B) Started, Running, Stopped
C) Good, Warning, Critical
D) Custom conditions vary per operator — no standards exist
✅ A — Available, Progressing, Degraded (standard conditions)

Standard K8s conditions: Available (service is ready and accepting requests). Progressing (reconciliation in progress — rolling update, scaling). Degraded (something is wrong — pod crashlooping, can't reach API). These map to the colors in kubectl/ArgoCD: Available=green, Progressing=yellow, Degraded=red. Using standard conditions makes your operator's status immediately understandable to anyone familiar with K8s.

APIs Q7 of 10
What does OLM (Operator Lifecycle Manager) do?
A) Manages pod lifecycles
B) Manages container image lifecycles
C) Manages Kubernetes version upgrades
D) Manages OPERATOR lifecycles — installation, upgrades (via channels: stable/fast/candidate), dependency resolution (Operator A requires Operator B v2+), and RBAC. OLM is to Operators what a package manager is to software.
✅ D — OLM = package manager for Operators

OLM manages Operators at scale: (1) Installation from catalogs (OperatorHub). (2) Upgrades via channels (stable, fast, candidate) with Manual or Automatic approval. (3) Dependency resolution — Operator A requires Operator B v2.1+. (4) RBAC generation from Operator metadata. (5) Health monitoring of installed Operators. Without OLM, you manage Operator CRDs, Deployments, RBAC, and upgrades manually. OLM automates all of it.

APIs Q8 of 10
The operator's reconcile function gets an error from the cloud API. What's the CORRECT error handling?
A) Panic and crash — let K8s restart the operator
B) Log the error. Set Degraded status condition with the error message. Return the error with RETRY + BACKOFF. The controller-runtime will re-queue the request with exponential backoff. Never panic — the operator should be resilient to transient failures.
C) Ignore the error — continue to the next resource
D) Delete and recreate the resource
✅ B — Log, set Degraded, requeue with backoff. Never panic.

Correct error handling: (1) Log the error with context. (2) Update status.conditions to Degraded=True with the error message. (3) Return the error with a requeue. The controller-runtime automatically applies exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s... up to a max). This handles transient cloud API failures gracefully. Panicking resets all watches and caches. Ignoring the error means the resource stays in a broken state silently. Deleting the resource is destructive and unnecessary.

APIs Q9 of 10
How does the Prometheus Operator discover which pods to scrape?
A) Prometheus Operator scans all pods automatically
B) Developers annotate their pods with scrape annotations
C) Developers create ServiceMonitor CRDs (or PodMonitor). The Prometheus Operator watches these CRDs and generates Prometheus scrape configurations. NO manual Prometheus config needed. Fully declarative.
D) Prometheus Operator reads Prometheus configuration files
✅ C — ServiceMonitor CRDs → Operator → Prometheus config

The Prometheus Operator pattern: (1) Developer creates a ServiceMonitor CRD referencing their Service. (2) Prometheus Operator watches ServiceMonitor resources. (3) Operator generates Prometheus scrape configuration from the ServiceMonitor. (4) Operator updates Prometheus's config and reloads it. This is the Operator pattern in action: CRD defines intent, Operator reconciles it into reality. No manual Prometheus YAML editing — ever.

APIs Q10 of 10
Design the anihpj JobBoard Operator — what should it do when a developer creates a JobBoard CR?
A) Reconcile creates: Deployment (Django app, 3 replicas) + Service (ClusterIP) + Ingress (TLS via cert-manager) + PVC (20Gi) + NetworkPolicy (web→api→db) + ServiceMonitor (Prometheus) + ConfigMap (Django settings) + Secret (DB password via ESO). Status reports Available/Progressing/Degraded. Finalizers clean up cloud resources before deletion. Owner references ensure cascade delete.
B) Just create a Deployment — the rest is manual
C) Send an email to the platform team to provision manually
D) Create a Jira ticket for the DBA team
✅ A — Full stack from ONE CR: 8 child resources, status, cleanup

The JobBoard Operator automates what would take a platform engineer 30+ minutes: creating 8 interconnected resources, configuring TLS, setting up monitoring, securing with NetworkPolicies, and managing secrets. One kubectl apply → production-ready in minutes. The operator handles Day 2: rolling upgrades when the image tag changes, PVC expansion when storage is full, and cleanup when the JobBoard is deleted. This is the Operator pattern — encoding human operational knowledge into software that runs 24/7 without fatigue.

21Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) Deep Dive
IDPs

21.1 What is an IDP? — The Self-Service Layer

An Internal Developer Platform (IDP) is the layer that sits between developers and infrastructure. Developers shouldn't need to understand K8s Deployments, Helm charts, ingress controllers, or AWS APIs — they should click a button or run a CLI command and get a production-ready service. The IDP is the sum of the platform engineering work — every CRD you built, every GitOps pipeline, every Kyverno policy — unified behind a self-service interface.

📊 IDP COMPONENTS — The Complete Picture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
