26.2 Deployment Frequency — How Often Do You Ship?

Deployment Frequency measures how often code reaches production. Elite performers deploy on-demand (multiple times a day). Low performers deploy once a month or less. The platform directly enables higher deployment frequency by making deployment fast, safe, and automated — no manual approvals, no ticket queues, no fear.

💡 Platform Impact on Deploy Frequency

Before platform: manual deploy process → fear of deployment → infrequent deploys → each deploy is HUGE (50 changes bundled) → high risk of failure → more fear. After platform: automated GitOps (ArgoCD) → deployments are routine → 5x/day deploys → each deploy is SMALL (1-3 changes) → low risk → no fear. The platform breaks the "deploy fear" cycle. Small, frequent deploys are safer than large, infrequent ones.

26.3 Lead Time for Changes — From Commit to Production

Lead Time measures: "How long from code committed to code running in production?" This captures the ENTIRE delivery pipeline: code review → CI build → automated tests → security scan → deployment. The platform optimizes every stage: automated CI, parallelized tests, automated security gates, and GitOps deployment.

0m
Developer Merges PR

Code review approved → merge to main → CI pipeline triggers

8m
CI Pipeline Complete

Build (3m) + Unit tests (2m) + Security scan (2m) + Image push (1m)

10m
ArgoCD Detects Change

Git commit changes K8s manifest → ArgoCD syncs (3 min polling interval)

12m
Deployment Rolls Out

Rolling update: new pods start → health check passes → old pods terminate

15m
Monitoring Confirms Healthy

No error rate spike, latency normal → deployment marked successful → total lead time: 15 minutes

26.4 Mean Time to Recover (MTTR) — How Fast Do You Fix Incidents?

MTTR measures: "From the moment an incident is detected to the moment service is restored." Elite performers recover in under 1 hour. Low performers take a week. The platform reduces MTTR through: automated rollback (ArgoCD one-click revert), AIOps correlation (identifies root cause in seconds), and runbook automation (pre-scripted recovery procedures).

❌ MTTR Without Platform
  • Alert fires → on-call wakes up (5 min)
  • Opens laptop, VPN, 3 dashboards (5 min)
  • Manually correlates: metrics + logs + traces (15 min)
  • Finds root cause: "bad query in v2.4.1" (10 min)
  • Manually reverts: kubectl, helm, or AWS console (10 min)
  • Total MTTR: 45-90 minutes
✅ MTTR With Platform
  • Alert fires with AIOps context: "DB pool exhaustion after v2.4.1 deploy" (0 min)
  • On-call opens Backstage → sees incident + rollback button (1 min)
  • Clicks "Rollback" → ArgoCD reverts to previous commit (2 min)
  • K8s rolling update restores previous version (3 min)
  • Monitoring confirms healthy → Total MTTR: 5-15 minutes

26.5 Change Failure Rate — What % of Deployments Fail?

Change Failure Rate measures the percentage of deployments that cause a failure in production (degraded service, outage, rollback required). Elite performers: 0-15%. Low performers: 46-60%. The platform reduces CFR through: automated testing in CI, Kyverno policy validation (catch anti-patterns before deploy), canary/progressive delivery (blast radius limited), and automated rollback (failures are quickly reverted, minimizing impact).

📖 Small Deploys = Lower CFR

There's a direct correlation: smaller, more frequent deploys have a LOWER failure rate than large, infrequent ones. Why? A deploy with 3 changes is easy to validate and easy to roll back. A deploy with 50 changes is impossible to fully test and catastrophic to roll back. The platform enables small deploys (automated, fast, low-friction), which naturally drives down CFR. Deploy frequency and change failure rate are inversely correlated — as frequency goes UP, failure rate goes DOWN.

26.6 DORA in Practice — Instrumenting Your Platform

DORA metrics aren't theoretical — they should be MEASURED automatically from your platform's data. Every deploy, every incident, every pipeline run generates data that can calculate DORA metrics. Build a DORA dashboard that updates in real-time.

📊
How to Measure Each Metric
  • Deploy Frequency: Count ArgoCD syncs or GitHub Releases per day/week
  • Lead Time: CI pipeline start time → ArgoCD sync complete time. Track in CI metadata.
  • MTTR: PagerDuty incident created → resolved time. Pull from PagerDuty API.
  • Change Failure Rate: (Deploys that triggered rollback or incident) / (Total deploys). Cross-reference ArgoCD rollbacks + PagerDuty incidents.
📈
DORA Dashboard (Grafana)
  • Panel 1: Deploy frequency trend (daily, weekly bar chart)
  • Panel 2: Lead time trend (line chart — should trend DOWN)
  • Panel 3: MTTR trend (line chart — should trend DOWN)
  • Panel 4: Change failure rate (percentage gauge — should stay LOW)
  • Panel 5: Performance tier: ELITE / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW badge

26.7 Continuous Improvement — The DORA Feedback Loop

DORA metrics aren't a one-time measurement — they're a continuous improvement engine. Measure → Analyze → Improve → Repeat. When a metric regresses (MTTR goes from 15 min → 45 min), investigate why, fix the root cause, and watch the metric recover. This is the same reconciliation loop pattern applied to platform performance.

26.8 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Measure Q1 of 10
What are the 4 DORA metrics?
A) CPU, Memory, Disk, Network
B) Uptime, Latency, Error Rate, Throughput
C) Deployment Frequency, Lead Time for Changes, Mean Time to Recover (MTTR), Change Failure Rate (CFR). These 4 metrics measure software delivery performance from Elite (on-demand deploys, <1h lead time) to Low (monthly deploys, 1-6 month lead time).
D) Cost, Speed, Quality, Satisfaction
✅ C — Deploy Frequency, Lead Time, MTTR, Change Failure Rate

The 4 DORA metrics: (1) Deployment Frequency — how often you deploy (Elite: on-demand). (2) Lead Time for Changes — commit to production (Elite: < 1 hour). (3) Mean Time to Recover — incident to resolution (Elite: < 1 hour). (4) Change Failure Rate — % of deploys causing failure (Elite: 0-15%). These four capture the throughput (speed) and stability (quality) of software delivery. Elite performers excel at both — proving speed and stability are complementary, not opposing.

Measure Q2 of 10
How does deployment frequency relate to change failure rate?
A) They are INVERSELY correlated: Elite performers deploy MORE often AND have LOWER failure rates. Small, frequent deploys (3 changes each) are safer than large, infrequent ones (50 changes). More deploys = smaller changes = easier to validate = lower failure rate. Speed ENABLES stability — they're not tradeoffs.
B) Higher frequency always means higher failure rate
C) There is no relationship between them
D) Higher frequency guarantees lower failure rate
✅ A — Inversely correlated: more deploys = smaller changes = lower failure rate

DORA research found that Elite performers (on-demand deploys) have the LOWEST change failure rates (0-15%), while Low performers (monthly deploys) have the HIGHEST failure rates (46-60%). The reason: small batches. A deploy with 3 changes is easy to review, easy to test, easy to roll back. A deploy with 50 changes is impossible to fully validate. The platform enables small, frequent deploys (automation removes the friction), which naturally drives up frequency AND drives down failures.

Measure Q3 of 10
How does the platform reduce Lead Time for Changes?
A) The platform doesn't affect lead time
B) By adding more manual approval gates
C) By slowing down deployments for safety
D) Automated CI (build+test+scan triggered on merge), automated CD (ArgoCD syncs on commit), parallelized tests (run tests concurrently), automated security gates (Kyverno policy check in pipeline), and small batch sizes (frequent small merges are faster than rare large ones).
✅ D — Automated CI, automated CD, parallel tests, automated gates, small batches

Lead time optimization through platform: (1) Automated CI triggers on every merge — no manual build step. (2) Parallel test execution (unit + integration + security run concurrently). (3) Automated security gates (Kyverno validates manifests, Trivy scans images — no manual security review). (4) GitOps deployment (ArgoCD auto-syncs — no manual deploy step). (5) Small batch sizes (encourage frequent small PRs instead of weekly mega-merges). Every manual step removed from the pipeline reduces lead time.

Measure Q4 of 10
How does the platform reduce MTTR?
A) MTTR is unaffected by platform
B) AIOps correlation (identifies root cause in seconds, not 15 min of dashboard clicking). Automated rollback (ArgoCD one-click revert). Runbook automation (pre-scripted recovery). Backstage incident view (all context in one page). Platform eliminates the slowest parts of incident response: diagnosis and manual recovery.
C) By adding more alerts
D) By hiding incidents from developers
✅ B — AIOps correlation + automated rollback + runbook automation + unified view

MTTR reduction through platform: (1) AIOps correlates: latency spike + DB errors + recent deploy → "Root cause: v2.4.1 DB pool exhaustion" in 10 seconds (vs 15 min human correlation). (2) ArgoCD rollback: one click (or API call) reverts to previous Git commit. (3) Runbook automation: pre-scripted recovery for known failures (restart, scale, clear cache). (4) Backstage: incident timeline, affected services, on-call, logs, and rollback button — all on one page. Result: MTTR drops from 45-90 min to 5-15 min.

Measure Q5 of 10
What's the difference between MTTR and Change Failure Rate?
A) They measure the same thing
B) MTTR is about deployment; CFR is about monitoring
C) MTTR measures RECOVERY SPEED (how fast you fix when things break — incident→resolution). CFR measures FAILURE FREQUENCY (what % of deploys cause a failure). Low CFR + Low MTTR = Elite (few failures, fast recovery). High CFR + High MTTR = Low (many failures, slow recovery). They measure different dimensions of stability.
D) CFR is a subset of MTTR
✅ C — MTTR = recovery speed. CFR = failure frequency. Different dimensions.

MTTR (Mean Time to Recover): measures how quickly you RESTORE service after an incident. Target: as low as possible. Platform impact: automated rollback, AIOps diagnosis, runbook automation. CFR (Change Failure Rate): measures how OFTEN your deploys cause problems. Target: as low as possible. Platform impact: automated testing, policy validation, canary deployments, small batch sizes. A team could have low MTTR (fast recovery) but high CFR (many failures) — they're fast at fixing but deploy buggy code. Or low CFR but high MTTR — they deploy clean code but take forever to fix when something does break.

Measure Q6 of 10
How do you automatically calculate DORA metrics from platform data?
A) Deploy Freq: count ArgoCD sync events. Lead Time: CI pipeline start timestamp → ArgoCD sync timestamp. MTTR: PagerDuty incident creation → resolution timestamps. CFR: (ArgoCD rollback events + PagerDuty deploy-triggered incidents) / total deploys. Pull data from APIs, build a Grafana dashboard.
B) Manually survey developers each week
C) DORA metrics cannot be automated
D) Use a spreadsheet updated monthly
✅ A — APIs: ArgoCD (deploys, rollbacks), CI system (timestamps), PagerDuty (incidents)

Automated DORA calculation: (1) Deploy Frequency = count of ArgoCD Application sync events per day/week (query ArgoCD API or Prometheus metrics). (2) Lead Time = for each deploy, CI pipeline start time → ArgoCD sync completion time (CI metadata + ArgoCD API). (3) MTTR = PagerDuty incident created_at → resolved_at (PagerDuty REST API). (4) CFR = (deploys that triggered a rollback OR incident) / total deploys. Cross-reference ArgoCD rollback events with PagerDuty incidents (deploy-triggered). Build a Grafana dashboard that auto-refreshes daily.

Measure Q7 of 10
What is the DORA continuous improvement cycle?
A) Deploy → Test → Fix → Deploy
B) Plan → Build → Run → Monitor
C) Sprint → Review → Retro → Plan
D) Measure (collect DORA metrics) → Analyze (find root cause of regression) → Improve (fix the platform bottleneck) → Repeat. When MTTR regresses, investigate why, fix it, and watch the metric recover. This is the same reconciliation loop applied to platform performance.
✅ D — Measure → Analyze → Improve → Repeat. Platform reconciliation loop.

The DORA improvement cycle mirrors the K8s reconciliation loop: (1) Measure: observe current state (MTTR 45 min). (2) Analyze: diff from desired state (why is MTTR up? outdated runbooks). (3) Improve: act to reconcile (automate runbooks, add rollback button). (4) Repeat: measure again (MTTR 12 min — reconciled!). This cycle runs continuously. Every sprint, review DORA trends. Investigate regressions. Plan improvements. The platform, like a K8s controller, should never stop improving.

Measure Q8 of 10
How do DORA metrics justify the platform investment to leadership?
A) DORA metrics are too technical for leadership
B) Show the BEFORE/AFTER transformation: "Before platform: Low performer (deploy 1x/month, lead time 2 weeks, MTTR 8 hours, CFR 40%). After platform: ELITE (deploy 5x/day, lead time 45 min, MTTR 15 min, CFR 3%). The platform moved us from the bottom tier to the TOP tier — and ELITE performers are 2x more likely to meet business goals." DORA metrics make platform value VISIBLE and BENCHMARKABLE.
C) Hide the metrics and just talk about features
D) Only show infrastructure cost savings
✅ B — Before/After: Low → ELITE. DORA tiers make improvement benchmarkable.

DORA metrics are the most leadership-friendly technical metrics because they have industry benchmarks. "We went from Low to Elite" tells a story anyone can understand. "ELITE performers are 2x more likely to meet or exceed business goals" (DORA research) ties platform investment to business outcomes. Compare: "We reduced MTTR from 8 hours to 15 minutes" (clear, benchmarkable) vs "We optimized our Kubernetes reconciliation loop efficiency" (nobody knows what that means). DORA metrics translate platform work into business language.

Measure Q9 of 10
anihpj's change failure rate is 3%. Is this good?
A) No — any failures are unacceptable
B) It's average
C) YES — 3% is ELITE (Elite: 0-15%). It means 97% of deploys succeed without issues. Combined with 5x/day deploy frequency, this means ~1 failure every 6-7 days, and with 15 min MTTR, each failure is quickly fixed. This is world-class delivery performance.
D) DORA doesn't define CFR benchmarks
✅ C — 3% is ELITE (0-15%). World-class. 97% success rate with 5x/day deploys.

CFR interpretation: Elite = 0-15%, High = 16-30%, Medium = 31-45%, Low = 46-60%. anihpj at 3% is well within Elite territory. Context matters: 3% CFR with 5 deploys/day means about 1 failure per week (5 × 20 working days × 0.03 = 3 failures/month). With MTTR of 15 minutes, each failure is quickly resolved. The GOAL is not 0% (that would mean you're not deploying enough, or you're over-testing). The goal is LOW failures + FAST recovery — which anihpj achieves.

Measure Q10 of 10
How should the platform team respond when a DORA metric regresses?
A) DON'T PANIC. Investigate: Is the regression real or a measurement error? What changed recently (new tool, process change, team growth)? Find the root cause. Make ONE improvement. Measure again. Regressions are feedback — they tell you where the platform needs attention. A team that never regresses is a team that stopped measuring.
B) Immediately revert all recent platform changes
C) Ignore it — metrics fluctuate naturally
D) Set more aggressive metric targets
✅ A — Investigate root cause. Single improvement. Measure again. Don't panic.

Metric regression response: (1) Verify the data — is the regression real or an instrumentation error? (2) Correlate with changes — what changed in the platform/process/team recently? (3) Root cause analysis — WHY did MTTR increase? (4) Make ONE targeted improvement — don't overhaul everything. (5) Measure — did the metric recover? (6) Document — what caused the regression and how was it fixed? Regressions are normal and expected. They're signals that drive improvement. A platform team that never sees regressions has either achieved perfection (impossible) or stopped measuring honestly.

  • Proctoring: Live remote proctor via webcam + screen share
  • Allowed: NOTHING — closed book! No external docs, no notes
  • Not Allowed: Phone, second monitor, headphones, papers, food
  • Allowed: Water in clear glass. Bathroom break (clock keeps running!)
  • System Check: Must complete 24 hours before exam

A.2 CNPA Exam Domain Weights

DomainWeightChaptersFocus Areas
1. Core Fundamentals36%Ch 1-6K8s architecture, Platform as Product, API design, Container runtimes, Service mesh, Platform architecture
2. Observability & Security20%Ch 7-11Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo, Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper, Falco, Network Policies, RBAC
3. Continuous Delivery16%Ch 12-16GitOps, ArgoCD, Helm, Kustomize, Progressive Delivery, CI/CD pipeline design
4. Platform APIs12%Ch 17-20Reconciliation loop, CRDs, Crossplane, Cluster API, Operator Pattern, OLM
5. IDPs & DevEx8%Ch 21-24Internal Developer Platforms, Backstage, Service Catalogs, AI/ML in platforms
6. Measuring Platform8%Ch 25-26Platform efficiency, SPACE framework, DORA metrics, Cost management
💡 Study Strategy by Weight

Domain 1 (36%) is worth more than Domains 4+5+6 combined (28%). Prioritize Core Fundamentals heavily — it's the foundation AND the biggest score contributor. But don't skip the smaller domains: you need to pass ALL domains, not just the big ones. A strong Domain 1 score can compensate for weaker areas, but can't save you if you fail a domain entirely.

A.3 Tips, Tricks & Time Management

1
First Pass: Quick Wins (30 min)

Read every question. Answer what you KNOW immediately. Flag uncertain questions (flag icon). Skip long scenario questions — they'll eat your time. Goal: answer 30-35 questions confidently in 30 minutes.

2
Second Pass: Flagged Questions (60 min)

Return to flagged questions. Read carefully. Eliminate obviously wrong answers FIRST (usually 2 of 4 are clearly wrong). Now you're choosing between 2 — much higher odds. For scenario questions: identify the CNPA pattern being tested (reconciliation? GitOps? platform as product?).

3
Third Pass: Review All (30 min)

Review ALL answers — even ones you were confident about. Look for misread questions ("Which is NOT..." vs "Which IS..."). Check for answer patterns (too many C's in a row?). Don't change answers unless you're SURE — first instinct is usually right.

⚠️ Common CNPA Exam Traps
  • K8s admin vs Platform engineering: Questions test platform concepts, not kubectl commands. "How would you design X?" not "What's the kubectl command for Y?"
  • "Platform as a Product": This mindset permeates the exam. Always choose answers that treat the platform as a product serving developers — not as infrastructure or ops.
  • CNCF tools vs proprietary: The CNPA favors CNCF/OSS tools (ArgoCD, Backstage, Crossplane, Kyverno) over proprietary alternatives.
  • Not ALL of the above: Be wary of "All of the above" — it's often a distractor. CNPA questions usually have ONE best answer that demonstrates platform engineering thinking.

A.4 Practice Lab Recommendations

🖥️
Hands-On Labs
  • KodeKloud CNPA Course: Structured labs covering all 6 domains. Hands-on K8s + platform tools.
  • Killer.sh CNPA Simulator: Realistic exam environment when available.
  • Build Your Own IDP: Install Backstage + ArgoCD + Crossplane + Kyverno on a local K8s cluster. Build Golden Path templates. This hands-on experience is THE best preparation.
📚
Supplementary Resources
  • PlatformEngineering.org: Community, articles, conference talks
  • CNCF Landscape: Understand the tool ecosystem
  • K8s Official Docs: CRDs, Operators, Reconciliation loop
  • Backstage Docs: Catalog, Scaffolder, TechDocs
  • DORA Research: Accelerate State of DevOps reports
📖 The anihpj Approach — Learn by Building

The best CNPA preparation is building a platform. Use the anihpj example throughout this guide as a template: deploy a Django app (jobpost) on K8s → add GitOps (ArgoCD) → add monitoring (Prometheus/Grafana) → add policies (Kyverno) → add a portal (Backstage) → add self-service infrastructure (Crossplane) → measure everything (DORA). Each chapter of this guide maps to a step in this journey. Build it. Break it. Fix it. The exam tests real platform engineering judgment — and that comes from building real platforms.

A.5 Exam Day Checklist

✅ 24 Hours Before
  • Run system check on exam portal
  • Test webcam, microphone, internet (wired preferred)
  • Prepare quiet, well-lit room
  • Clear desk completely — nothing on it
  • No papers, no notes, no books in reach
  • Close all unnecessary applications
  • Disable notifications, VPN, screen savers
✅ Exam Time
  • Join 15-30 minutes early
  • Government ID ready (passport, driver's license)
  • Proctor will ask to scan room with webcam
  • Show desk and under desk
  • Water in clear glass ONLY (no labels)
  • Read each question CAREFULLY — watch for "NOT" qualifiers
  • Use the flag system — don't get stuck
  • Trust your preparation — you've got this! 🏆

📖 Appendix D: CNPA Terminology Glossary

TermDefinitionChapter
IDPInternal Developer Platform — a self-service layer (Portal + API + Automation + Catalog) enabling developers to deploy and manage services without deep platform knowledge.Ch 21
Golden PathAn opinionated, supported, well-paved route from idea to production. Not mandatory but so smooth most developers choose it.Ch 21
GitOpsUsing Git as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications. An agent (ArgoCD/Flux) ensures the cluster state matches Git.Ch 12
Reconciliation LoopThe core K8s pattern: Observe (current state) → Diff (vs desired state) → Act (reconcile). Runs continuously, idempotently, forever.Ch 17
CRDCustom Resource Definition — extends the K8s API with new resource types. The foundation of Operators, Crossplane, and platform APIs.Ch 18
OperatorA CRD + Custom Controller that encodes human operational knowledge into software. Automates Day 0 (install), Day 1 (configure), and Day 2 (operate).Ch 20
OLMOperator Lifecycle Manager — manages Operator installation, upgrades (channels), dependency resolution, and RBAC. Like a package manager for Operators.Ch 20
CrossplaneA K8s-native infrastructure provisioning tool. Uses CRDs + Controllers to manage cloud resources. XRD + Composition + Claim = self-service infrastructure.Ch 19
XRDComposite Resource Definition (Crossplane) — defines the platform API schema developers see. Like a simplified CRD for cloud resources.Ch 19
CompositionCrossplane resource mapping your platform API (XRD) to actual cloud resources. One Composition, many cloud resources.Ch 19
KyvernoA K8s-native policy engine. Policies are K8s resources (not a separate language like Rego). Validate, Mutate, Generate, Verify Images.Ch 9
OPA/GatekeeperPolicy engine using Rego language. Gatekeeper integrates OPA into K8s as CRDs (ConstraintTemplate + Constraint). More expressive than Kyverno, steeper learning curve.Ch 10
BackstageSpotify's CNCF developer portal. React + Node.js + Plugins. Unifies Service Catalog, TechDocs, Scaffolder, and tool integrations.Ch 23
CatalogBackstage's central registry of all services, APIs, and resources. Defined by catalog-info.yaml files in Git repos. Auto-discovered via GitHub provider.Ch 22
ServiceMonitorA Prometheus Operator CRD that declaratively defines which services to scrape and how. Replaces manual Prometheus scrape configs.Ch 7
DORA Metrics4 key software delivery metrics: Deployment Frequency, Lead Time, MTTR, Change Failure Rate. Industry standard for measuring DevOps maturity.Ch 26
SPACE FrameworkA holistic developer productivity framework: Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication, Efficiency. Goes beyond lines of code.Ch 25
ToilManual, repetitive, automatable work that adds no enduring value. The platform's job is to eliminate toil through automation.Ch 25
Progressive DeliveryGradually rolling out changes: Canary → 5% traffic → 25% → 100%. Argo Rollouts + AnalysisTemplate. Reduces blast radius of bad deploys.Ch 15
CAPICluster API — uses K8s to manage K8s clusters. Define Cluster + Machine CRDs. "Clusters as cattle" — declarative cluster lifecycle management.Ch 19
GitOps AgentThe component (ArgoCD Application Controller) that pulls desired state from Git and pushes it to the cluster. Pull-based, not push-based CI/CD.Ch 12
HelmK8s package manager. Charts = templated K8s manifests. Values = configuration. Releases = installed instances. Repositories = chart storage.Ch 13
KustomizeK8s-native configuration customization. Base + Overlays. No templates — pure YAML patching. Built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k).Ch 14
Service MeshInfrastructure layer for service-to-service communication. Istio/Linkerd provide: mTLS, traffic splitting, observability, resilience patterns. Sidecar proxy (Envoy) per pod.Ch 5
Platform as a ProductTreating the platform like a product — with customers (developers), UX design (DevEx), metrics (adoption, satisfaction), and continuous improvement. The core CNPA philosophy.Ch 2

Week 4Security (Part 2 cont.)Ch 9-11: Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper, Falco, Security Best PracticesInstall Kyverno. Write policies (require labels, block latest tag). Create NetworkPolicies. Run Falco.10-12h
Week 5Continuous Delivery (Part 3)Ch 12-16: GitOps, ArgoCD, Helm, Kustomize, Progressive DeliveryInstall ArgoCD. Deploy anihpj via GitOps. Create Helm chart. Argo Rollouts canary deployment.10-12h

Weekly Routine

M-W
Read & Understand (6 hours)

Read chapters for the week. Take notes. Understand concepts, don't memorize. Focus on WHY, not just WHAT. Use the diagrams and tables in this guide as visual anchors.

Th-F
Hands-On Labs (4 hours)

Build what you read about. Deploy the tools. Configure them. Break them. Fix them. Hands-on experience is 10x more sticky than reading alone.

Sat
Practice MCQs (2 hours)

Answer the 10 practice questions at the end of each chapter. Review explanations. Identify weak areas. Re-read sections you got wrong.

Sun
Review & Rest

Review notes from the week. Skim chapter summaries. REST — burnout is real. The CNPA is a marathon, not a sprint.

💡 Study Tips That Actually Work
  • Explain it to someone else: The best test of understanding is explaining a concept to a colleague who doesn't know it. If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough.
  • Build a real project: Use the anihpj jobpost app as your testbed. Deploy it. Monitor it. Secure it. Build a platform around it. Real problems teach more than tutorials.
  • Focus on patterns, not details: The CNPA tests platform engineering JUDGMENT — which tool for which problem? What are the tradeoffs? Understanding the reconciliation loop pattern is more important than memorizing kubectl flags.
  • Use this guide actively: Don't just read — answer the MCQs, trace the diagrams, type the code blocks. Active recall > passive reading.
